## Performance Considerations
- Use bulk payloads to reduce network calls and enable atomic UI updates.
- Keep animations short and amplitudes modest to limit repaint costs.
- Preallocate LVGL objects in game loops and reuse them to avoid heap allocation.
- Debounce user interactions to minimize unnecessary service calls.
- Monitor loop time and memory usage via the console overlay.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and resolutions:
- Black screen after reboot: Ensure the required delay before display initialization and explicit LVGL resume steps are present in the boot sequence.
- Silent push failures: Verify service names and payload formats match between Home Assistant and firmware; mismatches cause silent drops.
- UI crashes during HA restarts: Confirm all LVGL updates are guarded by boot and API connection checks.
- Volume inconsistencies: Use the centralized volume apply script to sync UI and device state; debounce slider changes to avoid spamming the device.

Debugging tips:
- Open the system console overlay to check uptime, RSSI, core temperature, and HA connectivity.
- Log connectivity issues at boot and emit heartbeat events periodically.
- Use dismiss IDs consistently to ensure banners can be dismissed reliably.

## Conclusion
Tab5’s architecture emphasizes a push-only data flow, modular packaging, and a clear separation between declarative UI and executable logic. By leveraging bulk payloads, centralized helpers, and robust scripts, you can implement advanced configurations, custom components, and sophisticated automations while maintaining performance and reliability. Adhering to established patterns ensures scalability, security, and compatibility across versions.

## Introduction
This document explains how the Tab5 system is optimized for CPU efficiency and smooth user experience on an ESP32-P4 with LVGL. It covers:
- Push-only architecture benefits: zero polling overhead, event-driven processing, reduced network stack usage
- LVGL rendering optimizations: frame pacing, partial updates, efficient widget hierarchies
- Efficient data packing: delimited strings, binary-friendly parsing, compression considerations
- Interrupt handling, task scheduling, and background processing patterns
- CPU throttling strategies, power-aware processing, and performance monitoring via system metrics

## Project Structure
The system is organized into modular ESPHome packages that are composed by a single entry point. The key layers are:
- Hardware and peripherals (display, touch, audio, Wi-Fi co-processor)
- UI layout and pages (LVGL)
- API service handlers (push endpoints from Home Assistant)
- Central C++ logic (parsing, LVGL helpers, animations, state machines)
- Diagnostics and sensors (system metrics, SNTP, intervals)
- Scripts (reusable sequences, debounces, game lifecycle)
- IMU (adaptive polling for tilt input and tap-to-wake)

```mermaid
graph TB
HA["Home Assistant"] --> API["ESPHome API Services<br/>tab5_maj_*"]
API --> Logic["C++ Logic<br/>tab5_custom.cpp"]
Logic --> LVGL["LVGL UI<br/>tab5-lvgl.yaml"]
HW["Hardware Config<br/>tab5-hardware.yaml"] --> LVGL
Diag["Diagnostics<br/>tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml"] --> LVGL
Scripts["Scripts<br/>tab5-scripts.yaml"] --> LVGL
IMU["IMU<br/>tab5-imu.yaml"] --> Logic
Globals["Globals<br/>tab5-globals.yaml"] --> Logic
```

## Core Components
- Push-only API layer: Home Assistant calls ESPHome services to push payloads; device remains reactive with no polling.
- Central C++ parser and LVGL helpers: tokenizes bulk payloads, guards LVGL calls, animates icons, refreshes forecast widgets.
- LVGL page model: single-page dashboard with layered overlays and separate fullscreen game pages; styles centralized to reduce allocations.
- Adaptive IMU: dynamic update interval based on active game context; internal axes avoid saturating HA.
- Diagnostics and intervals: periodic updates for console metrics; SNTP drives clock/date without HA dependency.
- Scripts: debounce interactions, manage popups, orchestrate central rotator, and control game open/close lifecycle.

## Architecture Overview
The system uses a push-only data flow: Home Assistant detects changes and invokes ESPHome API services with compact payloads. The firmware parses them once and updates LVGL atomically. This eliminates polling loops, reduces TCP socket pressure, and keeps CPU idle when nothing changes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant API as "ESPHome API Service"
participant CPP as "C++ Parser<br/>tab5_custom.cpp"
participant LV as "LVGL UI<br/>tab5-lvgl.yaml"
HA->>API : "tab5_maj_previsions_jours_bulk(payload)"
API->>CPP : "parse_and_update_jours_bulk()"
CPP-->>LV : "refresh_daily_forecast() + icon roll-in"
Note over HA,CPP : "One network call replaces N per-field calls"
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Push-Only Data Flow and Network Efficiency
- Zero polling: Device never requests state; all updates are pushed from Home Assistant automations.
- Traffic pacing: Automations insert delays between service blocks and within loops to prevent TCP socket exhaustion alongside I2S audio streams.
- Payload contract: Delimited strings carry multi-value datasets; parsers use fixed-size buffers and strtok_r to avoid heap churn.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Push Received"]) --> Validate["Validate payload length"]
Validate --> |OK| Parse["Tokenize with strtok_r"]
Validate --> |Too long| Drop["Drop to avoid OOM"]
Parse --> Update["Update structs and LVGL widgets"]
Update --> End(["Done"])
Drop --> End
```

### LVGL Rendering Optimizations
- Single-page dashboard: All home automation features live on one 1280×720 page; games use dedicated fullscreen pages marked skip to avoid swipe navigation overhead.
- Partial updates: Only changed icons animate; temperature/humidity labels update without full redraws; crossfade transitions hide/show layers instead of recreating widgets.
- Style reuse: Global style definitions minimize PSRAM allocations; inline styles avoided across 80+ widgets.
- Gesture delegation: Swipe pagination delegated to C++ to keep YAML declarative and reduce runtime decisions in UI code.

### Efficient Data Packing and Parsing
- Delimited strings: Multi-value datasets serialized into semicolon-delimited strings; each item further split by pipe delimiters.
- In-place parsing: Fixed-size char buffers and strtok_r avoid std::string allocations in hot paths.
- Atomic updates: After parsing, LVGL updates occur in a single pass, preventing intermediate redraws.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
A["Receive payload"] --> B["Copy to fixed buffer"]
B --> C{"Length OK?"}
C --> |No| D["Log error and drop"]
C --> |Yes| E["strtok_r(';') loop"]
E --> F["strchr('|') split fields"]
F --> G["Write to DayForecastData/HourForecastData"]
G --> H["refresh_*_forecast() once"]
```

### Interrupt Handling and Background Processing
- Touch interrupt: Touchscreen uses an interrupt pin; polling stops after ISR attachment, reducing CPU wake-ups.
- Tap-to-wake: IMU acceleration Z triggers backlight on tap with debounce; internal axes avoid HA traffic.
- Interval-based tasks: Central rotator, diagnostics, and IMU adaptive polling run on intervals, not busy loops.

### Task Scheduling and Game Lifecycle
- lv_timer lifecycle: Games create timers on open and destroy on close; zero CPU cost when inactive.
- Pre-allocated LVGL pool: Sprites and labels created once, then recycled via show/hide and set_pos.
- Adaptive IMU polling: Switches between 10 Hz at rest and 30 Hz during tilt-controlled games.

### CPU Throttling and Power-Aware Processing
- Display update strategy: MIPI display configured with update_interval: never and auto_clear disabled; LVGL controls redraws explicitly.
- Backlight control: Light component pauses/resumes LVGL on off/on; tap-to-wake reactivates display efficiently.
- IMU adaptive rate: Lower poll rate when idle; higher rate only when tilt input is needed.
- Heartbeat and timeouts: OTA safe mode and reboot timeout guard against zombie states without constant polling.

- Console diagnostics: Uptime, RSSI, core temperature, free RAM, loop time updated periodically when console visible.
- SNTP-driven clock: Date/time updates independent of HA; avoids extra network calls.

## Performance Considerations
- Avoid polling: Rely on push events; do not add pull cycles unless absolutely necessary.
- Batch updates: Use bulk payloads and atomic LVGL refresh to minimize redraws.
- Reuse resources: Pre-allocate LVGL objects; recycle via visibility toggles rather than reallocating.
- Minimize allocations: Use fixed buffers and strtok_r; avoid std::string in hot paths.
- Throttle sensors: Publish only diagnostic IMU values at low rates; keep high-rate axes internal.
- Control display updates: Explicit redraws with update_interval: never; leverage LVGL’s dirty region optimization.
- Debounce inputs: Group rapid gestures into single HA calls to reduce network and CPU load.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- API connections exhausted: Caused by too many small service calls; prefer bulk payloads and paced pushes.
- Black screen after software restart: Ensure blocking delay before display reset pin activation; verify GPIO expander stabilization.
- Stale state: If an automation fails to fire, the device cannot self-catch up; ensure HA-side guards and continue_on_error.
- Audio glitches: Speaker ring buffer duration tuned to avoid gaps; microphone gain moved to analog stage to improve SNR.

**Section sources**
- [0003-data-packing-delimited-strings.md:13-18](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/decisions/0003-data-packing-delimited-strings.md#L13-L18)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-83](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L83)
- [architecture.md:191-220](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L191-L220)

## Conclusion
Tab5 achieves high CPU efficiency and smooth UI through a disciplined push-only architecture, compact data packing, and careful LVGL management. Adaptive IMU polling, interval-based tasks, and robust diagnostics provide responsive behavior while conserving power. Following these patterns ensures scalable performance on constrained embedded hardware.

## Introduction
This document explains how the Tab5 embedded system manages memory across PSRAM, internal SRAM, and flash (NVS). It focuses on:
- PSRAM utilization for LVGL rendering and large buffers
- String storage optimization to avoid heap fragmentation
- Dynamic allocation strategies and memory pooling patterns
- SRAM optimization via static vs dynamic allocation and efficient data structures
- Flash efficiency using NVS with delayed writes and minimal footprint
- Practical examples of memory-efficient string handling, array optimizations, and garbage collection avoidance
- Memory profiling via console diagnostics and leak prevention strategies

## Project Structure
The Tab5 firmware is organized around ESPHome YAML configuration files that declare UI, hardware, and runtime behavior, complemented by C++ modules implementing core logic, games, and memory-sensitive algorithms. Key areas relevant to memory management:
- Hardware and PSRAM configuration
- LVGL UI layout and pages
- Central custom logic for parsing, formatting, and diagnostics
- Game modules with NVS persistence and memory-conscious designs

## Core Components
- PSRAM configuration enables external RAM usage for SDIO buffers and audio task stacks, reducing internal SRAM pressure.
- LVGL UI is declared declaratively; heavy workloads are offloaded to C++.
- Central custom module handles bulk payload parsing with stack buffers and avoids std::string allocations in hot paths.
- Games implement NVS persistence with delayed writes and preallocated LVGL objects to prevent runtime allocations during gameplay.

Key memory-related behaviors:
- PSRAM used for SDIO buffers and microphone wake-word task stack
- Internal SRAM metrics exposed via console diagnostics
- NVS write throttling to minimize flash wear and CPU stalls
- Static arrays and module-level scratch buffers replace deep recursion and large local stacks

## Architecture Overview
The system separates concerns to optimize memory:
- YAML defines UI and hardware features without allocating runtime resources
- C++ centralizes parsing and rendering updates, using stack buffers and global caches
- Games encapsulate their own state and persistence, minimizing cross-module allocations

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HW as "ESP32-P4 + PSRAM"
participant LV as "LVGL (YAML)"
participant CORE as "tab5_custom.cpp"
participant GAME as "Game Modules"
participant NVS as "NVS (Flash)"
HW->>LV : Initialize display and PSRAM
LV->>CORE : Request UI updates (bulk payloads)
CORE->>CORE : Parse in-place with stack buffers
CORE-->>LV : Update labels/bars (no heap churn)
GAME->>GAME : Preallocate LVGL objects once
GAME->>NVS : Delayed persist_save() with min interval
CORE-->>HW : Report SRAM/PSRAM usage via console
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### PSRAM Utilization Patterns
- SDIO buffers moved to PSRAM to avoid internal SRAM exhaustion and crashes
- MicroWakeWord task stack placed in PSRAM to save ~3 KB of internal SRAM per task
- Online image decoding uses RGB565 format and resizing to reduce memory footprint

Practical implications:
- External RAM reduces contention on tight internal SRAM
- Lower risk of heap fragmentation in critical paths
- Image assets fit within constrained memory while maintaining acceptable quality

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:35-35](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L35-L35)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:290-293](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L290-L293)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:496-512](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L496-L512)

### LVGL Rendering in External RAM
- LVGL pages and widgets are declared in YAML; heavy logic stays in C++
- The system avoids creating or destroying LVGL objects at runtime in performance-critical paths
- Games preallocate all LVGL objects once and reuse them via show/hide/move operations

Optimization notes:
- Minimize dynamic LVGL object creation in loops
- Reuse containers and fonts defined at boot
- Keep UI updates lightweight; delegate complex calculations to C++

**Section sources**
- [tab5-lvgl.yaml:10-16](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml#L10-L16)
- [arkanoid_game.cpp:1-13](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/arkanoid_game.cpp#L1-L13)

### String Storage Optimization
- Bulk payloads parsed in-place using a fixed-size stack buffer and strtok_r to avoid heap copies
- UTF-8 normalization functions operate on small buffers and return compact results
- Avoid std::string in hot paths; prefer char arrays and tokenizers

Benefits:
- Prevents heap fragmentation from repeated allocations
- Reduces peak memory usage during parsing bursts
- Keeps latency predictable under load

**Section sources**
- [tab5_custom.cpp:338-353](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L338-L353)
- [tab5_custom.cpp:38-101](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L38-L101)

### Dynamic Allocation Strategies
- Prefer static arrays and module-level scratch buffers for algorithmic needs
- Use generation counters instead of memset to reset visited states efficiently
- Defer NVS writes to batch updates and reduce flash wear

Patterns observed:
- Module-level scratch arrays for graph traversal and board processing
- Generation-based marking to avoid costly resets
- Throttled NVS flushes with dirty flags and minimum intervals

**Section sources**
- [go_engine.cpp:27-43](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/go_engine.cpp#L27-L43)

- [go_game.cpp:324-396](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/go_game.cpp#L324-L396)

### SRAM Optimization Techniques
- Global and static arrays for frequently accessed data (e.g., weather slots, game boards)
- Stack buffers for temporary parsing and formatting
- Minimal use of dynamic containers in hot paths

Examples:
- Fixed-size arrays for day/hour forecast slots
- Local char buffers for tokenization and formatting
- Preallocated LVGL widget pools in games

**Section sources**
- [tab5_custom.cpp:27-32](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L27-L32)

### Flash Storage Efficiency Through NVS
- Persist settings and game state with a magic key and versioned structure
- Delay writes using a dirty flag and minimum interval to avoid frequent flash cycles
- Force saves only at meaningful boundaries (menu transitions, game end, close)

Flow of NVS persistence:
- Stash changes into RAM-backed save structure
- Mark dirty and schedule flush after a time window
- On flush, write entire structure and sync

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Change detected"]) --> Stash["Stash settings/position in RAM"]
Stash --> SetDirty{"g_dirty = true"}
SetDirty --> Wait["Wait until NVS_MIN_MS elapsed"]
Wait --> Flush{"Force or interval reached?"}
Flush --> |No| Wait
Flush --> |Yes| Save["persist_save()<br/>write struct + sync"]
Save --> ClearDirty["Clear g_dirty<br/>update last_nvs"]
ClearDirty --> End(["Idle"])
```

**Diagram sources**
- [go_game.cpp:324-396](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/go_game.cpp#L324-L396)

**Section sources**
- [go_game.cpp:324-396](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/go_game.cpp#L324-L396)

### Memory-Efficient Data Structures
- Board and position structures sized to maximum grid dimensions
- Bitmask or compact fields where possible (e.g., days mask, flags)
- Generation counters replace full resets for visited sets

Impact:
- Predictable memory usage regardless of input size
- Reduced CPU overhead for clearing or copying large buffers
- Better cache locality due to compact layouts

**Section sources**
- [go_engine.cpp:27-43](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/go_engine.cpp#L27-L43)

### Garbage Collection Avoidance Patterns
- No dynamic allocation in hot loops; reuse buffers and objects
- Avoid std::string in parsing; use char arrays and tokenizers
- Preallocate LVGL widgets once and toggle visibility

Guidelines:
- Keep hot paths free of new/delete and container growth
- Batch updates and defer expensive operations
- Use static/global caches for repeated computations

- Color-coded bars indicate thresholds for normal/warning/critical usage

Usage:

- Correlate UI interactions with memory changes

## Performance Considerations
- Use PSRAM for large buffers and task stacks to preserve internal SRAM
- Parse bulk payloads in-place with stack buffers to avoid heap churn
- Preallocate LVGL objects once; update visibility and positions instead of recreating
- Delay NVS writes to reduce flash wear and CPU stalls
- Monitor largest free block to detect fragmentation early

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and remedies:
- Black screen after software reboot: ensure proper delay before display reset pin toggles
- High SRAM usage: check for excessive std::string usage in parsing; switch to stack buffers
- Frequent NVS writes: verify dirty flag and minimum interval logic; force saves only at boundaries
- Audio glitches: adjust speaker buffer duration and ensure PSRAM usage for streaming buffers

Diagnostic steps:
- Open system console to inspect SRAM/PSRAM percentages and fragmentation
- Correlate UI actions with memory spikes
- Validate NVS flush timing and forced saves

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-79](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L79)
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1964-2010](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1964-L2010)
- [go_game.cpp:324-396](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/go_game.cpp#L324-L396)

## Conclusion
Tab5’s memory strategy centers on:
- Leveraging PSRAM for large buffers and task stacks
- Keeping internal SRAM lean with static arrays and stack buffers
- Deferring NVS writes to protect flash and reduce CPU overhead
- Preallocating LVGL objects and reusing them throughout runtime
- Monitoring memory via console diagnostics to catch fragmentation and leaks early

These practices collectively ensure stable, responsive performance on constrained embedded hardware while supporting rich UI and interactive games.

## Introduction
This document provides a comprehensive performance optimization guide for the Tab5 embedded system. It focuses on memory management (PSRAM utilization, SRAM optimization, flash efficiency), CPU optimization via push-only architecture and LVGL rendering strategies, efficient data packing, profiling with the console overlay’s SYSTEM card, and practical examples for memory allocation patterns, animation tuning, and battery life improvements. It also addresses common bottlenecks such as string handling, event-driven updates, and sensor polling patterns.

## Project Structure
The Tab5 firmware is organized into modular ESPHome packages that are composed at runtime:
- Hardware configuration and peripherals (display, touch, audio, Wi-Fi co-processor)
- UI layout and pages (LVGL)
- System diagnostics and sensors
- Central C++ logic layer for LVGL updates, parsing, and animations
- Decision records describing architectural choices (push-only, data packing)

## Core Components
- Push-only data flow: The device never polls; Home Assistant pushes state changes via ESPHome API services. This minimizes CPU and network usage when idle.
- Data packing: Multi-value datasets are serialized into single delimited strings to reduce network calls and socket contention.
- LVGL UI: Single-page dashboard with lightweight animations, preallocated game assets, and style reuse to minimize PSRAM allocations.
- Diagnostics console: A modal overlay showing SRAM/PSRAM usage, loop time, CPU temperature, Wi-Fi status, and HA connectivity.

Key implementation anchors:
- Push-only decision and traffic pacing
- Delimited-string payload strategy
- LVGL page structure and gesture handling
- Console overlay widgets and refresh intervals
- C++ parsing and LVGL update helpers

## Architecture Overview
The Tab5 uses a push-only architecture where Home Assistant detects state changes and pushes them to the device through ESPHome API services. The device parses payloads efficiently and updates LVGL widgets atomically.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram

participant LV as "LVGL UI"

CPP-->>ESP : "Parsed structs / flags"
ESP->>LV : "update_*_ui(...) (guarded)"
LV-->>HA : "UI reflects latest state"
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Memory Management: PSRAM Utilization Patterns
- PSRAM is enabled and configured at high speed to host large buffers and offload internal SRAM pressure.
- SDIO buffers for the Wi-Fi co-processor are placed in PSRAM to avoid crashes and free internal SRAM.
- Audio task stacks can be placed in PSRAM to save internal SRAM.
- Online images are decoded in RGB565 format and resized to fit target areas, reducing memory footprint during display.

Practical implications:
- Use PSRAM for large temporary buffers (e.g., image decoding, network payloads).
- Keep hot paths and small stack buffers in SRAM for speed and determinism.
- Prefer fixed-size char arrays over dynamic strings in tight loops to avoid heap churn.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:84-86](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L84-L86)

- [tab5_custom.cpp:7-8](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L7-L8)

### SRAM Optimization Techniques
- Avoid std::string in parsing loops; use char* and strtok_r to parse in-place.
- Preallocate global structures for UI slots and contexts to avoid repeated allocations.
- Reuse styles globally to minimize per-widget style allocations in PSRAM.
- Guard LVGL updates to prevent unnecessary redraws or invalid operations before boot completion.

Examples:
- Parsing weather and alert payloads using tokenizers with capped buffers.
- Global WeatherDaySlot/WeatherHourSlot arrays initialized once at boot.
- CentralPanelCtx consolidates references to multiple wrappers and flags.

- [tab5_custom.cpp:7-8](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L7-L8)

### Flash Storage Efficiency
- OTA settings include yield during erase to avoid CPU stalls and improve stability.
- Logging level set to INFO by default; DEBUG logs are compiled out unless explicitly enabled, saving flash space and runtime overhead.
- Avoid excessive logging in hot paths; rely on structured events and targeted diagnostics.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:17-21](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L17-L21)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-82](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L82)

### CPU Optimization: Push-Only Architecture Benefits
- Zero polling from the device means near-zero CPU/network usage when nothing changes.
- Traffic pacing on the HA side prevents TCP socket exhaustion alongside I2S streaming.
- Event-driven updates ensure the device only processes relevant changes.

Best practices:
- Ensure HA-side automations reliably push all state changes; add guard automations and continue_on_error where appropriate.
- Batch related updates into single service calls using delimited payloads.

**Section sources**
- [0001-push-only-zero-polling.md:5-17](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/decisions/0001-push-only-zero-polling.md#L5-L17)
- [architecture.md:191-220](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L191-L220)

### LVGL Rendering Optimizations for Smooth Animations
- Lightweight animations with reduced durations and amplitudes to minimize repaint cost.
- Crossfade transitions instead of heavy transforms for full-screen layers.
- Icon roll-in effects with staggered delays to create smooth visual feedback without excessive redraws.
- Preallocated LVGL pools for games; objects are recycled via show/hide and position updates.

Animation constants and helpers:
- UIAnim namespace centralizes durations and offsets for consistent, optimized motion.
- Helper functions encapsulate animation callbacks and lifecycle management.

**Section sources**

### Efficient Data Packing Methods
- Multi-valued datasets are serialized into semicolon-delimited strings and parsed in a single pass.
- Atomic LVGL updates after parsing avoid intermediate redraws and reduce UI jitter.
- Payload sizes are bounded to prevent buffer overflows and OOM conditions.

Parsing and update flow:
- Services receive payloads and invoke C++ parsers.
- Parsers tokenize and update structs; UI helpers then apply changes to LVGL widgets.

### Profiling Techniques Using the Console Overlay’s SYSTEM Card
- The SYSTEM card displays uptime, CPU temperature, and loop time.
- An interval updates diagnostic metrics when the console is visible, minimizing overhead when hidden.
- Network info (SSID, IP, RSSI) and HA connection status are shown for operational visibility.

Usage tips:
- Open the console via the dedicated button to view real-time diagnostics.
- Monitor loop time spikes to identify heavy operations or blocking code.
- Track CPU temperature under load to assess thermal throttling risks.

### Memory Allocation Patterns: Examples
- Fixed-size char buffers for parsing and formatting (e.g., snprintf into small buffers).
- Global arrays for forecast slots and UI contexts to avoid repeated allocations.
- PSRAM-backed stacks for audio tasks to preserve internal SRAM.

Where to look:
- Parsing utilities and UTF-8 normalization routines use local char buffers.
- Global slot arrays are declared and initialized at boot.
- Audio task stack placement is configured in hardware YAML.

- Reduce animation duration and offset to lower repaint cost.

- Stagger icon roll-ins to create fluid transitions without overwhelming the renderer.

- Forecast icon roll-in uses delayed entry to sequence visuals.

### Battery Life Optimization Strategies
- Push-only architecture eliminates polling, reducing Wi-Fi radio wake-ups.
- Adaptive IMU polling reduces frequency when not needed (games open vs. rest).
- Minimize logging verbosity in production builds to reduce CPU and serial overhead.
- Use PSRAM for non-critical buffers to keep SRAM available for fast operations.

**Section sources**
- [0001-push-only-zero-polling.md:13-17](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/decisions/0001-push-only-zero-polling.md#L13-L17)
- [architecture.md:224-235](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L224-L235)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-82](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L82)

### Common Bottlenecks and Solutions
- String handling: Replace std::string concatenation in hot paths with fixed buffers and tokenizers.
- Event-driven updates: Ensure HA pushes complete datasets via bulk services; avoid per-field calls.
- Sensor polling: Use adaptive rates and conditional updates (e.g., only when console is visible).

Mitigations:
- Tokenize payloads in-place with strtok_r and bounded buffers.
- Centralize LVGL updates behind guarded helpers to prevent redundant work.
- Gate diagnostic updates behind visibility checks to avoid unnecessary UI calls.

## Performance Considerations
- Prefer PSRAM for large, non-hot buffers; keep critical paths in SRAM.
- Use push-only updates and batched payloads to minimize network and CPU usage.
- Optimize LVGL animations with shorter durations and minimal repaint regions.
- Profile with the SYSTEM card to detect loop time spikes and adjust accordingly.
- Avoid dynamic allocations in tight loops; use fixed buffers and preallocated structures.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- If the screen remains black after software restarts, ensure proper reset timing for the display via GPIO expander and avoid relying solely on logger verbosity.
- Monitor loop time and CPU temperature via the SYSTEM card; high values indicate heavy processing or thermal throttling.
- Check Wi-Fi signal and HA connectivity in the console overlay; intermittent connections can cause stale UI if pushes fail.
- Validate payload formats between HA and device; mismatches can lead to silent failures due to lack of schema validation.

## Conclusion
The Tab5 achieves high performance through a combination of push-only architecture, efficient data packing, careful memory management leveraging PSRAM and SRAM, and optimized LVGL rendering. The diagnostics console enables continuous monitoring of loop times, CPU temperature, and resource usage. By following the outlined strategies—fixed buffers, preallocated structures, lightweight animations, and event-driven updates—you can maintain smooth interactions and extend battery life while avoiding common bottlenecks.

## Introduction
This document provides comprehensive profiling and diagnostics guidance for the Tab5 system, focusing on the SYSTEM card’s diagnostic capabilities: loop time monitoring, CPU temperature tracking, memory profiling via built-in counters, and resource usage visualization. It also covers performance bottleneck identification through systematic testing and measurement, interpreting diagnostic output, establishing baselines, identifying optimization opportunities, integrating debugging tools, logging strategies, and remote diagnostics for production deployments.

## Project Structure
The Tab5 diagnostics are implemented across ESPHome YAML components that expose sensors and UI updates, a C++ helper layer that reads platform metrics and updates LVGL widgets, and Home Assistant health automations that alert on anomalies. The SYSTEM console is a modal overlay with four glass cards: Memory (SRAM/PSRAM, largest free block, flash), Network (SSID/IP/signal + HA connection status), System (uptime, CPU temperature, loop time, volume), and Management (screen refresh, automation reload, restart HA, reboot device).

## Core Components
- Diagnostic sensors and intervals:
  - Uptime sensor updated every 60s; updates console label when visible.
  - WiFi RSSI sensor updated every 60s; updates console label when visible.
  - Internal core temperature sensor updated every 60s; updates console label when visible.
  - Debug free heap and loop time sensors exposed as entities for consumption.
  - Interval-based update every 2s refreshes memory bars, fragmentation, flash info, loop time, IP/SSID, and HA connection status.
- Console UI:
  - Glass cards render SRAM/PSRAM usage, largest free block, flash usage, network details, system metrics, and management actions.
- C++ metric aggregation:
  - Reads SRAM/PSRAM free/total and largest free block using platform APIs; formats values and colors; updates LVGL labels and progress bars.
- Home Assistant health automations:
  - Alerts if push gating boolean stays off, unexpected reboots detected via uptime drop, or ESPHome API disconnected for extended periods.

## Detailed Component Analysis

### SYSTEM Card: Loop Time Monitoring
- Exposed via debug loop_time sensor; refreshed by the 2s interval and displayed in the SYSTEM card.
- Interpretation:
  - Consistently high loop times indicate heavy processing or blocking operations in the main loop.
  - Spikes correlate with UI redraws, large payload parsing, or network activity.
- Baseline:
  - Record typical loop time under idle and active states (e.g., weather updates, games).
  - Track trends over days to detect gradual degradation.

### Memory Profiling: Built-in Counters and Custom Metrics
- Free heap and PSRAM metrics:
  - debug.free exposes free heap; interval updates memory bars and labels.
  - C++ reads SRAM/PSRAM free/total and largest free block; formats and renders.
- Fragmentation insight:
  - Largest free block indicates fragmentation; low values suggest memory pressure.
- Flash usage:
  - Displayed alongside memory metrics to understand storage footprint.
- Baseline:
  - Record free SRAM/PSRAM at boot and under load; track fragmentation trends.
  - Identify allocations causing spikes or leaks.

### Interpreting Diagnostic Output
- Loop time:
  - High sustained values point to bottlenecks; spikes during UI updates or network ops are expected.
- Temperature:
  - Elevated temps under load are normal; persistent highs warrant investigation into workload or cooling.
- Memory:
  - Declining free SRAM/PSRAM or shrinking largest free block suggests fragmentation or leaks.
- Network:
  - Low RSSI or frequent disconnects can cause delays; HA connection status helps isolate upstream issues.
- Uptime:
  - Drops indicate reboots; correlate with power events or firmware crashes.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml:135-198](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml#L135-L198)
- [tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml:266-310](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml#L266-L310)
- [console_sys.yaml:59-187](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/console_sys.yaml#L59-L187)

### Setting Up Performance Baselines
- Capture metrics under known conditions:
  - Idle: record loop time, temperature, free memory, RSSI.
  - Load: run games, voice assistant, OTA; record peaks and averages.
- Establish thresholds:
  - Define acceptable ranges for loop time and temperature.
  - Alert on memory drops below baseline or fragmentation increases.
- Monitor trends:
  - Use Home Assistant history graphs to track changes over time.

**Section sources**
- [tab5_health.yaml:43-176](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/HomeAssistant_Config/packages/tab5_health.yaml#L43-L176)
- [tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml:135-198](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml#L135-L198)

### Identifying Optimization Opportunities
- Reduce loop time:
  - Offload heavy tasks to background or chunk processing.
  - Minimize LVGL updates in tight loops.
- Improve memory efficiency:
  - Avoid large temporary buffers; reuse char arrays.
  - Monitor largest free block to detect fragmentation early.
- Network optimizations:
  - Batch payloads; reduce frequency of updates.
  - Handle reconnects gracefully to avoid repeated retries.

## Performance Considerations
- Logging level impacts boot and runtime overhead; INFO is balanced for production.
- Wi-Fi co-processor initialization requires careful timing to avoid black screens after reboots.
- API reboot timeout prevents zombie devices but must be tuned to avoid unnecessary reboots during HA outages.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Live logs:
  - Use ESPHome logs for boot sequence, API connections, and ESP_LOG lines.
  - Close sessions promptly to avoid exhausting API connections.
- On-screen console:
  - Access via the SYSTEM console button; view memory, network, system, and management cards.
  - Not a log viewer; use ESPHome logs for event payloads.
- Home Assistant logs:
  - Check automation triggers, template errors, and service call rejections.

The Tab5 system provides robust diagnostics through ESPHome sensors, a C++ helper, and a user-friendly SYSTEM console. By monitoring loop time, CPU temperature, memory usage, and network status, operators can establish baselines, identify bottlenecks, and optimize performance. Home Assistant health automations add a safety net for production deployments. Integrating logging strategies and remote diagnostics ensures reliable operation and quick issue resolution.

## Introduction
This document explains rendering performance for the Tab5 LVGL-based interface with a focus on animation optimization, efficient redraws, color and graphics tuning, modal popups, swipe navigation, real-time data visualization, touch responsiveness, gesture recognition, and battery impact. It synthesizes the LVGL layout, style definitions, global state, and C++ helpers that drive animations, gestures, and UI updates.

## Project Structure
The dashboard is a single LVGL page (page_main) with layered components: home area, central rotating card, bottom region (weather or switches), and multiple overlays (popups). Styles are centralized to minimize allocations. Global variables coordinate state across YAML and C++. The C++ layer provides all LVGL updates via helper functions, ensuring safe, efficient, and consistent rendering.

```mermaid
graph TB
A["LVGL Page<br/>page_main"] --> B["Central Card Rotator"]
A --> C["Bottom Region<br/>Weather / Switches"]
A --> D["Overlays<br/>Popups & Console"]
E["Styles (tab5-styles.yaml)"] --> A
F["Globals (tab5-globals.yaml)"] --> A
G["C++ Helpers (tab5_custom.*)"] --> A
G --> B
G --> C
G --> D
```

## Core Components
- LVGL page and layers: page_main defines widgets, gesture handling, and includes for forecast daily/hourly, switches, console, and popups. Swipe gestures delegate to C++ for pagination and crossfade transitions.
- Style system: Centralized styles reduce per-widget allocations; glassmorphism uses gradients and borders rather than heavy effects.
- Globals: Shared state such as active_page, forecast_page_index, show_switches, and panel visibility flags coordinate UI behavior between YAML and C++.
- C++ helpers: All LVGL updates go through typed helpers (e.g., refresh_daily_forecast, animate_swipe_horizontal, animate_crossfade_layers, animate_popup_open/close), which encapsulate animations, state checks, and redraw logic.

Key performance implications:
- Single-page layout avoids full screen reloads; layers are toggled via hidden flags and opacity animations.
- Bulk parsing and atomic UI updates prevent intermediate redraws.
- Short, tuned animation durations reduce frame counts and perceived latency.

## Architecture Overview
Data arrives from Home Assistant as compact payloads, parsed in C++, then applied to LVGL in one pass. Animations are short and purposeful: swipe transitions use horizontal slide + crossfade; popups fade in/out; alert banners slide-in; weather icons roll with staggered timing.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant API as "ESPHome API"
participant CPP as "C++ Helpers"
participant LV as "LVGL Engine"
HA->>API : "tab5_maj_* services (bulk payloads)"
API->>CPP : "parse_and_update_* (in-place tokenization)"
CPP->>LV : "refresh_*_forecast() / update_*_ui()"
Note over CPP,LV : "Atomic updates, no intermediate redraws"
HA->>API : "Gesture triggers (YAML on_gesture)"
API->>CPP : "handle_swipe_gesture()"
CPP->>LV : "animate_swipe_horizontal() / animate_crossfade_layers()"
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Animation Optimization Techniques
- Frame rate control: LVGL runs from ESPHome loop; animations use short durations (e.g., swipe 200ms, popup open 150ms, close 110ms) to limit frames and improve responsiveness.
- Motion smoothing: Easing curves (ease_in/ease_out) and small offsets create fluid motion without heavy repaints.
- Efficient state transitions: Crossfade layers avoid sliding when content overlaps; swipe animations cancel previous animations to prevent conflicts.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["User Gesture"]) --> Detect["Detect direction & region"]
Detect --> Decide{"Forecast window?"}
Decide --> |Yes| Swipe["animate_swipe_horizontal(out,in,dir)"]
Decide --> |No| Crossfade["animate_crossfade_layers(out,in)"]
Swipe --> Update["Update page index & title"]
Crossfade --> Update
Update --> End(["Render complete"])
```

### UI Component Rendering Strategies
- Lazy loading: Popups and overlays are hidden by default and shown only on interaction; inactive layers remain hidden to avoid unnecessary drawing.
- Virtual scrolling: Not used; instead, fixed slots (5-day/5-hour windows) are reused and updated in place.
- Efficient redraw regions: Layer toggling via LV_OBJ_FLAG_HIDDEN and opacity changes minimizes redraw scope; icon roll-in targets only changed icons.

Examples:
- Forecast pages reuse g_day_slots/g_hour_slots arrays; refresh functions update labels and icons conditionally.
- Central panel rotator hides non-active panels and animates only the active one.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-lvgl.yaml:631-674](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml#L631-L674)

- [tab5_custom.cpp:738-764](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L738-L764)

### Color and Graphics Optimization
- Palette usage: Centralized UIColor constants mirror YAML tokens; semantic colors ensure consistency and avoid hardcoding.
- Image compression: Custom fonts (IconeMeteo.ttf, MDI subsets) include only needed glyphs; chess pieces subset reduces font size.
- Font rendering efficiency: Small glyph sets and targeted sizes reduce memory and draw cost; Roboto Mono used for aligned Markdown tables in assistant responses.

Practical notes:
- Weather icons use two-layer composition with precise offsets; rolling animation only triggers when icon condition changes.
- Glassmorphism achieved via gradients and border opacities rather than expensive backdrop effects.

- [tab5-styles.yaml:129-298](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-styles.yaml#L129-L298)

### Modal Popup Performance
- Open/close animations: Fade-in (150ms) and fade-out (110ms) with scrim; closing hides both card and scrim automatically.
- Guard against re-entry: Close-if-open prevents flicker by checking visibility and ongoing animations.
- Foreground management: Popups moved to foreground to ensure correct z-order without extra redraws.

```mermaid
User->>YAML : "Tap overlay or ×"
YAML->>CPP : "animate_popup_close(card, scrim)"
```

### Swipe Navigation Optimization
- Gesture routing: on_gesture delegates to handle_swipe_gesture based on y-region; ensures swipe only affects forecast layers.
- Transition strategy: Horizontal slide + crossfade; cancels prior animations to avoid visual artifacts.
- Title overlay: Non-default forecast pages show a page-title wrapper; rotation pauses while overlay is visible.

```mermaid
flowchart TD

Route --> UpdateLayers["animate_swipe_horizontal / update page index"]
UpdateLayers --> RefreshTitle["update_central_forecast_page_ui()"]
```

### Real-Time Data Visualization Techniques
- Bulk payload parsing: In-place tokenization avoids heap fragmentation; O(n) parse on string length.
- Atomic UI updates: After parsing, LVGL updates occur once per batch, preventing intermediate redraws.
- Conditional icon roll: Rolling animation only when icon condition changes, reducing unnecessary repaints.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
PStart["Receive bulk payload"] --> Parse["strtok_r split (hours/days)"]
Parse --> Validate{"Length OK?"}
Validate --> |No| Drop["Drop payload (OOM guard)"]
Validate --> |Yes| Apply["Apply to structs (cal_heures_data/cal_jours_data)"]
Apply --> Render["refresh_*_forecast()"]
Render --> Animate{"Icon changed?"}
Animate --> |Yes| Roll["animate_icon_roll_in(staggered)"]
Animate --> |No| Skip["Skip roll"]
Roll --> PRestore["Restore central rotator if applicable"]
Skip --> PRestore
```

- Short animations: Reduced duration and amplitude cut frame counts, lowering CPU and display power.
- Minimal redraws: Hidden layers and conditional updates avoid unnecessary repainting.
- Adaptive IMU polling: Tilt-controlled games increase polling rate only when active; rest uses lower frequency.

## Performance Considerations
- Prefer bulk payloads and atomic updates to minimize network and render overhead.
- Use centralized styles to reduce allocations and keep draw calls efficient.
- Keep animations short and meaningful; cancel conflicting animations promptly.
- Reuse widget slots and update only changed elements (e.g., icon roll only on change).
- Avoid heavy effects; simulate glassmorphism with gradients and borders.
- Gate LVGL updates behind boot_complete and API connected checks to prevent crashes during restarts.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and mitigations:
- NaN values during HA restarts: Ensure boot_complete and api.connected() before LVGL calls.
- Conflicting animations: Cancel prior animations before starting new ones (e.g., lv_anim_delete before animate_swipe_horizontal).
- Stale layer positions: Reset X and opacity when switching layers to avoid leftover states.
- Payload size limits: Reject oversized payloads to prevent OOM conditions.

## Conclusion
The Tab5 LVGL interface achieves responsive rendering through a single-page architecture, centralized styles, and robust C++ helpers that manage animations, gestures, and data updates efficiently. By using bulk payloads, atomic UI updates, short animations, and careful redraw strategies, the system maintains smooth interactions while conserving battery. Modal popups, swipe navigation, and real-time visualizations are optimized for low latency and minimal resource usage.

## Introduction
This document explains the alarm clock system implemented for the Tab5 device, focusing on:
- The scheduling engine that computes the next ring time from fixed times, calendar work shifts, and safety bounds.
- The notification system that plays alarms locally (RTTTL or optional media URL), shows a full-screen ring overlay, and supports snooze and auto-stop.
- The integration with Home Assistant for appointment reminders and spoken briefings.
- Timezone handling via SNTP and local day calculations.
- Edge cases such as DST transitions, missed rings after reboot, voice assistant interruptions, and I2S bus conflicts between microphone and speaker.

The design ensures the alarm can ring without Home Assistant being available; HA only enhances comfort with TTS briefings and appointment reminders.

## Project Structure
The alarm system spans firmware logic, UI components, and Home Assistant configuration:
- Firmware core: alarm scheduling, labels, melodies, and LVGL rendering helpers live in C++.
- ESPHome orchestration: entities, scripts, intervals, and state management are defined in YAML.
- UI components: LVGL screens for settings and ring overlay.
- Home Assistant: pushes upcoming appointments and provides spoken briefing services.

## Core Components
- Scheduling engine (C++): Computes next ring time using fixed time, workday calendar data, and constraints like earliest/latest bounds and minimum rest after previous day’s closing. It caches results to keep the 1-second tick cheap.
- Ring controller (YAML): Orchestrates starting/stopping the ring, managing cycles, crescendo volume, snooze, max ring duration, and overlay visibility.
- UI layers: Settings popup for configuring alarms; full-screen overlay for active ringing with large stop/snooze targets.
- Appointment reminders: HA pushes upcoming events; firmware stores them and triggers announcements at configured lead time.
- Voice assistant coordination: Ensures I2S bus is free before playing alarm sounds and temporarily enables wake word “Stop” during ringing.

Key responsibilities by file:
- alarm_clock.h/.cpp: Pure logic for next-ring calculation, snooze, dismissal, labels, melodies, and LVGL render helpers.
- tab5-alarm.yaml: Entities, scripts, intervals, and runtime control flow bridging UI and firmware logic.
- alarm_popup.yaml: LVGL layout for alarm settings; delegates actions to scripts.
- alarm_ring_overlay.yaml: Full-screen ring overlay layout and interactions.
- tab5_reveil.yaml: HA scripts to push appointments and speak morning briefing.

## Architecture Overview
The system separates concerns cleanly:
- Firmware owns all scheduling and timing decisions.
- YAML defines the user-facing controls and runtime behavior.
- LVGL renders UI but does not implement business logic.
- HA enriches experience with appointment lists and spoken briefings.

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Scheduling Engine
Responsibilities:
- Compute next ring time across up to 8 days considering:
  - Fixed-time mode with weekly mask.
  - Workday-only mode using calendar shift data.
  - Opening-mode derived time based on shift start minus lead, clamped to earliest/latest, plus minimum rest after previous day’s closing.
- Handle timezone correctly by building local tm via helper and mktime.
- Cache next ring to avoid scanning every second; invalidate on config changes, calendar updates, or ring/snooze/dismiss.
- Provide labels for UI and diagnostic sensors.

Algorithm highlights:
- Next ring search uses a floor to prevent re-triggering already-passed times and a grace window on first boot to avoid missing early rings after OTA/restart.
- Snooze sets a future trigger time and increments a counter; dismiss advances the skip floor to prevent same-day re-ringing.
- Calendar readiness fallback ensures alarms still ring on fixed time if calendar data is unavailable.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["alarm_next_ring(now)"]) --> CheckCache{"Dirty or >1min?"}
CheckCache --> |No| ReturnCached["Return cached next_ts"]
CheckCache --> |Yes| Reset["Reset cache vars"]
Reset --> Enabled{"Enabled?"}
Enabled --> |No| ReturnZero["Return 0"]
Enabled --> |Yes| Floor["Compute floor = max(last_tick, skip_before)"]
Floor --> LoopDays["For offset 0..8"]
LoopDays --> DayCalc["ring_minute_for_day(offset)"]
DayCalc --> Valid{"Valid minute?"}
Valid --> |No| NextDay["Next day"]
Valid --> |Yes| Epoch["epoch_at(offset, minute)"]
Epoch --> AfterFloor{"ts > floor?"}
AfterFloor --> |No| NextDay
AfterFloor --> |Yes| SetNext["Set next_ts, offset, minute"]
SetNext --> ReturnNext["Return ts"]
NextDay --> LoopDays
ReturnZero --> End(["Exit"])
ReturnCached --> End
ReturnNext --> End
```

### Notification System and Ring Overlay
Responsibilities:
- Start ring sequence when alarm is due.
- Manage cycles with crescendo volume and optional custom media URL from HA.
- Show/hide full-screen overlay with large stop/snooze buttons.
- Coordinate with voice assistant to allow “Stop” command while ensuring I2S bus availability.
- Enforce maximum ring duration and clean up resources.

Key behaviors:
- On start: mark ringing, interrupt vocal activity, ensure backlight on, close games, show overlay, enable wake word “Stop”, then run ring loop.
- Ring loop: set gain per cycle, refresh UI, play either RTTTL or media URL, manage microphone/speaker bus, listen for “Stop” in silence windows, enforce max duration.
- Stop/Snooze: stop audio, clear flags, optionally dismiss scheduled ring, hide overlay, restore volume, restart/stop wake word appropriately.

### Alarm Popup Interface
Responsibilities:
- Present alarm configuration: enable/disable, fixed time, weekly mask, mode selection, calendar bounds, snooze duration, max ring duration, volume, crescendo, TTS, and appointment reminder settings.
- Delegate all interactions to ESPHome scripts; no logic in UI layer.
- Keep visual state synchronized through a central sync script that calls C++ render helpers.

User flows:
- Adjust time with hour/minute increment/decrement buttons.
- Toggle days of week chips; preset selector updates underlying mask.
- Choose mode (fixed, workdays, opening-derived).
- Configure lead time, earliest/latest bounds, and minimum rest hours.
- Preview melody and adjust volume; toggle crescendo.
- Enable spoken briefing and appointment announcements; configure lead time for reminders.

### Calendar Integration and Appointment Reminders
Responsibilities:
- HA periodically pushes upcoming appointments (up to 8) with epoch timestamps and titles.
- Firmware stores and deduplicates entries, marking announced ones to avoid repeats.
- At configured lead time before an appointment, firmware displays a banner and optionally speaks a reminder.

Data contract:
- Payload format: “epoch|title~epoch|title…” with cleaned separators.
- Matching by epoch ensures stability across repeated pushes.

### Timezone Handling
- Local day calculations use a dedicated helper to convert offsets to local tm structures, avoiding pitfalls of simple arithmetic across DST boundaries.
- Epochs for specific wall-clock minutes are built by constructing a full tm and calling mktime, ensuring correct DST-aware conversion.
- SNTP provides current time; the system relies on local time for user-facing schedules.

**Section sources**
- [alarm_clock.cpp:46-59](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.cpp#L46-L59)
- [alarm_clock.h:23-26](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.h#L23-L26)

### Configuration and Entity Mapping
Core configuration lives in C++ struct mirrored from ESPHome entities:
- enabled, days_mask, fixed_min, mode, lead_min, earliest_min, latest_min, rest_hours, rest_mode, snooze_min, max_ring_min.
- All entity changes call a refresh script that updates the struct and invalidates the next-ring cache.

Melodies and preferences:
- Built-in RTTTL melodies with approximate durations used to size ring cycles.
- Optional custom media URL played via media player; falls back silently to local melody if HA is unreachable.
- Crescendo support increases volume gradually across cycles.

**Section sources**
- [alarm_clock.h:31-73](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.h#L31-L73)
- [alarm_clock.h:149-166](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.h#L149-L166)
- [tab5-alarm.yaml:55-330](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-alarm.yaml#L55-L330)
- [alarm_clock.cpp:358-405](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.cpp#L358-L405)

### Edge Cases and Coordination
- Missed rings after reboot: Grace window allows catching a ring shortly after startup; otherwise, skipped times are honored to avoid immediate re-ringing.
- DST transitions: Handled by building tm and using mktime; recalculation occurs at least once per minute as a safety net.
- Voice assistant interruptions: During ringing, wake word “Stop” is enabled; I2S bus is managed by stopping microphone capture before playing sound and restarting it afterward.
- Max ring duration: Prevents indefinite ringing if user is absent; cleans up and publishes events.
- Snooze vs dismiss: Snooze schedules a future ring; dismiss advances the skip floor so the same day’s alarm won’t repeat.

## Performance Considerations
- The 1-second interval performs a single integer comparison against a cached next ring timestamp; recalculations occur only on config/calendar changes or at least once per minute.
- Scanning up to 8 days is bounded and infrequent; caching avoids heavy computation on hot path.
- Volume crescendo uses simple arithmetic per cycle; melody durations are approximate but sufficient for pacing.
- I2S bus coordination prevents silent alarms and ensures reliable playback by explicitly stopping microphone capture before speaker use and vice versa.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and resolutions:
- Alarm does not ring:
  - Verify SNTP time is valid and calendar data has been pushed.
  - Ensure alarm is enabled and at least one day or workday matches within the search window.
  - Check that the next ring is not in the past due to skip floor; dismiss or wait for next day.
- Missed ring after reboot:
  - Grace window covers short delays; if missed, the system will schedule the next occurrence.
- No sound during ringing:
  - Confirm I2S bus is free; microphone capture may block speaker. The system stops mic before playing and waits for release.
  - If using custom media URL, ensure HA is reachable; otherwise, local RTTTL melody will play.
- Voice assistant interference:
  - Wake word “Stop” is enabled during ringing; ensure microWakeWord is running and not blocked by ongoing TTS or media playback.
- Excessive ringing:
  - Max ring duration prevents indefinite loops; verify configuration and that dismiss/snooze clears state properly.

## Conclusion
The alarm clock system delivers robust, offline-capable scheduling with rich integrations for calendar-based work shifts and appointment reminders. Its design emphasizes reliability (caching, grace windows, DST-safe time math), usability (clear UI, snooze, crescendo), and resilience (voice assistant coordination, I2S bus management). Home Assistant enhances the experience without becoming a dependency for core alarm functionality.

## Appendices

### API and Data Contracts Summary
- Next ring computation:
  - Inputs: enabled flag, days mask, fixed time, mode, lead time, earliest/latest bounds, rest hours, rest mode.
  - Outputs: next ring timestamp and labels for UI.
- Appointment reminders:
  - Input payload: “epoch|title~epoch|title…”.
  - Behavior: store, deduplicate by epoch, announce at lead time, mark announced.
- Ring lifecycle:
  - Start on due, cycle with crescendo, allow snooze/dismiss, enforce max duration, cleanup resources.

## Introduction
This document explains the alarm notification and ring system for the device, covering:
- Full-screen ring overlay with large time display, alarm title, and snooze controls
- RTTTL melody system with built-in sounds, volume ramping (crescendo), and automatic ring duration limits
- Notification pipeline including speech announcements for upcoming appointments, coordination with voice assistant interruptions, and status icon behavior in the header bar
- Snooze functionality with configurable intervals and dismissal that prevents same-day recurrence
- Customization examples and integration with Home Assistant for custom sound URLs
- Troubleshooting common audio issues related to microphone/speaker bus contention

## Project Structure
The alarm system spans firmware logic, LVGL UI components, and Home Assistant configuration:
- Firmware engine: pure C++ alarm scheduler, melodies, and rendez-vous announcer
- LVGL overlays: full-screen ring overlay and settings popup
- ESPHome orchestration: entities, scripts, rtttl player, media player path, and state synchronization
- Home Assistant: calendar data push and optional custom sound URL

## Core Components
- Alarm scheduler and state machine: computes next ring time, handles snooze/dismiss, and enforces grace periods and skip floors to avoid immediate re-ringing or missed rings after restarts
- Ring overlay UI: full-screen layer with large clock, title, subtitle, stop and snooze buttons, and a scrim tap-to-stop
- Settings popup: mode selection (fixed, workdays, opening-time based), day mask, lead/bounds, rest hours, snooze interval, max ring duration, volume/crescendo, TTS and RDV announcement toggles
- Melody system: built-in RTTTL melodies with approximate durations; crescendo gain per cycle
- Announcement pipeline: stores upcoming appointments from HA, announces on screen and via TTS at configured lead times, coordinated with voice assistant interruptions
- Status icon: header bar alarm icon reflects enabled state and whether a future ring is actually scheduled

## Architecture Overview
The system is designed to ring without Home Assistant. Time comes from SNTP, work schedules are cached locally, and melodies are synthesized on-device. HA augments the experience with appointment lists and optional custom sound URLs.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Tick as "1s tick"
participant Sched as "alarm_due()"
participant UI as "Overlay + Popup"
participant ESP as "ESPHome scripts"
participant Audio as "rtttl / media_player"
participant VA as "Voice Assistant"
Tick->>Sched : check now
alt due
Sched-->>ESP : trigger ring start
ESP->>VA : interrupt vocal if needed
ESP->>UI : show overlay (time, title, snooze)
loop until stop/snooze/max
ESP->>Audio : play melody or HA URL with crescendo
Audio-->>ESP : finished
ESP->>UI : refresh snooze label
opt user says "Stop"
VA-->>ESP : wake word detected
ESP->>Audio : stop
ESP->>UI : hide overlay
end
end
else not due
Sched-->>Tick : wait
end
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Full-Screen Ring Overlay
- Purpose: Immediate, glanceable alarm interface with minimal interaction
- Elements:
  - Scrim background that stops the alarm when tapped
  - Large current time display
  - Title (“Réveil” or “Répétition N”)
  - Subtitle showing context (e.g., work schedule details)
  - Two large action buttons: Stop and Snooze
  - Bottom hint text guiding voice or touch stop
- Behavior:
  - Always brought to foreground and hidden only by explicit stop, snooze, or max ring duration
  - Not auto-closed by inactivity timers

**Section sources**
- [alarm_ring_overlay.yaml:1-95](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/alarm_ring_overlay.yaml#L1-L95)
- [alarm_clock.cpp:670-708](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.cpp#L670-L708)

### Alarm Scheduler and Next Ring Calculation
- Computes next ring across up to 8 days using:
  - Fixed time mode with day mask
  - Workday mode (calendar-driven)
  - Opening-time mode derived from calendar shift start minus lead, clamped to earliest/latest bounds and respecting minimum rest after previous day’s close
- Cache strategy:
  - Recomputes only on changes or once per minute for safety against DST/SNTP resync
  - Uses a skip floor to prevent immediate re-trigger after dismissal or during grace window post-restart
- Snooze and dismiss:
  - Snooze sets a future time and increments repetition count
  - Dismiss clears snooze and advances skip floor so the same day does not ring again

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start([Next ring computation]) --> CheckEnabled{"Enabled?"}
CheckEnabled --> |No| None["No ring scheduled"]
CheckEnabled --> |Yes| ComputeFloor["Compute floor = max(skip_before, last_tick or grace)"]
ComputeFloor --> LoopDays["For next 8 days"]
LoopDays --> DayMode{"Mode"}
DayMode --> |Fixed| UseFixed["Use fixed_min if day selected"]
DayMode --> |Workdays| UseCal["Use fixed_min on workdays"]
DayMode --> |Opening| Derive["Start - lead, clamp to bounds, apply rest_hours"]
UseFixed --> Candidate["Candidate timestamp"]
UseCal --> Candidate
Derive --> Candidate
Candidate --> Valid{"ts > floor?"}
Valid --> |Yes| ReturnNext["Return ts"]
Valid --> |No| NextDay["Next day"]
NextDay --> LoopDays
LoopDays --> |Done| None
```

### RTTTL Melodies and Crescendo Volume Ramping
- Built-in melodies defined as RTTTL strings with approximate durations used to size loops
- Volume ramping:
  - Base volume set by user entity
  - If crescendo enabled, each cycle increases effective gain from a floor (35%) toward full base over several cycles
  - Applied both to local rtttl playback and to media_player when playing a custom URL
- Safety:
  - Max ring duration prevents indefinite ringing if no interaction occurs

### Appointment Announcements and Voice Assistant Coordination
- Upcoming appointments are pushed from HA into a local list with epoch timestamps and titles
- At each tick, the system checks if any appointment is within the configured lead time and not yet announced
- On due:
  - Updates a screen banner with time and title
  - Produces a TTS announcement formatted for natural speech
- During active ringing, announcements are suppressed to avoid audio overlap and interference with wake-word listening for “Stop”
- Voice assistant interruption:
  - Before starting the ring, the system interrupts any ongoing voice response to free the I2S bus
  - While ringing, the system periodically stops the microphone to allow the speaker to play without contention, then restores it for wake-word detection between cycles

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant FW as "Firmware"
participant TTS as "TTS"
participant VA as "Voice Assistant"
participant SPK as "Speaker"
HA->>FW : push appointments (epoch|title~...)
loop every second
FW->>FW : rdv_due(now, lead_min)
alt due
FW->>SPK : announce (screen + TTS)
Note over FW,SPK : If alarm_ringing == true, skip to avoid overlap
end
end
FW->>VA : interrupt if speaking before ring
FW->>SPK : play ring (rtttl or HA URL)
loop between cycles
FW->>VA : stop mic capture temporarily
FW->>SPK : play next cycle
FW->>VA : resume mic capture
end
```

### Status Icon in Device Header Bar
- Displays an alarm icon whose color indicates:
  - Off: inactive color
  - Armed but no future ring: warning color (e.g., weekend-only or no workdays)
  - Armed with a future ring: success color
- Updated whenever settings sync or at ring start/end

### Snooze Functionality and Dismissal
- Snooze:
  - Configurable interval (1–30 minutes)
  - Sets a future time; each snooze increments repetition count
  - Overlay shows “Repeat · X min” updated per cycle
- Dismiss:
  - Clears snooze and advances skip floor so the same day will not ring again
  - Turning off the alarm also dismisses any active ring and cancels snooze

### Calendar Integration and Opening-Time Mode
- HA pushes daily codes and work hours for up to 31 days, including holidays, school vacations, and events
- The firmware uses this to:
  - Determine work vs rest days
  - Derive opening-time-based alarms: start time minus lead, bounded by earliest/latest and minimum rest after previous day’s close
- Labels in the settings popup reflect today’s work hours or “rest”

## Dependency Analysis

- tab5-alarm.yaml orchestrates entities, scripts, rtttl, and media_player; it calls into alarm_clock.cpp functions for scheduling, labels, and gain

## Performance Considerations
- One-second tick performs a single integer comparison; next ring is cached and recomputed only on changes or once per minute
- Grace window after restart avoids swallowing near-future alarms while preventing stale catch-up
- I2S bus mutex requires careful sequencing: microphone must be stopped before speaker plays and resumed afterward to avoid silent rings or stuck states
- Media player buffer and network pacing help prevent audio gaps during TTS/ring playback

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common audio issues and resolutions:
- Silent ring when wake word is active:
  - Cause: Microphone holds the I2S bus; speaker cannot acquire it
  - Resolution: Ensure the ring loop stops microphone capture before playing and waits for release; verify the relay sequence in the ring loop
- Speaker stuck in starting state after a ring:
  - Cause: Playback did not fully complete or was interrupted
  - Resolution: Wait for rtttl/media_player to finish; ensure timeouts are sufficient; re-run cleanup to restore volume and state
- No announcement during ring:
  - Cause: Announcements are suppressed while ringing to avoid overlap and wake-word interference
  - Resolution: This is expected; announcements occur outside ringing windows or when ringing is disabled
- Custom sound URL not playing:
  - Cause: Home Assistant unavailable or URL empty
  - Resolution: Verify HA connectivity and that the URL entity is set; fallback to local RTTTL automatically

## Conclusion
The alarm system combines a robust, offline-capable scheduler with a user-friendly full-screen ring overlay, flexible melody options, and intelligent announcements. It coordinates carefully with the voice assistant to ensure reliable audio output and responsive control. Configuration through the LVGL popup and Home Assistant enables customization of modes, schedules, snooze intervals, and sound sources, while safeguards like skip floors, grace windows, and max ring duration keep behavior predictable and safe.

## Introduction
This document explains the alarm scheduling engine core that powers wake-up and appointment announcements on the device. It covers:
- Three alarm modes (FIXE, TRAVAIL, EMBAUCHE) and their calculation algorithms
- Next-ring computation with calendar integration, timezone handling via local_day_from_offset(), and daylight saving transitions
- The alarm state machine including snooze, dismissal, and a grace period to prevent missed alarms after restarts
- Performance optimizations such as cached next-ring calculations, one-second tick processing, and skip floor persistence across reboots
- Examples of configuration scenarios, edge cases, and how alarm modes relate to Home Assistant calendar data

## Project Structure
The alarm system is split between:
- A pure C++ scheduling engine (no network calls) for date/time math, mode logic, and state management
- An ESPHome YAML layer that exposes configuration entities, scripts, and UI wiring to LVGL
- Home Assistant packages that push calendar and appointment data into the device

## Core Components
- AlarmCfg: mirrors ESPHome entities into a single configuration struct used by the engine
- Mode constants: FIXE (fixed time), TRAVAIL (fixed time on workdays), EMBAUCHE (derived from opening hours)
- Next-ring computation: alarm_next_ring() with caching and floor-based skipping
- Due detection: alarm_due() called once per second by the tick loop
- Snooze and dismissal: alarm_snooze(), alarm_dismiss()
- Calendar readiness: alarm_calendar_ready() ensures safe fallback when calendar data is missing
- Appointment reminders: rdv_* functions manage upcoming appointments and announcements
- UI rendering helpers: alarm_render_settings(), alarm_ring_show/refresh/hide(), status icon updates

## Architecture Overview
The engine is designed to be fully autonomous: it uses SNTP time and locally cached schedule data to compute alarms without requiring Home Assistant at ring time. HA provides comfort features like spoken announcements and custom media URLs.

```mermaid
Engine-->>Tick : true if due
alt ringing
Tick->>UI : show overlay
UI->>HA : optional TTS/media URL
UI-->>Engine : snooze/dismiss events

end
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Alarm Modes and Calculation Algorithms
- FIXE: Rings at fixed_min on selected days (bitmask). Ignores calendar.
- TRAVAIL: Rings at fixed_min only on days marked as work in the calendar; ignores day bitmask for workdays.
- EMBAUCHE: Derives ring time from calendar opening start minus lead_min, clamped within earliest_min/latest_min. Also enforces minimum rest after previous day’s closing time when configured.

Key behaviors:
- If calendar data is not ready, calendar-driven modes fall back to fixed time to avoid missing work shifts.
- For non-work days, behavior depends on rest_mode: silence or fixed time using the day mask.
- EMBAUCHE respects previous day’s closing time to enforce rest_hours, bounded by earliest/latest limits.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["ring_minute_for_day(offset, day)"])
CheckCal{"Calendar ready?"}
WorkDay{"Work day?"}
Mode{"Mode"}
Fixe["Return fixed_min if day selected else -1"]
Rest{"Rest day"}
Silence["Return -1 (silence)"]
FixedOnRest["Return fixed_min"]
Travail["Return fixed_min"]
EmbaucheStart["Parse shift start"]
Lead["m = clamp(start - lead_min, earliest, latest)"]
PrevClose{"Previous day closed?"}
RestMin["Apply rest_hours floor"]
ReturnM["Return m"]
Start --> CheckCal
CheckCal --> |No| Fixe
CheckCal --> |Yes| WorkDay
WorkDay --> |No| Rest
Rest --> |Silence| Silence
Rest --> |Fixed| FixedOnRest
WorkDay --> |Yes| Mode
Mode --> |TRAVAIL| Travail
Mode --> |EMBAUCHE| EmbaucheStart
EmbaucheStart --> Lead
Lead --> PrevClose
PrevClose --> |Yes| RestMin
PrevClose --> |No| ReturnM
RestMin --> ReturnM
```

### Next-Ring Computation and Calendar Integration
- Scans up to 8 days ahead to cover all weekday combinations plus a full week of silent rest days.
- Uses local_day_from_offset() to correctly handle DST transitions when converting wall-clock minutes to epoch.
- Skips any candidate times at or before the “floor” (skip floor or last tick), preventing immediate re-rings and missed catches during restarts.
- Caches results for up to 60 seconds unless invalidated by configuration changes, calendar pushes, or ring/snooze/dismiss actions.

```mermaid

Loop["For offset 0..8"]

Minute["ring_minute_for_day(offset, day)"]
Epoch["epoch_at(offset, minute)"]
Skip{"ts > floor?"}
Save["Save next_ts, offset, minute"]
ReturnNext["Return next_ts"]

NStart --> Cache
Cache --> |Yes| ReturnNext
Cache --> |No| Invalidate
Invalidate --> Enabled
Enabled --> |No| NoNext
Enabled --> |Yes| Floor
Floor --> Loop
Loop --> Day
Day --> Minute
Minute --> Epoch
Epoch --> Skip
Skip --> |Yes| Save
Save --> ReturnNext
Skip --> |No| Loop
```

### Timezone Handling and DST Transitions
- All date conversions go through local_day_from_offset(), ensuring correct handling of summer/winter time switches.
- epoch_at() builds a full tm structure and uses mktime() to convert wall-clock minutes to epoch safely around DST boundaries.

**Section sources**
- [tab5_custom.h:42-48](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.h#L42-L48)
- [alarm_clock.cpp:46-59](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.cpp#L46-L59)

### Alarm State Machine: Snooze, Dismissal, Grace Period
- Snooze: Sets a future time until which no ring will occur; when reached, alarm_due() returns true exactly once.
- Dismissal: Clears snooze and advances the skip floor so the current day’s ring does not repeat immediately.
- Grace period: On first call after boot, a 120-second window allows catching a missed ring shortly after restart or OTA.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
[*] --> Idle
Idle --> Snoozed : "alarm_snooze(minutes)"
Snoozed --> Idle : "now >= snooze_until"
Idle --> Ringing : "alarm_due() && next == now"
Ringing --> Snoozed : "user presses snooze"
Ringing --> Idle : "dismiss / stop"
Idle --> Idle : "tick continues"
```

### Persistence Across Reboots: Skip Floor
- The skip floor is persisted in NVS and restored at boot to avoid ringing again within a short window after a stop or restart.
- The refresh script restores the floor from ESPHome globals if present, then writes back periodically.

**Section sources**

### Appointment Reminders
- Appointments are stored and announced based on a lead time. Each entry is tracked by epoch to avoid re-announcing after repeated pushes.
- rdv_due() checks for upcoming appointments within the lead window and formats screen and speech outputs.

- Ring overlay shows current time, title, subtitle, and snooze button; refreshes with snooze count and remaining time.

## Performance Considerations
- One-second tick: alarm_due() performs a single integer comparison path; heavy computation is avoided by caching.
- Cached next-ring: Results are reused for up to 60 seconds unless invalidated by configuration/calendar changes or ring/snooze/dismiss events.
- Skip floor: Prevents unnecessary re-evaluation and avoids re-ringing after stop/restart; persisted to NVS every minute.
- Minimal I/O: Scheduling logic is pure C++; network calls are limited to optional TTS/media URL playback.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- No ring on workday: Ensure calendar data is ready; otherwise calendar-driven modes fall back to fixed time. Verify cal_jours_data contains work/rest flags and hours_ouverture.
- Missed ring after reboot: Confirm grace period behavior and skip floor restoration; check that alarm_skip_floor is loaded from NVS and written back periodically.
- DST issues: Validate that local_day_from_offset() is used for all date conversions; avoid direct minuit+offset arithmetic.
- Snooze not triggering: Verify snooze_until is set and alarm_due() is called each second; ensure snooze is not cleared by accidental dismiss.
- Volume or sound issues: During ringing, microphone capture can block I2S bus; the ring loop stops mic capture before playing rtttl to avoid silence.

- [alarm_clock.cpp:155-247](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.cpp#L155-L247)

## Conclusion
The alarm scheduling engine delivers reliable, low-overhead wake-up and appointment notifications with robust timezone handling and graceful recovery after restarts. Its three modes provide flexibility for fixed schedules, workday-aware alerts, and dynamic pre-opening alarms tied to calendar data. Performance is optimized through caching, minimal tick work, and persistent skip floors, while UI and HA integrations enhance usability without compromising autonomy.

## Introduction
This document explains the alarm user interface components and their integration with the device’s alarm engine and Home Assistant entities. It covers:
- The alarm settings popup layout (enable/disable toggle, day chips, mode buttons, configuration sliders for lead time, earliest/latest times, rest period).
- The real-time preview system showing next alarm time and details.
- Melody selection with volume control and TTS notification preferences.

- The rendering system that updates UI elements based on alarm configuration.
- Responsive design patterns used across the alarm interface.
- Common workflows such as setting work-day alarms, configuring vacation modes, and adjusting notification preferences.

## Project Structure
The alarm UI is split into two LVGL screens and a central YAML/ESPHome layer that binds to a C++ engine:
- Settings popup: defines the modal card with all controls and labels.
- Ring overlay: full-screen overlay shown when an alarm rings.
- Alarm logic and state: defined in C++ and exposed via ESPHome entities and scripts.
- Globals and persistence: stored in globals for skip floor, days mask, and ring state.

```mermaid
graph TB
```
