## Detailed Component Analysis

### Ball Physics Engine
- Fixed timestep loop at approximately 30 Hz with three sub-steps per frame to reduce tunneling through thin bricks.
- Ball speed is normalized each step to maintain a constant magnitude equal to the current game speed setting.
- Wall bounces clamp position and reflect velocity components.
- Paddle collision checks downward-moving balls and reflects based on relative hit position to vary angle.
- Glue mechanic allows balls to stick to the paddle until tapped to launch.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Tick Step"]) --> Normalize["Normalize ball speed"]
Normalize --> Substeps{"For each sub-step"}
Substeps --> Move["Move ball by vx*SDT, vy*SDT"]
Move --> Walls{"Hit walls?"}
Walls --> |Yes| ReflectWalls["Clamp position and reflect velocity"]
Walls --> |No| PaddleCheck{"Downward and near paddle?"}
ReflectWalls --> PaddleCheck
PaddleCheck --> |Yes| PaddleReflect["Compute angle from hit offset<br/>Set new vx/vy"]
PaddleCheck --> |No| Bricks["Check brick collisions"]
PaddleReflect --> Bricks
Bricks --> Floor{"Below floor?"}
Floor --> |Yes| LoseBall["lose_ball()"]
Floor --> |No| NextStep["Next sub-step or next ball"]
LoseBall --> End(["End Step"])
NextStep --> End
```

### Paddle Controls
- Two modes supported: IMU tilt and touch buttons, or both simultaneously.
- IMU path applies deadzone, smoothing, sensitivity scaling, and clamps to max tilt; then integrates acceleration with friction to compute paddle velocity and position.
- Touch mode moves paddle directly at a fixed speed when left/right buttons are pressed.
- Paddle width can be modified by power-ups within min/max bounds.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Inp["Input Frame"] --> IMUPart{"IMU enabled?"}
IMUPart --> |Yes| Tilt["Read raw Y, subtract calibration<br/>Smooth, deadzone, scale, clamp"]
IMUPart --> |No| Buttons{"Buttons enabled?"}
Tilt --> Combine["Combine with button input"]
Buttons --> |Yes| Dir["Left/Right direction"]
Buttons --> |No| NoDir["No direct input"]
Combine --> Mode{"Mode?"}
Mode --> |IMU or Mixed| Accel["Accumulate accel + friction<br/>Integrate to position"]
Mode --> |Buttons Only| Direct["Move by speed * DT"]
Accel --> Clamp["Clamp to playfield bounds"]
Direct --> Clamp
Clamp --> Update["Update paddle LVGL object"]
```

**Diagram sources**
- [arkanoid_game.cpp:1121-1164](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/arkanoid_game.cpp#L1121-L1164)

- [arkanoid_game.cpp:1121-1164](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/arkanoid_game.cpp#L1121-L1164)

### Brick Destruction Mechanics
- Grid-based layout per level with constants for columns, rows, spacing, margins, and brick dimensions.
- Brick types: normal, tough (multi-hit), indestructible, bonus (drops power-up).
- Collision uses AABB vs circle: find closest point on rectangle to ball center, check distance against radius.
- Reflection chooses axis based on overlap to avoid corner artifacts.
- Scoring uses combo window to multiply points; bonus bricks drop power-ups; normal bricks have a chance to drop power-ups.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Hit["Ball hits brick area"] --> Closest["Closest point on rect to ball center"]
Closest --> Dist{"Distance < radius?"}
Dist --> |No| Miss["No hit"]
Dist --> |Yes| Overlap["Compute overlap X/Y"]
Overlap --> Axis{"X overlap < Y overlap?"}
Axis --> |Yes| ReflectX["Reflect VX, adjust X"]
Axis --> |No| ReflectY["Reflect VY, adjust Y"]
ReflectX --> Type{"Brick type?"}
ReflectY --> Type
Type --> |Normal/Tough| Damage["Decrease HP"]
Type --> |Indestructible| NoDmg["No damage"]
Damage --> Dead{"HP == 0?"}
Dead --> |Yes| Remove["Hide, decrement alive, score+combo, maybe spawn PU"]
Dead --> |No| Color["Update color for remaining HP"]
Remove --> End(["Done"])
Color --> End
NoDmg --> End
Miss --> End
```

### Power-Up System
- Power-ups spawn from bonus bricks or randomly from normal bricks with weighted probabilities.
- Types include expand/shrink paddle, slow/fast ball, multi-ball, glue, and extra life.
- Power-ups fall at a constant speed and are collected by the paddle via simple AABB checks.
- Effects are applied immediately and may change paddle size, ball speed, active ball count, or lives.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Brick as "Brick"

participant World as "PowerUp Pool"
participant Paddle as "Paddle"
participant Apply as "apply_powerup()"
Brick->>Spawn : On destroy (bonus or random)
Spawn->>World : Allocate slot, set type/color/position
World-->>Spawn : Active power-up
loop Each frame
World->>World : Fall down by speed*DT
World->>Paddle : AABB overlap?
alt Collected
Paddle->>Apply : apply_powerup(type)
Apply-->>World : Hide and deactivate
else Offscreen
World->>World : Deactivate
end
end
```

### Level Progression and Scoring
- Eight predefined levels with distinct patterns: solid wall, pyramid, columns, checkerboard, corridors with indestructible pillars, fortress with tough/bonus mix, zigzag, and boss row.
- Difficulty increases via higher base ball speed per level and tougher brick configurations.
- Scoring awards more points for tough bricks and benefits from combos within a time window.
- High scores are stored locally with level reached and control mode used.

### Touch and Tilt Controls
- IMU tilt is mapped to horizontal paddle movement with deadzone, smoothing, sensitivity scaling, and maximum tilt clamping.
- Touch buttons provide direct left/right movement.
- Control mode can be switched between tilt-only, buttons-only, or both, and is persisted.

**Section sources**
- [arkanoid_game.cpp:1121-1164](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/arkanoid_game.cpp#L1121-L1164)
- [tab5-imu.yaml:60-65](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L60-L65)

### Collision Detection Algorithms
- Ball-to-wall: clamp position and invert relevant velocity component.
- Ball-to-paddle: only when moving downward and overlapping vertically; angle computed from relative hit position to vary bounce direction.
- Ball-to-brick: AABB vs circle using closest-point distance and reflection along the axis of least penetration.

- Retro palette derived from NTSC colors for brick rows; distinct styles for tough and indestructible bricks.
- Death vignette: four red border strips flash briefly on losing a life.
- Power-ups use colored rectangles with borders to indicate type.
- HUD labels are updated only when values change to reduce redraw overhead.

## Performance Considerations
- Fixed timestep with sub-steps ensures stable physics without heavy CPU spikes.
- Object pooling: All LVGL objects (bricks, balls, power-ups, buttons) are created once and reused by moving/hiding them each frame.
- Minimal allocations in hot path: No dynamic memory allocation during gameplay; HUD text is cached and only rewritten when changed.
- Efficient collision loops: Early exits for inactive bricks; sub-stepping reduces missed collisions.
- NVS persistence only at key moments (start, pause, quit) to avoid frequent writes.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Game not starting: Ensure the LVGL page containers exist and are passed correctly via the script before opening the game.
- Paddle not responding to tilt: Verify IMU callback is wired and calibration is set; re-calibrate from settings if needed.
- Balls passing through bricks: Confirm sub-stepping is active and brick dimensions/margins match expectations; check for extreme speeds beyond configured caps.
- Power-ups not appearing: Check that bonus bricks are present in the level layout and that spawn slots are available.
- Scores not saving: Ensure NVS preference object is initialized and saved at appropriate times; verify permissions and storage availability.

## Conclusion
Arkanoid delivers a polished breakout experience optimized for embedded display hardware. Its design emphasizes deterministic physics, efficient rendering, and accessible controls via tilt and touch. The modular structure separates UI containers from gameplay logic, enabling easy maintenance and extension. With persistent scoring, configurable settings, and a variety of power-ups and levels, it offers engaging progression while maintaining performance and responsiveness.

## Introduction
Coureur d’Or is a faithful, self-contained implementation of the classic Lode Runner platformer for the Tab5 device. It features tile-based movement, ladder and rope mechanics, gold collection objectives, enemy AI with pathfinding, hole digging, and a progressive 10-level campaign. The game runs full-screen at 1280x720, uses LVGL for rendering, and persists progress locally via NVS without requiring Home Assistant during gameplay.

Key highlights:
- Grid-locked movement model identical to the original Lode Runner
- Touch controls (D-pad + dig buttons) and IMU tilt control modes
- BFS-based guard AI that chases the player and steals gold
- Hole creation and closure with traps and hazards
- Save system storing scores, unlocked levels, and settings

## Project Structure
The game is implemented as a standalone module integrated into the Tab5 HMI:
- UI containers are declared in YAML; all gameplay UI is built in C++
- Game logic, state machine, rendering, and persistence live in lode_game.cpp
- Public API and types are exposed in lode_game.h
- A documentation patch file summarizes usage and rules

```mermaid

CPP --> LVGL["LVGL runtime<br/>(rendering, timers, events)"]
CPP --> NVS["NVS storage<br/>(esphome::global_preferences)"]
CPP --> IMU["IMU input<br/>(on_imu callback)"]
```

## Core Components
- Tile grid and level maps: 30x16 grid with brick, solid, ladder, bar, exit, gold, player start, and guard start
- Actors: Player and up to 4 guards with states (idle, fall, dig, trap, out, gone)
- Holes: Temporary pits that close after a duration, trapping or killing entities
- Gold: Collectibles that open the exit when all are gathered
- HUD: Score, lives, level name, remaining gold, best score
- Menus: Hub, level select, settings, pause, scores, confirm
- Persistence: Local NVS save for scores, unlocked levels, control mode, sensitivity, speed, calibration, assist mode

## Architecture Overview
The game runs on an LVGL timer loop. Each tick updates holes, player movement, guard AI, collision detection, and rendering. Input comes from touch zones or IMU tilt. Menus are overlays on top of the game field.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Timer as "lv_timer"
participant Tick as "tick_cb()"
participant Player as "player_step()"
participant Guards as "guard_step()"
participant Render as "draw_actor()/update_hud()"
Timer->>Tick : every TICK_MS (playing) / IDLE_TICK_MS (menus)
Tick->>Tick : update_holes(now)
Tick->>Player : player_step(now)
Tick->>Tick : rebuild_dist() every 4 ticks
Tick->>Guards : guard_step(i, now)
Tick->>Render : draw actors + update HUD
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Tile-Based Movement System
- Movement is locked to the grid: each actor commits to a step of one tile and advances pixel-by-pixel until reaching the next cell
- Horizontal movement requires support under the current cell; vertical movement depends on ladders or bars
- Falling occurs when unsupported; falling speed differs from running speed
- Ladder and bar interactions:
  - Ladders allow climbing up/down and can be stood on
  - Bars allow hanging and dropping down at falling speed
- Exit activation: once all gold is collected, exit ladders become climbable to row 0 to clear the level

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Actor step"]) --> CheckMove{"Moving?"}
CheckMove --> |Yes| Advance["Advance sub by speed"]
Advance --> Reached{"Reached next cell?"}
Reached --> |No| End(["Wait next tick"])
Reached --> |Yes| EnterCell["Enter cell effects (gold, exit)"]
CheckMove --> |No| Gravity{"Supported?"}
Gravity --> |No| Fall["Set state FALL, move down if passable"]
Gravity --> |Yes| Idle["State IDLE"]
Idle --> DigWant{"Dig requested?"}
DigWant --> |Yes| TryDig["try_dig(d)"]
DigWant --> |No| ChooseDir["Choose direction (input)"]
ChooseDir --> End
```

### Ladder and Rope Mechanics
- Ladders:
  - Climb up if above cell is passable
  - Stand on ladders as platforms
  - Exit ladders activate only after all gold is collected
- Bars (ropes):
  - Hang below bars; can drop down at falling speed
  - Cannot dig while on a bar or ladder

### Gold Collection Objectives
- Gold tiles spawn visible objects; collecting gold removes the object and decrements remaining count
- When all gold is collected, exit ladders become active and a toast notifies the player
- Guards may steal gold temporarily and drop it later, forcing strategic retrieval

```mermaid
Exit-->>Player : Show exit ladders + toast
```

### Enemy AI Patterns
- Guards use inverse BFS from the player to compute distance fields, then choose moves that reduce distance
- Guards move slightly slower than the player (skip 1 tick every 5), maintaining consistent difficulty across speeds
- Guards can pick up gold and occasionally drop it; trapped guards cannot kill the player and can be walked over
- Respawn logic places guards near the top, avoiding immediate proximity to the player

```mermaid
classDiagram

+int8_t cx, cy
+int8_t mdx, mdy
+int16_t sub
+uint8_t st
+bool carry
+lv_obj_t* body, head
}
class GuardAI {
+rebuild_dist()
+guard_choose(Actor&)
+guard_step(Actor&, int, uint32_t)
+guard_respawn(Actor&)
}
Actor <.. GuardAI : "moves and decisions"
```

### Hole Digging Mechanics
- Digging is allowed only when standing on solid ground (not on ladders or bars)
- Target must be a brick tile directly below and diagonally adjacent; the space above must be passable
- Holes last a fixed duration, blink before closing, and trap or kill entities inside
- Trapped guards die when holes close; players die if inside when closing

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Try dig"]) --> ValidPos{"On solid ground?"}
ValidPos --> |No| Abort["Abort"]
ValidPos --> |Yes| CheckTarget{"Below is brick?"}
CheckTarget --> |No| Abort
CheckTarget --> |Yes| AboveClear{"Above target passable?"}
AboveClear --> |No| Abort
AboveClear --> |Yes| CreateHole["Create hole, set animation, add to list"]
CreateHole --> UpdateTiles["Hide tile object"]
UpdateTiles --> End(["Wait for closure"])
```

### Level Design Principles
- 10 handcrafted levels with increasing complexity
- Maps encoded as character grids with specific symbols for bricks, solids, ladders, bars, gold, exits, player start, and guard starts
- Levels are validated to ensure all gold is reachable and the exit remains accessible from any gold position after activation
- Maximum limits enforced for LVGL objects and gold to maintain performance

### Touch Controls and Interaction
- D-pad and two dig buttons rendered as semi-transparent touch zones
- Control modes:
  - Buttons: D-pad + dig buttons
  - Tilt: IMU-based 4-directional movement + dig buttons
  - Mixed: Tilt and D-pad combined, with touch taking priority
- Calibration adjusts tilt offsets; sensitivity adjusts dead zone and hysteresis
- Pause is triggered by tapping the HUD band

## Performance Considerations
- Preallocated LVGL object pools avoid allocations during gameplay
- Rendering cache prevents redundant updates to unchanged positions/colors
- Adaptive timer reduces CPU usage in menus (200ms vs 25ms during play)
- Guard AI distance field recalculated every 4 ticks to balance responsiveness and cost
- Solid tile runs merged into single LVGL objects to reduce draw calls

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and resolutions:
- Stuck controls: Ensure calibration is performed in flat orientation; adjust sensitivity if too sensitive
- Digging not working: Verify standing on solid ground (not ladder/bar) and target is brick with clear space above
- Guards not moving: Check that distance field rebuild is occurring; verify no invalid grid access
- Save corruption: Magic mismatch resets to defaults; reconfigure settings and replay

## Conclusion
Coureur d’Or delivers a polished, authentic Lode Runner experience optimized for the Tab5’s hardware constraints. Its grid-locked movement, robust AI, and careful resource management create a challenging yet fair puzzle-platformer. The modular design keeps the game self-contained while integrating seamlessly with the broader HMI ecosystem.

## Introduction
Dames Tab is a polished, embedded draughts (checkers) game for the Tab5 device. It implements international 10x10 draughts by default and supports English 8x8 checkers as an alternative variant. The game features:
- Full rule set including forced captures, multi-jump sequences, king promotion, and flying kings (international variant).
- An embedded AI engine with four difficulty levels, iterative deepening, alpha-beta pruning, and quiescence search at expert level.
- A responsive LVGL-based UI with clear piece visualization, move highlighting, undo/hint controls, and persistent settings and statistics.
- Time-sliced AI execution to keep the UI smooth on constrained hardware.

## Project Structure
The implementation is split across a header defining shared structures and constants, a large C++ file implementing rules, UI, persistence, and orchestration, an AI module with search logic, and a minimal YAML page layout that reserves containers for runtime construction.

```mermaid
graph TB
subgraph "UI Layer"
YML["draughts_game.yaml<br/>Page containers"]
CPP_UI["draughts_game.cpp<br/>LVGL UI, input, menus"]
end
subgraph "Game Engine"
H["draughts_game.h<br/>Engine types, Pos, Move"]
CPP_RULES["draughts_game.cpp<br/>Rules, board state, moves"]
end
subgraph "AI"
AI_H["draughts_ai.h<br/>Level, State, API"]
AI_CPP["draughts_ai.cpp<br/>Search, evaluation, time-slicing"]
end
YML --> CPP_UI
CPP_UI --> H
CPP_UI --> AI_H
CPP_RULES --> H
CPP_UI --> CPP_RULES
AI_CPP --> H
AI_CPP --> AI_H
```

## Core Components
- Game Engine (rules and state):
  - Board representation using a fixed-size array with dynamic board size (8 or 10).
  - Piece encoding: man and king for both sides; helpers to determine side, type, and square color.
  - Move structure capturing from/to, capture list, path for multi-jumps, and promotion flag.
  - Move generation covering silent moves and mandatory captures per variant.
  - Terminal detection and draw-by-no-progress rule.
- AI Engine:
  - Four levels: Beginner (weighted random), Amateur/Solid/Expert (iterative deepening negamax with alpha-beta).
  - Expert uses quiescence search limited to captures to avoid horizon effects.
  - Time-sliced step function to stay within a tight budget per tick.
- UI and Interaction:
  - LVGL full-screen page with HUD, field, and overlay panel.
  - Preallocated widgets for squares, pieces, highlights, and rings.
  - Input handling via coordinate mapping to board cells; selection and legal move highlighting.
  - Undo and Hint buttons; IMU shake triggers hint when enabled.
  - Persistent settings and stats via NVS preferences.

## Architecture Overview
The system separates concerns into three layers:
- UI layer builds and updates LVGL objects based on game state.
- Engine layer enforces rules, generates legal moves, applies moves, and evaluates terminal states.
- AI layer computes best moves using search algorithms and integrates with the UI through a non-blocking timer.

```mermaid

participant Eng as "Engine (rules)"
participant AI as "Ai (search)"

UI->>Eng : gen_moves(Pos)
UI->>UI : Highlight legal moves
User->>UI : Tap destination
UI->>Eng : apply_move(Pos, Move)
UI->>UI : Update board, history, HUD
UI->>UI : after_human_or_ai_move()
alt Human vs AI turn
UI->>AI : begin(Pos, Level)
loop Timer ticks
UI->>AI : step()
AI-->>UI : ready?
end
UI->>Eng : apply_move(Ai : : best())
UI->>UI : Update board, history, HUD
end
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Rules and Board State Management
- Board initialization sets up pieces according to variant:
  - International 10x10: more rows for black and white setup.
  - English 8x8: standard checkers setup.
- Move generation prioritizes captures:
  - Mandatory capture enforcement differs by variant:
    - International: maximum capture length required.
    - English: any legal capture suffices.
- Multi-jump sequences are represented via a path array and captured squares list; captures are removed only after the entire sequence completes.
- King movement:
  - International: flying kings can move any distance along diagonals.
  - English: short-range king jumps (one square).
- Promotion occurs when a man reaches the opponent’s back rank at the end of a move or capture sequence.
- Draw rule: no progress (no captures or promotions) for a threshold number of plies results in a draw.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Generate Moves"]) --> CheckCaps["Enumerate all captures"]
CheckCaps --> CapsFound{"Any captures?"}
CapsFound --> |Yes| EnforceMax{"Variant enforces max capture?"}
EnforceMax --> |Intl| FilterMax["Keep only longest capture sequences"]
EnforceMax --> |English| KeepAll["Keep all legal captures"]
FilterMax --> ReturnMoves["Return capture moves"]
KeepAll --> ReturnMoves
CapsFound --> |No| SilentMoves["Generate silent moves"]
SilentMoves --> Kings{"King moves?"}
Kings --> |Intl| FlyingKings["Flying king moves"]
Kings --> |English| ShortKings["Short king moves"]
FlyingKings --> ReturnMoves
ShortKings --> ReturnMoves
```

### AI Engine: Strategic Evaluation and Adaptive Difficulty
- Levels:
  - Beginner: weighted random choice favoring captures and promotions.
  - Amateur/Solid/Expert: negamax with alpha-beta pruning and iterative deepening.
  - Expert adds quiescence search limited to captures to stabilize evaluations near tactical sequences.
- Node budget and depth targets scale with difficulty to balance strength and responsiveness.
- Evaluation combines material count, mobility, and pawn advancement to guide decisions.

```mermaid

+abort() void
}

+gen_moves(Pos, Move*, int) int
+apply_move(Pos, Move) void
+eval_full(Pos) int
+is_terminal(Pos, int*) bool
}
Ai --> Engine : "uses"
```

### Interactive Gameplay Features and UI

### Capture Logic and Multi-Jump Sequences
- Captures are enumerated first; during a sequence, captured pieces remain on the board to block further movement but are marked to prevent re-capturing the same piece.
- After the final landing of a sequence, captured pieces are removed from the board.
- International variant allows long-range king captures; English variant restricts kings to single-step jumps.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Enter(["Start Capture Search"]) --> DirLoop["For each diagonal direction"]
DirLoop --> FindEnemy{"Find enemy piece"}
FindEnemy --> |Not found| NextDir["Next direction"]
FindEnemy --> |Found| LandCheck["Check empty landing squares beyond"]
LandCheck --> AnyLand{"Any landing?"}
AnyLand --> |No| NextDir
AnyLand --> |Yes| RecordPath["Record landing and captured piece"]
RecordPath --> Recurse["Recurse from landing"]
Recurse --> Extended{"Extension found?"}
Extended --> |Yes| Continue["Continue search"]
Extended --> |No| EmitMove["Emit capture move"]
Continue --> DirLoop
EmitDirLoop --> End(["Done"])
```

- Promoted pieces become kings and gain movement capabilities per variant rules.

## Performance Considerations
- Time-sliced AI: Each step consumes a bounded node budget to keep UI responsive.
- Efficient move generation: Arrays and inline helpers minimize allocations and overhead.
- Quiescence search at expert level limits tactical horizon issues without excessive cost.
- Preallocated LVGL widgets reduce runtime allocation during gameplay.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- No legal moves:
  - Terminal condition detected; game ends with winner determined by remaining pieces or lack of moves.
- Stuck in thinking state:
  - Ensure timer callback invokes AI::step(); verify node budget and depth target appropriate for device performance.
- Incorrect variant behavior:
  - Confirm Pos.variant is set correctly; international vs English rules branch on this flag.
- Hint not showing:
  - Verify IMU hint option enabled and shake threshold met; ensure hint timeout clears highlights properly.

Dames Tab delivers a robust draughts experience with comprehensive rule support, a capable AI, and a polished UI tailored for embedded devices. The architecture cleanly separates rules, AI, and presentation, enabling maintainable enhancements and consistent gameplay across variants and difficulty levels.

## Introduction
Fil d'Or is a tilt-controlled marble roguelite built for a 1280x720 full-screen LVGL surface on ESPHome. The player navigates a marble through six themed rooms using IMU tilt data from a BMI270 sensor. It features:
- Procedural room layouts with deterministic seeding per run
- A roguelite progression system (souls currency, level-ups, shop, equipment slots, and run-time boons)
- Robust physics with sub-stepped collision to prevent tunneling at high speeds
- Tilt control with deadzone, smoothing, clamping, and dash impulse
- Visual style using gradients and layered objects for depth without extra draw passes
- NVS persistence for meta-progression across sessions
- An experimental AI-generated prototype nature with careful hot-path constraints

## Project Structure
The game is implemented primarily in C++ with minimal YAML scaffolding:
- UI containers are declared in the LVGL component YAML; all gameplay visuals are created at runtime in C++
- IMU polling and callbacks feed tilt data into the game loop
- A custom color palette centralizes visual tokens used by the game

```mermaid

D --> B
E["Color Palette<br/>tab5_custom.h"] --> B
B --> F["NVS Persistence<br/>esphome::global_preferences"]
```

## Core Components
- Game state machine and screens: hub, settings, stats, shop, equip, reward selection, pause, game over, victory
- Room definitions and entity specs defining walls, hazards, pickups, portals, chests, runes
- Physics tick with sub-stepping, friction, speed limiting, bounce, and zone effects
- Tilt input pipeline: calibration offset, smoothing, deadzone, clamping, dash trigger
- Collision detection: circle vs rectangle resolution, safe pickup placement checks
- Progression systems: souls economy, stat upgrades, items/equipment, run-time boons
- Rendering: preallocated LVGL object pools, gradient-based shading, detail layers as children
- Persistence: save/load via esphome preferences with magic versioning

## Architecture Overview
The architecture separates concerns cleanly:
- YAML defines only four empty containers (root, HUD, field, panel). All visuals are constructed once and reused.
- The IMU driver publishes acceleration samples; the Z-axis callback batches axes and calls each game’s on_imu handler.
- The game loop runs at ~30 Hz via an LVGL timer, updating physics, entities, and rendering.
- Persistence uses NVS with a magic constant to detect schema changes and reset when needed.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant IMU as "BMI270 IMU"
participant ESP as "ESPHome Callback"
participant Game as "Marble : : on_imu()"
participant Tick as "tick_cb()"
participant LV as "LVGL Timer"
IMU-->>ESP : Acceleration x,y,z
ESP->>Game : on_imu(ax, ay, az)
Note over Game : Store raw samples, no heavy math
LV->>Tick : Call every ~33ms
Tick->>Tick : Apply calibration, smoothing, deadzone, clamp
Tick->>Tick : Integrate velocity, friction, zones, substeps
Tick->>Tick : Resolve collisions, update entities
Tick->>LV : Update LVGL positions/styles
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Tilt Control and Gravity Simulation
- Calibration offsets are stored in NVS and subtracted from raw IMU values
- Smoothing reduces jitter; a radial deadzone prevents micro-movements
- Vector magnitude is clamped to avoid excessive acceleration
- Screen rotation maps physical axes to screen axes correctly
- Dash impulse triggers on sharp tilts with cooldown

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["IMU Sample"]) --> Calib["Apply Calibration Offset"]
Calib --> Smooth["Smooth X/Y"]
Smooth --> Deadzone{"Within Deadzone?"}
Deadzone -- Yes --> Zero["Zero Input"]
Deadzone -- No --> Normalize["Normalize and Scale"]
Normalize --> Clamp["Clamp Magnitude"]
Clamp --> DashCheck{"Sharp Tilt?"}
DashCheck -- Yes --> DashImpulse["Add Dash Impulse"]
DashCheck -- No --> Accel["Compute Acceleration"]
Zero --> Accel
Accel --> Next(["Physics Integration"])
```

### Physics and Collision Detection
- Sub-stepping (3 steps per frame) prevents tunneling at high speeds
- Circle-vs-rectangle collision resolves overlap and reflects velocity with bounce factor
- Friction applied per sub-step; speed capped per frame
- Zones (glue, boost, wind) modify acceleration or damping while inside
- Safe pickup placement ensures connectivity to original position

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Enter(["Frame Start"]) --> Zones["Read Zone Effects"]
Zones --> SubstepLoop{"For Each Substep"}
SubstepLoop --> Integrate["Integrate Velocity + Acceleration"]
Integrate --> Limit["Cap Speed"]
Limit --> Move["Move Ball"]
Move --> Walls["Resolve Wall Collisions"]
Walls --> Entities["Update Moving Entities"]
Entities --> Pickups["Check Pickup/Trap/Exit"]
Pickups --> Render["Render Ball + Effects"]
Render --> Exit(["End Frame"])
```

### Roguelite Progression System

- Stat upgrades cost increasing amounts based on total level; six stats affect health, invulnerability, size, control, speed, and loot
- Items can be bought/sold in shop and equipped in two slots with persistent effects
- Run-time boons provide temporary buffs like magnet, brake, speed, revive, velvet (invulnerability), eye (visible portal), bronze shield, heart, control, purse

## Performance Considerations
- Hot path avoids dynamic allocations, string conversions, and heavy operations
- LVGL objects are preallocated once and recycled between rooms
- HUD labels are only rewritten when values change to minimize invalidations
- Sub-stepping improves collision robustness without excessive overhead
- Gradient shading provides visual depth with single draw passes
- IMU polling rate adapts dynamically: fast when games are open, slow otherwise

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- If the marble drifts unexpectedly, recalibrate tilt with the tablet flat
- If pickups appear unreachable, verify room specs and segment_clear logic during placement
- If performance drops, check for unintended LVGL invalidations or excessive label updates
- If progress doesn’t persist, confirm NVS write success and magic validation
- If tilt feels unresponsive, adjust deadzone and smoothing in configuration

- [marble_game.cpp:2307-2312](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/marble_game.cpp#L2307-L2312)

- [marble_game.cpp:508-524](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/marble_game.cpp#L508-L524)

## Conclusion
Fil d’Or delivers a polished tilt-controlled marble roguelite with careful attention to performance, visual clarity, and progressive challenge. Its architecture cleanly separates input, physics, rendering, and persistence, enabling smooth gameplay on embedded hardware. The roguelite systems offer meaningful choices and replayability, while the codebase maintains strict hot-path constraints for reliable real-time operation. As an experimental AI-generated prototype, it demonstrates how structured design and disciplined implementation can produce engaging interactive experiences within constrained environments.

## Introduction
This document explains the shared arcade game module architecture that enables eight games to run as fullscreen LVGL pages on ESP32-P4 hardware. It covers:
- The skip:true declaration pattern for dedicated game pages
- Empty YAML containers with C++-built content
- lv_timer lifecycle management per game
- NVS persistence for scores and settings
- Common UI patterns (fullscreen rendering at 1280x720, modal navigation without standard chrome, autonomous modules)
- Input handling (touch controls, tilt sensing via BMI270 IMU, adaptive polling)
- Performance considerations for maintaining smooth gameplay and memory management under embedded constraints

## Project Structure
The arcade system is composed of:
- A main dashboard page and a dedicated Arcade selector page
- Eight fullscreen game pages, each declared with skip:true to opt out of swipe navigation
- Per-game YAML files that declare only minimal empty containers
- Per-game C++ modules that build all runtime UI and logic
- Shared configuration for display, touch, audio, and IMU
- Global state and animation helpers used across the UI

## Core Components
- Dedicated game pages: Each game has its own LVGL page with skip:true so swipe gestures do not navigate away during gameplay.
- Minimal YAML shells: Game YAML files define only root containers and fonts; all gameplay UI is built in C++.
- Autonomous modules: Each game encapsulates its own state, input, rendering, and persistence.
- Shared infrastructure: Display/touch/audio/IMU configuration, global state, and animation utilities are centralized.

Key responsibilities:
- Navigation: YAML selectors trigger close-all, page show, and open scripts.
- Rendering: Fullscreen 1280x720 (or portrait for pinball), no standard chrome, modal overlays for menus.
- Input: Touch zones and IMU-driven tilt; adaptive polling rate based on active game.
- Persistence: Local NVS storage for high scores and settings without Home Assistant dependency.

## Architecture Overview
The arcade subsystem follows an autonomous-module-per-game model:
- YAML declares lightweight page shells and a grid-based selector
- C++ builds the full UI once, reuses objects, and drives a per-game lv_timer loop
- Input flows from LVGL events and IMU callbacks into each game’s namespace
- Settings and scores persist to NVS using ESPHome preferences

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant Selector as "Game Selector (YAML)"
participant LVGL as "LVGL Pages"
participant Game as "Game Module (C++)"
participant IMU as "BMI270 IMU"
participant NVS as "NVS Preferences"
User->>Selector : Tap game card
Selector->>LVGL : lvgl.page.show(page_<game>)
Selector->>Game : script.execute(tab5_<game>_open)
Game->>Game : Build UI once (if needed)
Game->>Game : Start lv_timer (tick loop)
IMU-->>Game : on_imu(ax,ay,az) (adaptive poll)
Game->>Game : Update physics/state
Game->>LVGL : Move/Show/Hide widgets
Game->>NVS : Save scores/settings on key events
User->>Game : Exit via hub/menu
Game->>Game : Stop lv_timer, persist, hide overlay
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Skip:true Declaration Pattern
- Each game page is declared with skip:true to disable swipe navigation while playing.
- Navigation uses explicit lvgl.page.show calls from the selector and C++ page switching.
- This ensures immersive fullscreen gameplay without accidental page changes.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-lvgl.yaml:686-747](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml#L686-L747)
- [game_selector.yaml:101-129](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/game_selector.yaml#L101-L129)

### Empty YAML Containers with C++-Built Content
- Game YAML files provide only root containers and fonts; all gameplay elements are created in C++.
- This keeps YAML declarative and avoids complex logic there, while allowing rich dynamic UI in C++.

Example: Arkanoid page shell defines HUD, field, and panel containers; C++ constructs bricks, balls, paddles, and menus.

**Section sources**
- [arkanoid_game.yaml:14-74](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/arkanoid_game.yaml#L14-L74)
- [arkanoid_game.cpp:479-593](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/arkanoid_game.cpp#L479-L593)

### lv_timer Lifecycle Management
- Each game starts an lv_timer when opened and stops it when closed, ensuring zero CPU usage when hidden.
- The timer drives the game tick at a fixed step (e.g., ~30 Hz for many games), with substeps for collision stability.
- Pinball adjusts tick frequency between menu and gameplay modes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start([Open Game]) --> BuildUI["Build UI once if needed"]
BuildUI --> StartTimer["Create lv_timer (tick)"]
StartTimer --> TickLoop{"lv_timer callback"}
TickLoop --> |Update| Physics["Physics & State"]
Physics --> Render["Move/Show/Hide LVGL objects"]
Render --> TickLoop
TickLoop --> |Close| StopTimer["Delete lv_timer"]
StopTimer --> End([Idle])
```

### NVS Persistence System
- Games use ESPHome preferences to store scores and settings locally without Home Assistant dependency.
- Each game defines a magic number and a dedicated preference key; mismatched formats reset to defaults.
- Persistence occurs at key moments (settings changes, game over, high score insertion).

## Performance Considerations
- Fixed timestep loops: Most games use ~30 Hz with substeps for stable collisions
- Object pooling: LVGL objects preallocated once and reused via show/hide/move
- Adaptive IMU polling: Switches between 10 Hz and 33 Hz depending on active games
- Portrait mode optimization: Pinball runs in portrait to avoid software rotation overhead
- Memory management: Avoid std::string/new/delete in hot paths; use static buffers and caches
- NVS writes: Throttled to key events to minimize flash wear

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Screen stays black after reboot: Ensure boot delay allows GPIO expander to stabilize before display reset
- IMU not responding: Verify I2C bus and address; check adaptive polling intervals
- Game not starting/stopping: Confirm lv_timer creation/destruction and page visibility flags
- NVS corruption: Magic mismatch resets to defaults; verify save/load functions

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-83](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L83)
- [tab5-imu.yaml:125-144](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L125-L144)
- [arkanoid_game.cpp:370-417](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/arkanoid_game.cpp#L370-L417)

## Conclusion
The arcade module architecture delivers a robust, scalable framework for running eight fullscreen games on ESP32-P4. By combining skip:true page isolation, minimal YAML shells, C++-driven UI, lv_timer lifecycle control, and NVS persistence, each game operates autonomously while sharing common infrastructure. Input handling leverages both touch and IMU with adaptive polling, and performance optimizations ensure smooth gameplay within embedded constraints.

## Introduction
Go Tab is a complete implementation of the strategy game Go embedded on an ESPHome-based device with LVGL UI and a built-in AI opponent. It supports 9×9, 13×13, and 19×19 boards, multiple difficulty levels, handicap stones, territory preview, move history, pause/resume, and persistent settings via NVS. The engine enforces Go rules (liberties, captures, suicide prohibition, simple ko), scoring uses Chinese area scoring with komi, and the AI provides time-sliced search to keep the UI responsive.

## Project Structure
The Go module is split into three layers:
- Engine layer: pure C++ rules, state, and scoring without UI dependencies.
- AI layer: candidate generation, static evaluation, alpha-beta search, and time-bounded planning.
- UI/Game layer: LVGL rendering, input handling, menus, persistence, and game flow.

```mermaid

end
subgraph "AI Layer"
AI["go_ai.*"]
end
subgraph "Engine Layer"
ENG["go_engine.*"]
end
YAML --> GO_UI
GO_UI --> AI
GO_UI --> ENG
AI --> ENG
```

## Core Components
- Engine: board representation, liberties calculation, legality checks, capture application, ko rule, eye detection, territory mapping, Chinese scoring, and handicap placement.
- AI: four difficulty levels, candidate move generation, influence-based evaluation, alpha-beta search with time slicing, and resign sentinel for large score gaps.
- UI/Game: full-screen LVGL page, preallocated widgets, stone placement, capture feedback, territory preview, move list, pause menu, stats, NVS persistence, IMU hint trigger, and game state machine.

Key responsibilities:
- Engine ensures correctness and performance by using module-level scratch buffers and avoiding deep recursion or large stack allocations.
- AI balances strength and responsiveness by bounding search by time and limiting candidates per node.
- UI integrates inputs, renders efficiently with minimal LVGL invalidations, and persists progress/settings safely.

## Architecture Overview
The system runs as a single-threaded LVGL loop. A periodic timer advances AI thinking in small slices so the UI remains fluid. The UI constructs LVGL objects once and reuses them across games. NVS writes are deferred to avoid flash wear.

```mermaid

UI->>AI : begin(root, level, seed, komi)
loop Timer tick
UI->>AI : step(slice_ms)
AI-->>UI : best_sq() or PASS
UI->>UI : render move/hint/progress
end
else Illegal
UI-->>User : show invalid
end
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Engine: Rules, State, Scoring
- Board state: grid array, board size, side to move, ko square, consecutive passes, move counter, captured counts.
- Liberties: efficient chain traversal with generation stamps to avoid memset overhead; returns group info optionally.
- Legality: fast path checks direct liberty, friendly extension with another liberty, or capturing adjacent enemy atari; no full simulation.
- Play: applies move, removes captured groups, updates counters, sets ko if applicable, resets passes, switches side.
- Moves generation: enumerates legal placements (excluding pass).
- Eyes: detects simple eyes to prevent self-destructive moves in AI.
- Territory map and scoring: builds live board excluding marked dead stones, floods empty regions to assign territory, computes Chinese area scores with komi.
- Handicap: places standard star-point stones and sets White to start.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["play(sq)"]) --> CheckPass{"sq == PASS?"}
CheckPass --> |Yes| IncPass["passes++, side=opp, ko=PASS, move_no++"] --> End(["true"])
CheckPass --> |No| Legal{"is_legal(sq)?"}
Legal --> |No| Fail(["false"])
Legal --> |Yes| Place["place stone, check neighbors"]
Place --> CaptureLoop["for each neighbor:<br/>if enemy and libs==0 remove group"]
CaptureLoop --> KoCheck{"captured==1 and new group libs==1?"}
KoCheck --> |Yes| SetKo["ko = last_cap"]
KoCheck --> |No| ClearKo["ko = PASS"]
SetKo --> Update["update counters, passes=0, side=opp, move_no++"]
ClearKo --> Update
Update --> End
```

### AI: Difficulty Levels, Evaluation, Search
- Levels: Beginner (weighted random), Amateur (1-ply), Solid (2-ply alpha-beta), Expert (deeper search with iterative refinement).
- Candidate generation: focuses on contacts, captures, saves, atari, extensions; avoids filling own eyes; includes positional bias (opening lines, edge penalties).
- Static evaluation: material (living stones), safety (liberty scarcity), influence (distance-weighted control of empty points).
- Search: negamax/alpha-beta with time gating every 32 nodes; depth targets vary by board size; fallback to legal moves if candidates filtered too aggressively.
- Resign sentinel: indicates AI concedes when score gap exceeds threshold.

```mermaid
classDiagram

+step(slice_ms)
+state()
+ready() bool
+best_sq() int
+progress_pct() int
+abort()
+level_name(level) const char*
}
class Engine {
+Pos
+Color

+play(Pos&, int) bool
+gen_moves(Pos, int*, int) int

}
Ai --> Engine : "uses"
```

## Performance Considerations
- Engine avoids large stack arrays by using module-level scratch buffers; this prevents stack overflow during deep AI searches.
- Liberty computation uses generation stamps to avoid repeated memset operations, keeping O(N) behavior critical for AI efficiency.
- AI bounds search by time rather than node count to guarantee responsiveness; it also limits candidates per node to reduce branching factor.
- UI minimizes LVGL invalidations by caching visibility and updating only changed intersections; gradients provide visual depth without extra widgets.
- NVS writes are deferred and batched to reduce flash wear and maintain smooth gameplay.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Illegal moves: ensure the move is not on an occupied intersection, respects ko, and is not suicide; use is_legal before play.
- Captures not applied: verify that adjacent enemy chains have zero liberties after placement; check capture loops and removed tracking.
- Ko issues: confirm ko square is set correctly when exactly one stone is captured and the placed stone has one liberty; ko clears after any other move or pass.
- Scoring discrepancies: mark dead stones before scoring; territory map should reflect removed dead stones and neutral dame areas.
- UI freezes: ensure AI step is called within the timer slice; do not block the main loop with long computations.

## Conclusion
Go Tab delivers a robust, performant Go experience with accurate rules enforcement, sophisticated AI, and an elegant LVGL interface. The separation of concerns between engine, AI, and UI enables maintainability and testing, while performance optimizations ensure smooth gameplay even on constrained hardware.

## Appendices

### Rules Summary
- Liberties and captures: groups are removed when they have no liberties; captures take precedence over suicide prevention.
- Suicide rule: placing a stone that would result in zero liberties is illegal unless it captures first.
- Ko rule: immediate recapture of a single-stone capture is forbidden until the opponent plays elsewhere.
- Scoring: Chinese area scoring with komi; dead stones can be marked and removed prior to counting.

### AI Difficulty Levels
- Beginner: weighted random selection among tactical candidates.
- Amateur: shallow search (1 ply).
- Solid: deeper search (2 plies) with alpha-beta pruning.
- Expert: increased depth and iterative refinement, tuned per board size.

## Introduction
Neon Apron is a portrait-mode pinball game built for the Tab5 embedded platform. It reimagines classic pinball mechanics in a vertical playfield optimized for handheld orientation, using tilt-based controls and a plunger to launch the ball. The game features a neon visual theme, dynamic scoring modes (Frenzy, Multiball, Skill Shot), bumpers, drop targets, rollovers, slingshots, and flippers that respond to touch zones on screen. Physics runs at 50 Hz with sub-stepping to prevent tunneling, while rendering avoids expensive transforms by pre-building static geometry and animating only moving elements.

## Project Structure
The game is implemented as a self-contained module with three primary files:
- C++ implementation and header for logic, physics, UI construction, and input handling
- A minimal LVGL YAML page declaring four containers (root, field, HUD, panel) and a line probe to enable line drawing
- Documentation notes describing performance characteristics and constraints

```mermaid

B --> C["LVGL runtime<br/>Widgets, timers, events"]
B --> D["ESPHome preferences<br/>NVS persistence"]
B --> E["IMU input<br/>Tilt/nudge detection"]
```

## Core Components
- Orientation management: The game switches LVGL to portrait mode when opened and restores landscape on close, ensuring the playfield fits vertically and touch coordinates remain correct.
- Playfield geometry: Static rails, arch, guides, and lanes are constructed once; only balls, flippers, flashes, and plunger rod animate each frame.
- Physics engine: Gravity pulls the ball downward; collisions use capsule-segment tests for rails/guides, circular constraint for the top arch, circle-circle for bumpers, segment tests for slingshots and targets, and rotating segments for flippers with angular velocity transfer.
- Scoring and modes: Bumpers, slingshots, targets, rollovers, and skill shots award points; Frenzy and Multiball multiply scores; bonus balls trigger at thresholds.
- Input: Touch zones control left/right flippers and plunger; IMU nudge imparts lateral impulses; tilt penalty disables flippers temporarily after repeated heavy nudges.
- Persistence: High scores, settings, and career stats are saved to NVS via ESPHome preferences.

## Architecture Overview
Neon Apron uses a state machine across hub, scores, settings, playing, paused, and game over screens. The main loop runs an LVGL timer that updates physics, handles inputs, renders animations, and syncs HUD text. UI is built once from LVGL containers declared in YAML; gameplay widgets are created programmatically.

### Flipper Mechanics and Controls
- Two flipper zones on the left and right sides of the field; holding triggers the corresponding flipper.
- Flippers rotate toward active/rest angles at a fixed speed; collision computes angular velocity and applies impulse plus punch when pressed.
- Tilt penalty temporarily disables flippers to prevent abuse.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Tick"]) --> StepFlippers["step_flippers(dt)<br/>update target angle"]
StepFlippers --> CollideFlipper{"Ball near flipper?"}
CollideFlipper --> |Yes| ComputeOmega["Compute omega from angle change"]
ComputeOmega --> ApplyImpulse["Apply relative velocity + punch if pressed"]
CollideFlipper --> |No| Next["Next collision"]
ApplyImpulse --> Next
```

### Ball Physics and Collision Detection
- Gravity acts downward; friction reduces velocity per sub-step; maximum speed capped.
- Rails and guides: capsule-segment collision with restitution; one-way flap prevents reverse travel in plunger lane.
- Top arch: circular constraint keeps ball inside the upper curve efficiently.
- Bumpers: circle-circle pushback with strong kick and flash effect.
- Slingshots: segment collision with normal-directed kick and random jitter.
- Drop targets: segment collision flips target down; bank complete alternates between Frenzy and Multiball.
- Rollovers: trigger zones along the arch; skill shot lane yields bonus points.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
S(["physics_step(dt)"]) --> Integrate["Integrate gravity + velocity<br/>apply friction"]
Integrate --> Walls["Collide walls/guides<br/>capsule-segment"]
Walls --> Arch["Collide arch<br/>circular constraint"]
Arch --> Flippers["Collide flippers<br/>angular velocity"]
Flippers --> Bumpers["Collide bumpers<br/>circle-circle"]
Bumpers --> Slings["Collide slingshots<br/>segment + normal"]
Slings --> Targets["Collide targets<br/>flip down"]
Targets --> Rollovers["Check rollover triggers"]
Rollovers --> CapSpeed["Cap max speed"]
CapSpeed --> Drain{"Drained or launched?"}
Drain --> |Drained| End(["Ball lost"])
Drain --> |Launched| Next(["Plunger launch"])
```

### Scoring Zones and Special Features
- Bumpers: high-score hits with flash and optional frenzy multiplier.
- Slingshots: quick kicks near flippers for rapid scoring opportunities.
- Targets: drop targets form a bank; completing all alternates rewards.
- Rollovers: three lanes along the arch; skill shot lane grants large bonus if hit within time window.
- Modes:
  - Frenzy: bumper score tripled for a limited duration.
  - Multiball: additional ball(s) launched; multiplier increases; jackpots on bumpers.
  - Skill Shot: targeted rollover yields big points.

### Tilt-Based Nudge and Tilt Penalty
- IMU readings are filtered through a high-pass to detect short shakes (nudge).
- Nudge imparts horizontal momentum to active balls; vertical component reduced for readability.
- Repeated nudges accumulate hits; exceeding threshold triggers TILT, disabling flippers briefly and marking the game.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
IMU["on_imu(ax, ay)"] --> Filter["High-pass filter<br/>compute jerk"]
Filter --> Threshold{"Magnitude > threshold?"}
Threshold --> |No| Wait["Wait next tick"]
Threshold --> |Yes| Apply["Apply vx/vy impulse to balls"]
Apply --> Count["Increment tilt_hits"]
Count --> Check{"hits >= TILT_HITS?"}
Check --> |Yes| Tilt["Set tilted, disable flippers"]
Check --> |No| Wait
```

### Plunger and Launch Mechanics
- Hold bottom-center zone to charge; release to launch with power proportional to charge time.
- Auto-launch safety prevents stalls; returning ball rests in plunger lane until launched again.
- Visual spring compresses with charge; HUD shows power bar while charging.

## Performance Considerations
- Fixed 50 Hz physics with 4 sub-steps to prevent tunneling; menu states run at slower intervals to save CPU.
- Rendering avoids transform rotations; static geometry built once; only dynamic elements updated per frame.
- Efficient collision math: circular constraint for arch, capsule-segment for rails, circle-circle for bumpers.
- Minimal allocations and string operations in hot paths; cached label updates reduce invalidations.
- Line drawing enabled via a hidden line widget in YAML to satisfy LVGL compile-time requirements.

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Screen remains rotated after closing: Ensure all exit paths call close() to restore landscape rotation.
- Compilation error lv_line_create not declared: Keep the hidden line widget in YAML; it enables LV_USE_LINE.
- Balls stuck in plunger lane: Verify drain thresholds and auto-launch timing; ensure return-to-lane logic resets position and visibility.
- Tilt too sensitive or inverted: Adjust nudge sensitivity and invert_nudge setting; recalibrate flat before playing.
- Poor performance: Confirm no transform rotations are used; verify only necessary objects are invalidated each frame.

## Conclusion
Neon Apron delivers a compact, responsive pinball experience tailored for portrait orientation on embedded hardware. Its design balances authentic gameplay mechanics—gravity-driven ball motion, realistic flipper interactions, and engaging scoring modes—with efficient rendering and robust collision detection. The tilt-based controls and plunger mechanic provide intuitive interaction, while persistent settings and scores enhance long-term engagement. By avoiding expensive transforms and optimizing hot paths, the game maintains smooth performance even on constrained devices.

## Introduction
Roi Noir is a complete, embedded FIDE chess game for the Tab5 device. It implements full chess rules (including castling, en passant, pawn promotion, and check/checkmate detection), provides a sophisticated AI engine with five difficulty levels, and offers a rich LVGL-based UI with move highlighting, captured pieces display, chess notation, clocks, statistics, and an Elo rating system. The implementation is fully local: no network or external dependencies, with settings and progress persisted to NVS.

## Project Structure
The project separates concerns into three primary layers:
- UI layer (LVGL): builds the board, HUD, panels, menus, and animations; handles user input and rendering.
- Game state layer: manages moves, history, clocks, modes, and end conditions.
- Engine layer (pure C++ model): represents positions, generates legal moves, evaluates positions, and searches using time-sliced negamax with alpha-beta pruning.

```mermaid
graph TB
UI["UI Layer<br/>chess_game.cpp"] --> Engine["Engine Model<br/>chess_ai.cpp"]
UI --> YAML["Page Layout<br/>chess_game.yaml"]
Engine --> Rules["Rules & Search<br/>gen_moves/make/unmake/eval/search"]
UI --> Persist["NVS Persistence<br/>ChessSave"]
```

## Core Components
- Position representation and rules: mailbox 0x88 board encoding, move flags, make/unmake, legality filtering, FEN/SAN support.
- Move generation: pseudo-legal generator unified for all piece types, captures-only mode for quiescence, castling checks, en passant handling, promotion branching.
- Evaluation: material + piece-square tables + pawn structure bonuses + king safety + tempo.
- Search: iterative deepening with time slicing, MVV/LVA move ordering, killer heuristic, quiescence search, mate scoring, hard/soft deadlines.
- UI: preallocated LVGL objects, two-layer piece rendering (filled + outline), move dots, coordinates, animated moves, HUD with clocks and evaluation, side panel with move list and controls.
- Persistence: NVS save/load of settings, stats, and current game state (FEN + clocks).
- Modes and features: Player vs AI, hotseat (player vs player), demo (AI vs AI), optional Fischer increments, gesture hints, 50-move rule toggle, evaluation display.

## Architecture Overview
The system uses a clean separation between UI and engine. The UI constructs LVGL widgets once and reuses them, while the engine operates on integer-only structures without LVGL dependencies. Time-sliced search ensures responsiveness by yielding to LVGL every ~18 ms.

## Detailed Component Analysis

### FIDE Rules Implementation
- Castling: generated only when rights exist, squares empty, and king does not pass through or land on attacked squares.
- En passant: generated when opponent double-pushes and adjacent enemy pawns can capture; handled in make/unmake with special victim square.
- Pawn promotion: four distinct moves generated upon reaching the last rank; UI prompts selection.
- Check/checkmate/stalemate: legality filter rejects moves leaving own king in check; end-game detection counts legal moves and checks for insufficient material, 50-move rule, triple repetition.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Move Attempt"]) --> Gen["Generate Pseudo-Legal Moves"]
Gen --> Filter{"Legal?"}
Filter --> |No| Reject["Reject Move"]
Filter --> |Yes| Apply["Apply Move (make)"]
Apply --> Check{"King in Check?"}
Check --> |Yes| Unmake["Unmake and Reject"]
Check --> |No| EndCheck["Check Game End Conditions"]
EndCheck --> Result{"Game Over?"}
Result --> |Yes| End(["End Game"])
Result --> |No| Next(["Next Turn"])
```

### AI Engine: Evaluation and Search
- Evaluation combines material values, piece-square tables, pawn structure (doubled, isolated, passed), rook open/semi-open columns, bishop pair bonus, king safety shield, and tempo.
- Search uses iterative deepening with time slicing, MVV/LVA move ordering, killer heuristics, and quiescence search to avoid horizon effects. Hard/soft deadlines ensure responsiveness.
- Difficulty levels control max depth, quiescence depth, budget, randomization window, and approximate Elo.

## Performance Considerations
- Preallocated LVGL objects minimize allocations during gameplay.
- Time-sliced search yields every ~18 ms to keep UI responsive.
- MVV/LVA ordering and killer heuristics improve pruning efficiency.
- Quiescence search reduces horizon effects in tactical positions.
- Hard/soft deadlines prevent runaway computation; retries allow completing expensive root moves.
- Efficient move generation avoids bitboards on 32-bit ESP32-P4, favoring mailbox checks.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Perft self-test validates move generator correctness against known node counts.
- If search appears stuck, verify time slicing and deadlines; check that search_step is called each tick.
- For incorrect end conditions, ensure legality filtering and end-game checks are invoked after each move.
- Use hints sparingly; cooldown prevents spam. Gesture hints require IMU enabled.

## Introduction
Trial Poursuite is a full-screen trivia quiz game inspired by classic board games, implemented as an LVGL-based console on the Tab5 device. It supports 1–6 teams, a faithful wheel-and-spokes board layout, category-based questions with difficulty levels, a timer, and persistent stats across sessions. The game runs entirely locally without Home Assistant dependencies during play, using NVS for persistence and LVGL for rendering.

Key highlights:
- Authentic board topology: outer ring of 42 cells, 6 spokes of 5 cells each, and a central hub cell (73 nodes total).
- Category system with 6 color-coded categories and wedge collection toward a final challenge at the center.
- Question database of 720+ French questions distributed across categories and difficulties.
- Timer options and shake-to-roll dice via IMU input.
- Persistent settings, team rosters, and live game state saved to NVS.

## Project Structure
The trivia game spans C++ logic, a question bank, and a minimal YAML page definition that only provides container slots. All gameplay UI is built dynamically in C++.

```mermaid
graph TB
A["tab5-scripts.yaml<br/>Launch script"] --> B["Trivia::open(ui)<br/>Builds UI once"]
B --> C["LVGL containers<br/>(root, hud, board, panel)"]
C --> D["Board graph<br/>42 ring + 6 spokes + hub"]
C --> E["Right panel<br/>dice, status, teams"]
C --> F["HUD<br/>turn, team, clock, menu"]
B --> G["Question bag<br/>per category"]
B --> H["NVS persistence<br/>settings/stats/game"]
B --> I["IMU input<br/>shake to roll"]
```

## Core Components
- Game state machine and phases: manages menus, setup, rules, stats, settings, confirmation, playing, category selection, question display, reveal, pause, and victory states; plus rolling, choosing, moving phases.
- Board model: defines cell types (category, HQ, roll, hub), builds the authentic wheel/spoke topology, computes neighbors and screen positions.
- Persistence layer: saves and loads settings, team roster, current game state, RNG seed, and global stats to NVS.
- UI construction: preallocates LVGL objects once and reuses them; uses caches to avoid redundant redraws.
- Question system: per-category bags shuffled via Fisher-Yates; draws without replacement until reshuffled.
- Timer and IMU integration: configurable timer and shake detection to trigger dice rolls.

## Architecture Overview
The game follows a clear separation between configuration (YAML), runtime UI (C++), data (question bank), and persistence (NVS). The launch script injects LVGL pointers into a UI struct and calls open(), which constructs the UI once and starts a tick loop.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant Script as "tab5-scripts.yaml"
participant Game as "Trivia : : open/close"
participant LVGL as "LVGL Containers"
participant Persist as "NVS"
participant QBank as "trivia_questions.h"
User->>Script : Launch trivia
Script->>Game : open(UI with root/hud/board/panel/fonts)
Game->>Persist : persist_load()
Game->>LVGL : build_board_ui()/build_panel_ui()/build_hud_ui()
Game->>QBank : init_bags() shuffle per category
loop tick()
Game->>Game : handle states/phases
Game->>LVGL : update UI (cached)
Game->>Persist : persist_save() periodically
end
User->>Game : close()
Game->>Persist : persist_save()
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Board Topology and Movement
- Nodes: 0–41 on the outer ring, 42–71 on spokes, 72 as the hub.
- Cell types: ordinary category cells, HQ category cells (grant wedges), “roll again” cells, and the hub (final challenge or category choice when missing wedges).
- Neighbors computed per node type to allow movement along ring edges and spokes without backtracking during a turn.
- Screen coordinates calculated from angles and radii for accurate placement.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Roll Dice"]) --> ComputeReach["Compute reachable nodes within N steps<br/>without reversing direction"]
ComputeReach --> Highlight["Highlight valid destinations"]
Highlight --> Choose{"Player taps destination?"}
Choose --> |Yes| Move["Animate pawn hop-by-hop"]
Choose --> |No| Wait["Wait for input"]
Move --> Land["Land on cell"]
Land --> Type{"Cell type?"}
Type --> |HQ| AwardWedge["Award wedge if not owned"]
Type --> |Roll| ReRoll["Immediate re-roll"]
Type --> |Hub| HubChoice{"Has all wedges?"}
HubChoice --> |Yes| Final["Final challenge"]
HubChoice --> |No| CatPick["Choose category"]
Type --> |Category| Ask["Ask question"]
AwardWedge --> NextTurn["Next turn or replay"]
ReRoll --> Start
Final --> End(["Victory?"])
CatPick --> Ask
Ask --> Result{"Correct?"}
Result --> |Yes| Replay["Replay turn"]
Result --> |No| NextTurn
```

### Question Database and Random Selection
- Data structure: compact fixed-size records with category, difficulty, question text, correct answer, and three distractors.
- Distribution: ~120 questions per category, balanced across easy, medium, and hard difficulties.
- Randomization: per-category bags are shuffled once per game using Fisher-Yates; questions drawn without replacement until exhausted.
- Difficulty filtering: masks select subsets based on configured difficulty level.

```mermaid

+next()
}
```

### Scoring and Progress Tracking
- Global stats: number of games played, correct/incorrect answers overall, per-category correctness, wedges won, best win in turns.
- Per-team progress: wedge mask (bitfield), position on board, name and color.
- Live game counters: correct/incorrect answers tracked during the current session.
- Persistence: entire save struct written to NVS with magic validation and bounds checks to prevent corruption.

## Performance Considerations
- Preallocated LVGL object pool avoids allocations during gameplay; reuse via show/hide and style updates.
- Render caches prevent redundant redraws by tracking signatures of pawns, rows, dice, and question state.
- Tick rates tuned for animations versus idle phases to balance responsiveness and CPU usage.
- No dynamic memory operations in hot paths; string formatting minimized and reused buffers used.

**Section sources**
- [trivia_game.cpp:392-490](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/trivia_game.cpp#L392-L490)
- [trivia_game.cpp:52-61](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/trivia_game.cpp#L52-L61)

## Troubleshooting Guide
- NVS corruption: load routine validates magic and clamps out-of-range values; defaults restored if invalid.
- Team names: null-terminated copies ensure safe storage; buffer sizes enforced.
- RNG seed: persisted to resume random sequence across sessions; reset to default if needed.
- IMU shake: debounced to prevent accidental triggers; can be disabled in settings.

**Section sources**
- [trivia_game.cpp:329-389](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/trivia_game.cpp#L329-L389)
- [trivia_game.cpp:289-291](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/trivia_game.cpp#L289-L291)

## Conclusion
Trial Poursuite delivers a polished, educational trivia experience with a faithful board design, robust question management, and thoughtful UI optimizations. Its modular architecture separates concerns cleanly, enabling maintainability and extensibility while running efficiently on embedded hardware. Players benefit from diverse topics, adjustable difficulty, and engaging presentation that encourages learning through play.

## Introduction
This document explains the calendar and planning system that renders a monthly 7×6 grid on the device, computes dates locally from SNTP time, and enriches each day with Home Assistant calendar data. It covers:
- Monthly grid rendering and local date math (weekday calculation, month length, today/past/weekend detection).
- Color-coded markers for work hours, public holidays, school holidays, appointments, and birthdays.
- Tap-to-detail sub-popup showing enriched day content from Home Assistant.
- Integration with multiple Home Assistant calendar entities and scripts that compute per-day codes and details.
- Date calculation algorithms, timezone handling via SNTP, and holiday detection mechanisms.
- Entity mapping, payload contracts, and relationship between work schedule data and visual indicators.
- Performance considerations for efficient rendering and synchronization with Home Assistant.

## Project Structure
The calendar spans two layers:
- Device UI and logic (LVGL + ESPHome C++):
  - UI layout for the monthly popup and day detail sub-popup.
  - Local rendering of the 7×6 grid using SNTP-based dates.
  - In-memory cache for monthly payloads with TTL and eviction.
- Home Assistant backend:
  - Scripts to fetch events from multiple calendars and push compact payloads back to the device.
  - Day detail generation for the tap-to-detail sub-popup.

## Core Components
- Monthly grid UI:
  - 7×6 grid of reusable cells with labels for day number, optional work hours, and indicator dots for appointments and birthdays.
  - Header navigation (previous/next month, “Today”) and legend explaining visual markers.
- Local rendering engine:
  - Computes weekday using an algorithm independent of system timezones.
  - Determines days-in-month including leap years.
  - Highlights today, past days, weekends, and applies background/border styles based on HA-provided codes.
- Month cache:
  - Stores per-month payloads (codes, work hours, optional embedded details) with timestamps.
  - Supports stale-while-revalidate and eviction to keep only adjacent months.
- Day detail sub-popup:
  - Shows up to six lines of enriched information for the selected day.
  - Uses embedded details when available; otherwise triggers a request to HA for on-demand enrichment.

## Architecture Overview
The system uses a split architecture:
- Device-side:
  - Renders the grid immediately using SNTP-derived dates.
  - Applies color coding and indicators from cached HA payloads.
  - Opens a day detail sub-popup on cell taps, either from embedded details or by requesting fresh data.
- Home Assistant-side:
  - Aggregates events from multiple calendar entities.
  - Produces compact payloads: per-day bitmasks and work hour ranges for the month view; structured lines for the day detail view.
  - Pushes updates back to the device via ESPHome services.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant Device as "Device UI<br/>calendar_popup.yaml"
participant Render as "Local Render<br/>cal_render_month()"
participant Cache as "Month Cache<br/>s_cal_month_cache"
participant Scripts as "ESPHome Scripts<br/>tab5-scripts.yaml"
participant HA as "HA Scripts<br/>tab5_calendar.yaml"
participant Calendars as "Calendar Entities"
User->>Device : Open calendar popup
Device->>Render : cal_render_month(view_year, view_month)
Render->>Cache : Check if month present
alt Month missing or stale
Device->>Scripts : Execute tab5_cal_render
Scripts->>HA : Call script.tab5_calendrier_mois(year, month)
HA->>Calendars : calendar.get_events(start,end)
Calendars-->>HA : Events
HA-->>Scripts : Payload (codes, heures, details?)
Scripts-->>Device : Update service call
Device->>Cache : Store month data
Device->>Render : Re-render with HA data
else Month cached
Render->>Cache : Read codes/heures/details
Render-->>Device : Apply colors, hours, dots
end
User->>Device : Tap cell
Device->>Render : cal_date_for_cell()
alt Embedded detail available
Render-->>Device : Show day detail instantly
else No embedded detail
Device->>HA : script.tab5_calendrier_jour(date)
HA-->>Device : Day detail payload
Device->>Render : cal_render_day_detail(payload)
end
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Monthly Grid Rendering and Visual Indicators
- Grid layout:
  - 42 cells arranged in 7 columns × 6 rows, Monday-first alignment.
  - Each cell includes: day number label, optional work hours label, appointment dot, birthday dot, and a transparent button to open the day detail.
- Local date math:
  - Weekday computed via an algorithm independent of system timezones.
  - Days-in-month computed with leap year rules.
  - Today detection compares view year/month/day against SNTP-derived current date.
  - Past detection compares view date against current date.
- Visual encoding:
  - Background tint for school holidays.
  - Border highlight for today.
  - Weekend dimming for Saturday/Sunday.
  - Work hours displayed inside cells; early shifts (< 9:00 start) highlighted.
  - Appointment and birthday dots shown when corresponding bits are set.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Open Month View"]) --> ComputeFirstCol["Compute first column offset<br/>weekday of 1st"]
ComputeFirstCol --> LoopCells["Loop 42 cells"]
LoopCells --> ValidDay{"Cell within month?"}
ValidDay --> |No| ClearCell["Clear text, hide dots,<br/>transparent bg/border"]
ValidDay --> |Yes| LoadCode["Load bitmask from cache"]
LoadCode --> SetNumber["Set day number"]
SetNumber --> DetectTodayPastWeekend["Detect today/past/weekend"]
DetectTodayPastWeekend --> ApplyColors["Apply number color,<br/>background tint,<br/>border highlight"]
ApplyColors --> HoursCheck{"Has work hours?"}
HoursCheck --> |Yes| ShowHours["Show HH:MM-HH:MM,<br/>early shift color if <9h"]
HoursCheck --> |No| HideHours["Hide hours"]
ShowHours --> DotsCheck{"Bits RDV/Anniv?"}
HideHours --> DotsCheck
DotsCheck --> ShowDots["Show appointment/birthday dots"]
ShowDots --> NextCell["Next cell"]
NextCell --> LoopCells
ClearCell --> NextCell
```

### Day Detail Sub-popup and On-Demand Enrichment
- Opening:
  - Tap on a cell computes the ISO date for that cell.
  - If embedded detail exists in the month cache, it is rendered instantly.
  - Otherwise, the sub-popup shows a loading status and requests HA to build detailed lines.
- Payload parsing:
  - Up to six lines, each typed (work, holiday, school holidays, appointment, birthday, civil holiday).
  - Icons and colors mapped per type; UTF-8 normalization applied.
- Fallback behavior:
  - When embedded details are absent (e.g., older HA versions or clamped event windows), the system falls back to the day script to generate lines.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant Device as "Device UI"
participant Render as "cal_date_for_cell()<br/>cal_cached_day_detail()"
participant HA as "script.tab5_calendrier_jour"
participant Parser as "cal_render_day_detail()"
User->>Device : Tap cell
Device->>Render : Get ISO date and check embedded detail
alt Embedded detail present
Render-->>Device : Return detail string
Device->>Parser : Parse and render lines
Parser-->>Device : Show icons + texts
else No embedded detail
Device->>HA : Request day detail
HA-->>Device : Payload "type|text;..."
Device->>Parser : Parse and render lines
Parser-->>Device : Show icons + texts
end
```

### Home Assistant Scripts and Calendar Entity Mapping
- Month script:
  - Queries four calendar entities over a bounded window:
    - Work calendar (events containing “Travail”).
    - Public holidays and other French holidays.
    - Family calendar (appointments).
    - Birthdays calendar.
  - Builds per-day bitmask:
    - Bit 1: Work
    - Bit 2: Public holiday
    - Bit 4: School holidays (Zone A static table)
    - Bit 8: Appointment
    - Bit 16: Birthday
  - Builds per-day work hours range (HH:MM-HH:MM) for work events starting on that day.
  - Optionally builds embedded day details (31 fields separated by ~).
  - Sends payload via ESPHome service to update the device.
- Day script:
  - Queries the same calendar entities for the selected day.
  - Produces up to six lines with typed entries and sanitized text.
  - Sends payload via ESPHome service to update the day detail sub-popup.

```mermaid
classDiagram
class HAMonthScript {
+variables : year, month
+get_events() : events[]
+build_bitmask() : codes
+build_work_hours() : heures
+build_details() : details?
+push_to_device()
}
class HADayScript {
+variables : date
+get_events() : events[]
+build_lines() : payload
+push_to_device()
}
class CalendarEntities {
+Work
+PublicHolidays
+Family
+Birthdays
}
HAMonthScript --> CalendarEntities : "queries"
HADayScript --> CalendarEntities : "queries"
```

### Date Calculation Algorithms and Timezone Handling
- Local weekday computation:
  - Uses a well-known algorithm to determine the weekday without relying on system time functions, ensuring correctness across all Gregorian dates.
- Days-in-month:
  - Includes leap year checks for February.
- Today and past detection:
  - Compares view year/month/day against SNTP-derived current date.
- Timezone handling:
  - The device relies on SNTP for accurate local time; date calculations use this time to avoid DST edge cases near midnight by normalizing to noon before computing offsets.
  - HA scripts use HA’s own timezone-aware datetime handling for event queries and boundaries.

### Holiday Detection Mechanisms
- Public holidays:
  - Filtered from the public holidays calendar by a whitelist of known holiday titles to avoid marking non-holiday civil events as holidays.
- School holidays:
  - Static table for Zone A (Bordeaux/Landes) with intervals expressed in local dates; verified against official sources and includes estimated future periods where necessary.
- Appointments and birthdays:
  - Derived from family and birthdays calendars; marked as appointments or birthdays respectively.

### Relationship Between Work Schedule Data and Visual Indicators
- Work hours:
  - Displayed inside cells as a range; early shifts (< 9:00 start) are highlighted distinctly.
- Work bit:
  - Sets the “work” flag for the day, used primarily for alarm scheduling and planning context elsewhere in the system.
- Visual hierarchy:
  - Today > Past > Holiday > Weekend > Normal for day number coloring.
  - Background tint for school holidays; border highlight for today.
  - Dots for appointments and birthdays overlay the cell corner.

## Performance Considerations
- Immediate rendering:
  - The grid is drawn locally using SNTP-derived dates so the UI remains responsive even without HA connectivity.
- Stale-while-revalidate:
  - Cached month data is displayed immediately; background refresh occurs if data is older than a threshold.
- Eviction policy:
  - Only three months (M-1, M, M+1) are kept in memory to minimize SRAM usage.
- Efficient payload formats:
  - Compact bitmask strings and delimited fields reduce network overhead and parsing cost.
- Event window bounds:
  - HA scripts bound event queries to avoid fetching unnecessary past events, improving performance.
- Pre-fetching:
  - Adjacent months are silently pre-fetched during rendering to improve navigation speed.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Calendar not updating:
  - Verify SNTP time is valid; without it, reliable date calculations cannot occur.
  - Ensure HA scripts are reachable and that calendar entities are configured correctly.
- Missing day details:
  - If embedded details are absent, the system falls back to the day script; confirm the day script runs and returns a payload.
- Incorrect holiday marking:
  - Confirm the whitelist of known holidays matches your calendar source and that events have expected titles.
- Performance issues:
  - Check cache eviction and TTL settings; ensure only adjacent months are cached.
  - Validate event query windows in HA scripts to avoid excessive data retrieval.

- [tab5-scripts.yaml:660-675](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml#L660-L675)

## Conclusion
The calendar and planning system combines robust local rendering with dynamic enrichment from Home Assistant. It delivers a responsive monthly grid with clear visual indicators for work, holidays, school breaks, appointments, and birthdays. The design emphasizes performance through caching, bounded event queries, and compact payloads, while maintaining accuracy via SNTP-based date calculations and careful timezone handling. The tap-to-detail sub-popup provides rich contextual information on demand, ensuring users can quickly understand their schedule at a glance.
