## Core Components
- Preset toggle button: Implements a toggle that sets the preset to a named value or resets to "none" when tapped again. It updates a global, triggers centralized recoloring, then calls the Home Assistant preset service.
- HVAC mode button: Sets the HVAC mode optimistically, recolors icons immediately, then calls the set_hvac_mode service.
- Temperature card: Provides +/- buttons and an arc to adjust target temperature with optimistic UI updates and debounced service calls.
- Centralized recoloring script: Reads globals for mode, preset, fan, and swing; applies active/inactive colors to all relevant icons consistently.
- Climate state update API: Receives authoritative state from Home Assistant, updates globals, and delegates to the recolor script.

## Architecture Overview
The control flow combines optimistic UI updates with authoritative state reconciliation:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant UI as "Climate Popup UI"
participant Script as "Recolor Script"
participant HA as "Home Assistant Climate"
participant API as "tab5_maj_clim"
User->>UI : Tap Preset / Fan / Swing / Windnice
UI->>UI : Update global clim_* optimistically
UI->>Script : Execute tab5_clim_recolor
UI->>HA : Call climate.set_* service
HA-->>API : Push new state (target/current/mode/preset/fan/swing)
API->>UI : Update globals and labels
API->>Script : Execute tab5_clim_recolor
Script-->>UI : Apply consistent active/inactive colors
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Preset System (Eco/Boost)
- Behavior: Tapping a preset toggles it on; tapping again returns to "none". For Daikin, "eco" maps to "away".
- Implementation: Each preset button updates a global, executes the centralized recolor script, then calls climate.set_preset_mode.
- Visual feedback: Icons are colored immediately; authoritative state later reconciles any discrepancies.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Preset Button Pressed"]) --> CheckCurrent["Read current preset global"]
CheckCurrent --> IsSame{"Is current == preset?"}
IsSame -- Yes --> SetNone["Set preset to 'none'"]
IsSame -- No --> SetPreset["Set preset to selected value"]
SetNone --> Recolor["Execute tab5_clim_recolor"]
SetPreset --> Recolor
Recolor --> CallService["Call climate.set_preset_mode"]
CallService --> End(["Done"])
```

### Fan Mode (Quiet/Auto)
- Behavior: Toggling the fan mode switches between quiet and auto.
- Implementation: Updates the fan global, triggers recoloring, then calls climate.set_fan_mode.
- Visual feedback: Icon highlights when quiet; otherwise inactive.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant UI as "Fan Button"
participant Script as "Recolor Script"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
User->>UI : Tap Quiet/Auto
UI->>UI : Toggle clim_fan_mode between "quiet" and "auto"
UI->>Script : Execute tab5_clim_recolor
UI->>HA : Call climate.set_fan_mode
HA-->>UI : Future state push via tab5_maj_clim
```

### Airflow Controls (Swing Stop/Oscillation/Windnice)
- Behavior: Two separate controls:
  - Oscillation toggles between swing and stop.
  - Windnice toggles between windnice and stop.
- Implementation: Each control updates the swing global accordingly, triggers recoloring, and calls climate.set_swing_mode.
- Manufacturer adaptation: Windnice is specific to Daikin Onecta; other manufacturers may not support it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Airflow Button Pressed"]) --> Type{"Control Type"}
Type -- Oscillation --> ToggleSwing["Toggle swing <-> stop"]
Type -- Windnice --> ToggleWindnice["Toggle windnice <-> stop"]
ToggleSwing --> Recolor["Execute tab5_clim_recolor"]
ToggleWindnice --> Recolor
Recolor --> CallService["Call climate.set_swing_mode"]
CallService --> End(["Done"])
```

### Optimistic UI Updates
- Pattern: On every user action, the UI first updates the relevant global (clim_hvac_mode, clim_preset_mode, clim_fan_mode, clim_swing_mode), then executes the centralized recolor script to highlight the active control immediately. Only after that does it send the Home Assistant service call.
- Benefit: Immediate visual feedback even if the cloud/device response is delayed.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant UI as "UI Control"
participant Global as "Global clim_*"
participant Script as "Recolor Script"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
UI->>Global : Update optimistic state
UI->>Script : Recolor icons now
UI->>HA : Send service call
Note over UI,HA : UI reflects intent instantly; authoritative state arrives later
```

### Centralized Recoloring Mechanism
- Purpose: Single source of truth for icon colors across all climate controls.
- Inputs: Current values of clim_hvac_mode, clim_preset_mode, clim_fan_mode, clim_swing_mode.
- Outputs: Active/inactive colors applied to each control’s icon; target temperature color adapts to mode (cool/heat/off).

```mermaid

+preset string
+fan string
+swing string
+applyColors() void
}
class UIControls {
+ModeIcons
+PresetIcons
+FanIcon
+SwingIcon
+WindniceIcon
}
RecolorScript --> UIControls : "sets active/inactive colors"
```

### Authoritative State Reconciliation
- Source: Home Assistant pushes climate state via tab5_maj_clim.
- Action: Updates globals (target, current, mode, preset, fan, swing), refreshes labels, and triggers the centralized recolor script to ensure UI matches device reality.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant API as "tab5_maj_clim"
participant UI as "Climate UI"
participant Script as "Recolor Script"
HA->>API : Push {target, current, mode, preset, fan, swing}
API->>UI : Update globals and labels
API->>Script : Execute tab5_clim_recolor
Script-->>UI : Apply consistent colors
```

### Device-Specific Adaptations
- Daikin Onecta:
  - Eco preset mapped to "away".
  - Windnice supported as a swing mode; separate control from general oscillation.
- Other manufacturers:
  - May not support windnice; the UI still works by toggling swing modes like "swing"/"stop".
  - Fan mode names may vary; recolor logic accounts for multiple variants (e.g., "low", "quiet", "Silence").

- UI components depend on:
  - Globals for optimistic state (clim_hvac_mode, clim_preset_mode, clim_fan_mode, clim_swing_mode)
  - Centralized recolor script for consistent visuals
  - Home Assistant services for actual device control
- Back-end depends on:
  - tab5_maj_clim to reconcile authoritative state
  - Climate entity capabilities (may vary by manufacturer)

## Performance Considerations
- Optimistic updates reduce perceived latency by updating UI immediately.
- Debounced temperature adjustments group rapid taps into a single service call to avoid flooding the backend.
- Centralized recoloring minimizes redundant UI updates by applying colors in one pass.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- If a control appears unresponsive:
  - Verify the Home Assistant climate entity supports the requested mode/preset/fan/swing.
  - Check that tab5_maj_clim is receiving and pushing state back to the device.
- Manufacturer-specific issues:
  - Windnice may not be available on non-Daikikin devices; use generic swing modes instead.
  - Fan mode names can differ; ensure your device exposes values recognized by the recolor logic (e.g., "low", "quiet", "Silence").
- Fallback behavior:
  - If a service call fails or is unsupported, the UI will still show the optimistic change until the authoritative state reconciles. If the device rejects the command, the next state push will revert the UI to the real state.

**Section sources**
- [climate_popup.yaml:212-309](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/climate_popup.yaml#L212-L309)
- [tab5-scripts.yaml:470-489](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml#L470-L489)
- [tab5-api-logic.yaml:162-198](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-api-logic.yaml#L162-L198)

## Conclusion
The climate control system uses a robust pattern of optimistic UI updates combined with centralized recoloring and authoritative state reconciliation. This ensures immediate responsiveness while maintaining consistency with the actual device state. Manufacturer-specific adaptations (like Daikin’s windnice and eco mapping) are handled gracefully, and the design allows easy extension for additional controls or device types.

## Introduction
This document provides ready-to-use examples and templates for integrating the Tab5 HMI with Home Assistant. It focuses on:
- Weather data pushing to the device
- Climate control automations
- Light management scripts and popups
- Plant monitoring setups
- Template sensors for derived values
- Automation patterns for state change detection
- The user_entities.yaml template and naming conventions
- Copy-paste-ready integration patterns for popular integrations
- Validation techniques, error handling, and troubleshooting guidance

The project uses a push-only architecture: Home Assistant detects changes and pushes updates to the device via ESPHome services. The device never polls HA; it renders last-known state when offline.

**Section sources**
- [README.md:82-158](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/README.md#L82-L158)

## Project Structure
At a high level:
- HomeAssistant_Config contains example automations, scripts, template sensors, and packages (alerts, calendar, health).
- Tab5 contains LVGL UI components, firmware configuration, and the user entity mapping file that binds HA entities to UI elements.
- docs holds troubleshooting and architectural decisions.

## Core Components
Key building blocks you will reuse across examples:
- Push automation chain: triggers on weather/climate/calendar/state changes, builds payloads, and calls ESPHome services to update the screen.
- Template sensors: compute concise strings or counts on HA side to reduce device-side logic.
- Scripts: invoked from the device to execute HA actions (e.g., toggle lights).
- Packages: reusable modules for alerts, calendar, and health monitoring.
- UI components: LVGL cards and popups bound to HA entities via user_entities.yaml.

## Architecture Overview
The system follows a push-only flow:
- HA automations detect changes and build compact payloads.
- ESPHome services receive payloads and update LVGL widgets.
- Device displays last known state when offline.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant AUT as "Automation<br/>automations_examples.yaml.example"
participant SVC as "ESPHome Services"
participant DEV as "Tab5 Firmware"
participant UI as "LVGL UI"
HA->>AUT : Trigger (weather/climate/calendar/state)
AUT->>AUT : Build payload (templates, calendars, forecasts)
AUT->>SVC : Call esphome.* services with payload
SVC->>DEV : Push data over ESPHome API
DEV->>UI : Update labels, icons, colors
Note over DEV,UI : If HA is unreachable, UI keeps last known state
```

**Diagram sources**
- [automations_examples.yaml.example:25-295](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/HomeAssistant_Config/automations_examples.yaml.example#L25-L295)
- [README.md:82-158](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/README.md#L82-L158)

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Weather Data Pushing
- Main automation triggers on weather, climate, rain sensor, time pattern, connection events, and calendar changes.
- It pushes:
  - Current weather (temperature, humidity)
  - Short-term rain intensity bars
  - Daily and hourly forecasts (bulk payloads)
  - Info banner with weather alerts and system status
- Use `continue_on_error` and `is defined` guards to avoid breaking the whole chain if one external API call fails.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Trigger"]) --> BuildWeather["Build current weather payload"]
BuildWeather --> RainBars["Build 1h rain bars (9 slots)"]
RainBars --> Daily["Fetch daily forecast + calendar events"]
Daily --> Hourly["Fetch hourly forecast"]
Hourly --> InfoBanner["Build info banner (alerts + updates + problems)"]
InfoBanner --> End(["Push to device"])
```

**Diagram sources**
- [automations_examples.yaml.example:25-295](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/HomeAssistant_Config/automations_examples.yaml.example#L25-L295)

### Climate Control Automations
- The main automation pushes climate target, current temperature, mode, preset, fan, and swing to the device.
- The climate card supports optimistic target updates and debounced set_temperature calls to avoid excessive network traffic.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant UI as "Climate Card"
participant DEV as "Firmware"
participant AUT as "Automation"
participant CLIM as "Climate Entity"
UI->>DEV : Tap +/- (optimistic UI update)
DEV->>AUT : Debounce script executes
AUT->>CLIM : Set target temperature (once per gesture)
AUT->>DEV : Push updated climate state
DEV->>UI : Refresh target and current temps
```

### Light Management Scripts and Popups
- Scripts are triggered from the device to perform HA actions (e.g., toggle lights).
- The light popup provides:
  - Light selector (room-based)
  - Brightness arc with live percentage and shortcuts
  - Color presets (named whites and color swatches)
- All actions target a dynamic entity ID resolved at runtime.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant UI as "Light Popup"
participant DEV as "Firmware"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant LIGHT as "Light Entity"
UI->>DEV : Adjust brightness arc
DEV->>HA : Debounced light.turn_on with brightness
HA-->>DEV : Acknowledge
DEV->>UI : Update arc and % label
UI->>HA : Toggle power or set color preset
```

### Integration Patterns for Popular Integrations
- Calendar: Use calendar.get_events with bounded windows and format dates explicitly to avoid validation failures.
- Weather: Use weather.get_forecasts for daily/hourly data; build bulk payloads and send via ESPHome services.
- Climate: Push target/current/mode/preset/fan/swing; use optimistic UI updates with debouncing on the device.
- Lights: Use light.toggle/turn_on with brightness/color_name; debounce rapid adjustments.
- Alerts: Use persistent notifications and notify services; track dismissed alerts to avoid repeated banners.

## Performance Considerations
- Use bulk payloads to minimize network calls (daily/hourly forecasts, rain bars).
- Add delays between service calls to avoid saturating the ESP32-P4 TCP socket while audio I2S is active.
- Format datetimes explicitly to prevent silent validation failures.
- Debounce rapid UI interactions (brightness, climate target) to reduce unnecessary HA calls.
- Offload heavy computations to templates and packages; keep firmware logic minimal.

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and fixes:
- Black screen after software reboot: add display reset delay before toggling reset_pin.
- Missing weather/planning/climate data: ensure the shared primary instance flag is ON and its guard automation is enabled.
- STT/TTS broken due to entity ID collisions: disable mirroring integration causing duplicates.
- Touch not working: enable “Allow service calls” in ESPHome integration options.
- Calendar/weather push breaks rest of automation: format datetime explicitly and add continue_on_error guards.
- ESPHome API connections exhausted: close orphaned CLI sessions holding connections.
- Device reboots periodically when HA is unreachable: adjust api reboot_timeout appropriately.
- Black screen + no network after OTA: perform a full power cycle to recover Wi-Fi co-processor link.

**Section sources**
- [troubleshooting.md:13-118](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L13-L118)
- [troubleshooting.md:131-212](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L131-L212)

## Conclusion
This guide consolidates practical examples and templates for weather pushing, climate control, light management, and plant monitoring within the Tab5 ecosystem. By following the push-only architecture, using robust templates, debounced UI interactions, and package-based helpers, you can build a responsive and resilient home automation dashboard. Always validate entity IDs, format datetimes explicitly, and leverage continue-on-error patterns to maintain reliability.

## Introduction
This guide helps you set up the M5Stack Tab5 V2 as a Home Assistant dashboard using ESPHome and LVGL. You will:
- Prepare hardware and software prerequisites
- Configure user entities and secrets
- Flash the device via USB, then update wirelessly via OTA
- Optionally test with a standalone demo script without installing Home Assistant
- Connect to Home Assistant and verify everything works
- Troubleshoot common issues like connection problems, compilation errors, and OTA failures

The project is push-only: the device never polls for data; it only reacts to service calls from Home Assistant or any client that speaks the ESPHome native API.

**Section sources**
- [README.md:82-87](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/README.md#L82-L87)

## Prerequisites Checklist
Before starting, ensure you have:
- A working Home Assistant instance (any installation method)
- ESPHome add-on or standalone CLI installed
- ESPHome version at least 2026.7.0 (enforced by the main configuration file)
- M5Stack Tab5 V2 (ESP32-P4 variant)
- Optional but commonly used:
  - Weather integration (e.g., Météo-France if you are in France)
  - Google Calendar integration (for planning screen)
  - Home Assistant Voice pipeline configured (for voice assistant features)

Expected outcome: Your environment can compile and run ESPHome projects targeting the Tab5 V2.

## Step-by-Step Installation
Follow these steps to install and flash the Tab5:

1. Clone the repository and locate the entry point
   - The main file is tab5-ha-hmi.yaml at the repository root
   - All other YAML files in Tab5/ are included as packages by this entry point

2. Create your entity substitutions file
   - Copy Tab5/user_entities.example.yaml to Tab5/user_entities.yaml
   - Replace placeholder entity IDs with your Home Assistant entities
   - These substitutions propagate throughout all packages

3. Create your secrets file
   - Create secrets.yaml at the repository root
   - Add Wi-Fi SSID/password, api_encryption_key, and ota_password
   - Generate a valid api_encryption_key using the provided Python command

4. Set up Home Assistant automations
   - Copy example files from HomeAssistant_Config/ into your Home Assistant configuration
   - Merge automations, scripts, and template sensors into your existing configuration
   - Replace placeholder entity names with your actual entities

5. First flash via USB
   - Connect the Tab5 to your computer via USB-C
   - Compile and flash using ESPHome CLI or Dashboard
   - The first flash must be done over USB; subsequent updates can use OTA

Expected outcomes after each step:
- After step 1: You have the correct entry point identified
- After step 2: Your device knows which Home Assistant entities to display
- After step 3: Your device has network credentials and security keys
- After step 4: Home Assistant can push data to your device
- After step 5: Your Tab5 is running the firmware and connected to Wi-Fi

**Section sources**
- [installation.md:23-117](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/installation.md#L23-L117)
- [user_entities.example.yaml:9-12](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/user_entities.example.yaml#L9-L12)

## Demo Mode Without Home Assistant
If you want to test the device without setting up Home Assistant, use the standalone demo mode:

1. Flash normally but keep user_entities.example.yaml unmodified
   - Copy it to user_entities.yaml without changes
   - You still need secrets.yaml with Wi-Fi credentials and api_encryption_key

2. Find your device's IP address
   - Check ESPHome dashboard, router, or use esphome logs

3. Install demo dependencies and run the script
   - Install aioesphomeapi from requirements.txt
   - Run demo_pusher.py with your device IP and encryption key
   - The script connects using the same ESPHome API library that Home Assistant uses

4. Watch the screen cycle through demo scenes
   - Weather, climate, planning, plant moisture, and alerts
   - Every ~20 seconds, different scenes are pushed to demonstrate functionality

5. Stop the script with Ctrl+C when done
   - Nothing persists outside the device itself

The demo mode is purely additive and doesn't modify any firmware files. It proves the touchscreen and UI work before investing time in full Home Assistant setup.

- [demo_mode.md:7-35](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/demo_mode.md#L7-L35)

## WiFi Configuration
WiFi settings are stored in secrets.yaml and referenced by the ESPHome configuration:

- wifi_ssid: Your Wi-Fi network name
- wifi_password: Your Wi-Fi password  
- api_encryption_key: Base64-encoded 32-byte key for secure communication
- ota_password: Password for wireless updates

Generate the encryption key using the Python command provided in the installation documentation. The device will connect to your network during the flashing process and register with ESPHome's OTA server for future updates.

Expected outcome: Your Tab5 connects to Wi-Fi and appears in your ESPHome dashboard.

**Section sources**
- [installation.md:69-86](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/installation.md#L69-L86)
- [installation.md:121-130](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/installation.md#L121-L130)

## Home Assistant Integration Setup
After flashing, configure Home Assistant to communicate with your Tab5:

1. Enable the ESPHome integration in Home Assistant
   - Your device should appear automatically once connected to Wi-Fi
   - If not, add it manually using the device's IP address

2. Copy Home Assistant configuration files
   - Move automations_examples.yaml.example content to your automations.yaml
   - Include scripts_examples.yaml in your scripts section
   - Add template_sensors_examples.yaml to your template configuration
   - Enable packages directory if using package-based configuration

3. Replace placeholder entities
   - Update city names, climate entities, calendar integrations
   - Ensure all entity IDs match your actual Home Assistant setup

4. Test the connection
   - Check that Home Assistant can see the Tab5 device
   - Verify that service calls work from Developer Tools
   - Monitor device logs for successful connections

Expected outcome: Home Assistant can push data to your Tab5, and the device responds to commands.

**Section sources**
- [HomeAssistant_Config/README.md:20-38](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/HomeAssistant_Config/README.md#L20-L38)
- [HomeAssistant_Config/README.md:118-135](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/HomeAssistant_Config/README.md#L118-L135)

## Initial Device Verification
Verify your Tab5 is working correctly with these checks:

1. Physical verification
   - Screen displays the dashboard interface
   - Touchscreen responds to taps and gestures
   - Device shows stable Wi-Fi connection in diagnostics

2. Network verification
   - Device appears in ESPHome dashboard
   - Can connect via `esphome logs` command
   - OTA updates work for subsequent flashes

3. Home Assistant verification
   - Device entity exists in Home Assistant
   - Service calls succeed from Developer Tools
   - Push notifications update the display

4. Feature verification
   - Clock and basic sensors display correctly
   - Weather data updates (if weather integration configured)
   - Climate controls respond to commands

Expected outcome: Your Tab5 is fully operational and integrated with Home Assistant.

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

### Connection Problems
**Symptom**: Device won't connect to Wi-Fi or Home Assistant
- Check that secrets.yaml contains correct Wi-Fi credentials
- Verify the device is on the same network as Home Assistant
- Ensure firewall rules allow ESPHome API port 6053
- Check for exhausted API connections from previous debugging sessions

**Fix**: 
- Regenerate api_encryption_key if corrupted
- Close orphaned `esphome logs` processes
- Restart both device and Home Assistant

### Compilation Errors
**Symptom**: ESPHome compilation fails
- Verify ESPHome version is 2026.7.0 or later
- Check that user_entities.yaml exists and is properly formatted
- Ensure all required files are included in the build

**Fix**:
- Update ESPHome to required version
- Validate YAML syntax in user_entities.yaml
- Check include paths for custom components

### OTA Flashing Failures
**Symptom**: OTA updates fail or device becomes unresponsive
- Perform a full power cycle (unplug USB-C for 15 seconds)
- Check that Wi-Fi co-processor came up successfully
- Verify network connectivity between development machine and device

**Fix**:
- Use USB cable for initial flashing if OTA fails
- Power cycle the device completely
- Check serial console output for detailed error messages

### Black Screen After Reboot
**Symptom**: Device reboots but screen stays black
- This is a known issue with the display reset sequence
- Requires a delay before resetting the display through the GPIO expander

**Fix**:
- The firmware includes a built-in delay to handle this
- If modifying boot sequences, preserve the critical delay
- Full power cycle may be necessary in some cases

### Missing Data Updates
**Symptom**: Device is online but weather/planning/climate data not updating
- Check that Home Assistant push automations are enabled
- Verify the primary active flag is turned on
- Ensure no condition guards are blocking the automation flow

**Fix**:
- Enable the shared state flag that gates push automations
- Manually trigger the push automation once
- Check for disabled guard automations that should auto-enable on HA boot

**Section sources**

## Introduction
This document provides a hardware reference for the M5Stack Tab5 V2 (ESP32-P4) implementation as used by this project. It consolidates ESP32-P4 specifications, memory architecture with PSRAM utilization, GPIO mappings for display, touch, audio, and sensors, MIPI-DSI display interface details, touch controller integration, ES8388 DAC and amplifier chain, I2C bus connections for IMU and other peripherals, power management considerations, and thermal constraints that influence software design. It also explains how the hardware abstraction layer is configured via ESPHome YAML and C++ to initialize and control components at runtime.

## Project Structure
The hardware configuration and behavior are primarily defined in:
- Low-level hardware configuration (display, touch, I2C/I2S, audio, PSRAM, hosted co-processor): tab5-hardware.yaml
- IMU sensor configuration and adaptive polling: tab5-imu.yaml
- LVGL UI layout and pages: tab5-lvgl.yaml
- Global state variables shared across modules: tab5-globals.yaml
- Runtime diagnostics and memory usage reporting: tab5_custom.cpp
- High-level hardware overview and pin references: docs/hardware.md

## Core Components
- Main processor: ESP32-P4 (RISC-V dual-core), configured to run at 360 MHz in this project; internal SRAM 768 KB; Flash 16 MB; PSRAM 16 MB (OCT-SPI).
- Co-processor: ESP32-C6 handling Wi-Fi 6 and BLE 5, connected via SDIO at 20 MHz; buffers use PSRAM to avoid internal SRAM pressure.
- Display: MIPI-DSI 16-bit RGB565, 1280×720 resolution; reset controlled through GPIO expander; update interval set to never (LVGL-driven).
- Touch: ST7123 capacitive multi-touch over I2C with interrupt-driven updates; calibration mapped to display coordinates; backlight auto-on on release.
- Audio input: ES7210 ADC streaming over I2S at 16 kHz, 16-bit mono; analog gain tuned to improve SNR before digital amplification.
- Audio output: ES8388 DAC driving stereo speaker; buffer duration increased to reduce TTS artifacts over WiFi; noise suppression disabled to preserve speech quality.
- Sensors: BMI270 IMU on I2C bus with adaptive polling rate depending on active game; tap-to-wake implemented via acceleration threshold.
- Power: USB-C powered; peak consumption can exceed 1.5A at 5V; backlight dimmable via PWM; no ambient light sensor.

## Architecture Overview
The system uses a layered approach:
- Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) via ESPHome YAML defines pins, buses, and device drivers.
- LVGL manages UI rendering using PSRAM-backed framebuffer.
- Audio pipeline integrates microphone capture (ES7210) and playback (ES8388) with Home Assistant voice assistant and wake word detection.
- IMU data drives both gameplay and tap-to-wake functionality.
- Co-processor offloads networking while main CPU focuses on UI and media.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant P4 as "ESP32-P4"
participant DSI as "MIPI-DSI Display"
participant TOUCH as "ST7123 Touch"
participant I2C as "I2C Bus"
participant IMU as "BMI270 IMU"
participant I2S as "I2S Audio"
participant MIC as "ES7210 ADC"
participant DAC as "ES8388 DAC"
participant C6 as "ESP32-C6 (Wi-Fi/BLE)"
P4->>DSI : Initialize MIPI-DSI (RGB565)
P4->>TOUCH : Configure ST7123 (I2C + IRQ)
P4->>I2C : Setup bus (GPIO31/32 @400kHz)
I2C->>IMU : Poll accelerometer/gyro
P4->>I2S : Start mic capture (16kHz/16bit)
I2S->>MIC : Stream audio data
P4->>I2S : Start speaker playback (48kHz/16bit)
I2S->>DAC : Output audio to speaker
P4-->>C6 : SDIO traffic (Wi-Fi/BLE)
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### ESP32-P4 Specifications and Memory Architecture
- CPU: RISC-V dual-core, configured to 360 MHz for stable OTA and performance balance.
- Internal SRAM: 768 KB, insufficient for full framebuffer at 1280×720 RGB565 (~1.8 MB).
- External PSRAM: 16 MB OCT-SPI, critical for LVGL framebuffer and large buffers.
- Flash: 16 MB for firmware and assets.
- PSRAM mode: hex, speed 200 MHz for optimal bandwidth.

Memory optimization techniques:
- Framebuffer stored entirely in PSRAM to prevent tearing and enable 60 FPS rendering.
- SDIO buffers for co-processor communication placed in PSRAM to free internal SRAM.
- Wake word task stack allocated in PSRAM to save ~3 KB internal SRAM.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:9-21](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L9-L21)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:84-86](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L84-L86)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:290-296](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L290-L296)
- [hardware.md:11-22](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L11-L22)

### MIPI-DSI Display Interface
- Resolution: 1280×720 pixels, RGB565 color format.
- Interface: MIPI-DSI with 16-bit pixel mode.
- Reset control: Via GPIO expander (PI4IOE5V6408) for reliable boot sequence.
- Update strategy: Manual updates only (update_interval: never) to avoid tearing.
- Calibration: Touch coordinates mapped to display dimensions.

Boot sequence considerations:
- Display reset pin requires stabilization time after GPIO expander initialization.
- Blocking delay ensures reliable display startup after software restarts.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:116-129](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L116-L129)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-79](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L79)

### Touch Controller Integration (ST7123)
- Platform: Official ESPHome ST7123 component.
- Interrupt-driven: Uses GPIO23 for touch interrupts to reduce polling overhead.
- Calibration: Maps touch coordinates to display resolution (0-720 X, 0-1280 Y).
- Auto-backlight: Turns on backlight when screen is touched while off.
- Polling: Initial polling stops once interrupt is attached.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:130-149](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L130-L149)

### Audio System - ES8388 DAC and Amplifier Chain
- DAC platform: Native ESPHome ES8388 driver.
- Speaker output: Stereo I2S audio at 48 kHz, 16-bit.
- Buffer duration: 500ms to handle network latency during TTS streaming.
- Noise suppression: Disabled to preserve speech quality for Whisper recognition.
- Amplifier enable: Software-controlled to prevent pop sounds during boot.

Audio routing:
- Media player configured for FLAC format at 24 kHz to match both local Piper and cloud TTS engines.
- Announcement pipeline prioritizes speaker output for voice responses.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:199-220](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L199-L220)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:242-288](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L242-L288)
- [hardware.md:43-68](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L43-L68)

### Microphone Input - ES7210 ADC
- ADC platform: ES7210 external ADC over I2S.
- Capture format: 16 kHz, 16-bit mono matching wake word and voice assistant requirements.
- Analog gain: 30 dB to improve signal-to-noise ratio before digital processing.
- DC offset correction: Enabled to remove any DC bias from ES7210 output.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:170-197](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L170-L197)
- [hardware.md:72-83](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L72-L83)

### I2C Bus and Sensor Connections
- Bus configuration: GPIO31 (SDA), GPIO32 (SCL) at 400 kHz.
- IMU (BMI270): Address 0x68, accelerometer range 4G, gyroscope range 2000DPS.
- Adaptive polling: 100 Hz when idle, 33 Hz during active games for responsive tilt controls.
- Tap-to-wake: Acceleration magnitude threshold >2.5g with 500ms debounce.

Sensor data flow:
- Accelerometer axes processed locally for game input and tap detection.
- Pitch, roll, and temperature published to Home Assistant with 60-second throttling.

### Power Management and Thermal Considerations
- Power source: USB-C, minimum 5V/2A charger recommended due to peak consumption exceeding 1.5A.
- Backlight control: Software dimming via PWM reduces power consumption; auto-on on touch interaction.
- Thermal monitoring: CPU temperature exposed as diagnostic sensor.
- Safe mode: Configured with 10 attempts and 30-second boot validation window.

Power optimization techniques:
- Backlight dimming through Home Assistant controls.
- Adaptive IMU polling reduces sensor overhead when not gaming.
- PSRAM usage prevents internal SRAM exhaustion during high-load scenarios.

## Performance Considerations
- Display performance: PSRAM-backed framebuffer enables smooth 60 FPS LVGL rendering without tearing.
- Audio quality: Increased buffer duration (500ms) compensates for network latency during TTS streaming over WiFi.
- Memory optimization: Wake word task stack moved to PSRAM, saving ~3KB internal SRAM.
- Sensor efficiency: Adaptive IMU polling reduces CPU load during non-gaming periods.
- Network stability: TCP window size increased to 16KB for more reliable OTA updates.

Runtime monitoring:
- Memory usage displayed in console showing SRAM and PSRAM utilization percentages.
- CPU temperature and WiFi RSSI available for system diagnostics.

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and solutions:

### Display Black Screen After Restart
- Cause: Display reset pin via GPIO expander requires stabilization time after boot.
- Solution: Blocking delay ensures GPIO expander stabilizes before display reset.
- Prevention: Maintain blocking delay in boot sequence; do not rely on non-blocking delays.

### Audio Pop During Boot
- Cause: Amplifier enable fires before I2S clock is stable.
- Solution: Proper boot sequencing turns on backlight first, sets volume, then enables amplifier.
- Prevention: Follow documented boot order in ESPHome configuration.

### Memory Exhaustion
- Symptoms: System crashes or freezes during heavy UI operations.
- Monitoring: Use console to check SRAM and PSRAM usage percentages.
- Optimization: Ensure framebuffers and large buffers use PSRAM; monitor memory trends.

### Touch Not Responding
- Check: Verify interrupt pin (GPIO23) is properly configured.
- Calibration: Ensure touch coordinates match display resolution mapping.
- Power: Confirm backlight is on (touch triggers backlight activation if off).

- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-79](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L79)
- [hardware.md:58-68](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L58-L68)
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1760-1787](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1760-L1787)

## Conclusion
The M5Stack Tab5 V2 implementation leverages the ESP32-P4's capabilities with careful attention to memory management, audio quality, and user experience. The combination of PSRAM for graphics, optimized audio buffering, and adaptive sensor polling creates a responsive embedded system suitable for home automation and interactive applications. The hardware abstraction layer through ESPHome provides a clean separation between hardware configuration and application logic, enabling maintainable and extensible code organization.

Key success factors include proper boot sequencing, adequate power supply, and continuous monitoring of system resources. The modular architecture allows for easy upgrades and feature additions while maintaining system stability.

## Appendices

### Configuration Parameters Reference
- CPU frequency: 360 MHz (balanced performance/stability)
- PSRAM speed: 200 MHz (hex mode)
- I2C bus: 400 kHz (optimal for all connected devices)
- Display: 1280×720 RGB565 (MIPI-DSI)
- Audio input: 16 kHz, 16-bit mono (ES7210)
- Audio output: 48 kHz, 16-bit stereo (ES8388)
- Network: SDIO 20 MHz (ESP32-C6 co-processor)

### Hardware Limitations Influencing Software Design
- Limited internal SRAM necessitates PSRAM usage for graphics and large buffers
- Network-dependent TTS requires robust buffering to handle latency variations
- Sensor polling must be adaptive to balance responsiveness with power consumption
- Boot sequence timing is critical for display and audio reliability

## Introduction
This document explains the brightness control system centered on a 320px LVGL arc gauge with live percentage display. It covers:
- The LVGL arc implementation and smooth user interactions
- Value range and mapping from 0–255 to percentage
- Real-time feedback during drag operations
- Debounced update mechanism using tab5_debounce_light_brightness to prevent excessive network calls
- Four preset shortcut buttons (10%, 35%, 65%, 100%) with immediate visual feedback and service call optimization
- Arc styling, knob behavior, and performance considerations for embedded hardware

## Project Structure
The brightness control is implemented as part of the light popup UI and coordinated by scripts and C++ helpers:
- UI definition and LVGL widgets are declared in light_popup.yaml
- Debounce logic and Home Assistant service calls are defined in tab5-scripts.yaml
- Synchronization between HA state and LVGL widgets is handled in tab5_custom.cpp
- Visual styles and color tokens are centralized in tab5-styles.yaml

```mermaid
graph TB
A["User Interaction<br/>Arc + Preset Buttons"] --> B["LVGL Arc Widget<br/>(light_popup.yaml)"]
B --> C["on_value Handler<br/>Update % Label + Execute Debounce Script"]
C --> D["Debounce Script<br/>(tab5-scripts.yaml)"]
D --> E["Home Assistant Service<br/>light.turn_on(entity_id, brightness)"]
F["HA State Updates<br/>(brightness sensor)"] --> G["C++ Sync Helper<br/>(tab5_custom.cpp)"]
G --> B
```

## Core Components
- 320px LVGL arc gauge with adjustable knob and live percentage label
- Debounced script that coalesces rapid value changes into a single Home Assistant call
- Preset shortcut buttons for quick brightness levels with immediate UI updates
- C++ synchronization helper that keeps the arc and label in sync with HA state without interfering with user interaction

Key responsibilities:
- UI: Define arc, label, and preset buttons; handle on_value events
- Scripts: Debounce and issue light.turn_on with current brightness
- C++: Update LVGL elements from HA state while avoiding conflicts during drag

## Architecture Overview
The brightness control follows a clear separation of concerns:
- LVGL handles input and rendering
- ESPHome scripts manage timing and network calls
- C++ ensures consistent UI state with backend data

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant U as "User"
participant L as "LVGL Arc<br/>(light_popup.yaml)"
participant S as "Debounce Script<br/>(tab5-scripts.yaml)"
participant H as "Home Assistant"
participant C as "Sync Helper<br/>(tab5_custom.cpp)"
U->>L : Drag knob / Tap preset
L->>L : Update % label immediately
L->>S : Execute debounce script
Note over L,S : Each tick restarts delay
S-->>H : After idle, call light.turn_on(brightness)
H-->>C : Push brightness state change
C->>L : Update arc + label if not dragging
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### LVGL Arc Gauge and Live Percentage
- Arc dimensions: 320x320 pixels
- Value range: 0–255 (mapped to percentage for display)
- Live percentage label updates instantly on every value change
- The arc is adjustable and styled with a track color and indicator color
- Knob is fully opaque with padding for comfortable touch interaction

Behavior highlights:
- on_value handler formats and sets the percentage text
- Triggers debounced script to avoid flooding Home Assistant during drag

**Section sources**
- [light_popup.yaml:154-189](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml#L154-L189)

### Debounced Update Mechanism (tab5_debounce_light_brightness)
Purpose:
- Prevent excessive network calls during continuous dragging
- Ensure only one light.turn_on is sent after the user stops interacting

Mechanism:
- Each value change restarts a 200ms delay
- When the delay completes (user is idle), the script reads the current arc value and calls light.turn_on with the entity and brightness
- Uses dynamic entity resolution via current_light_entity

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Value Change"]) --> Restart["Restart 200ms Delay"]
Restart --> Idle{"Idle for 200ms?"}
Idle --> |No| Restart
Idle --> |Yes| CallHA["Call light.turn_on<br/>with current brightness"]
CallHA --> End(["Done"])
```

**Diagram sources**
- [tab5-scripts.yaml:370-381](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml#L370-L381)

**Section sources**
- [tab5-scripts.yaml:370-381](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml#L370-L381)

### Preset Shortcut Buttons (10%, 35%, 65%, 100%)
Functionality:
- Immediate visual feedback by updating the arc value and percentage label
- Optimized service call using brightness_pct to set exact percentages
- Each button targets the currently selected light entity

Interaction flow:
- User taps a preset
- UI updates instantly (arc + label)
- Home Assistant service is called with the corresponding brightness percentage

**Section sources**
- [light_popup.yaml:192-271](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml#L192-L271)

### C++ Synchronization Helper
Role:
- Keeps the LVGL arc and percentage label synchronized with Home Assistant brightness state
- Avoids overriding user interaction during drag to prevent knob jumping

Key behaviors:
- Guards against updating when popup is hidden or arc is being pressed
- Converts brightness values to arc values and percentage strings
- Ensures safe updates even with NaN or out-of-range values

**Section sources**
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1646-1665](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1646-L1665)

### Arc Styling and Knob Behavior
Styling details:
- Track color uses a dedicated token for consistency across controls
- Indicator color provides visual feedback for current brightness level
- Knob is fully opaque with padding for better touch target size
- Arc width is set to provide clear visual indication of progress

Visual design principles:
- Consistent use of theme tokens for colors
- Clear contrast between track and indicator
- Touch-friendly knob sizing and spacing

## Performance Considerations
Optimizations for smooth operation on embedded hardware:

- **Debouncing**: Prevents network flooding during drag operations by coalescing multiple value changes into a single service call
- **Immediate UI Feedback**: Percentage label updates instantly without waiting for network responses
- **Conditional Updates**: C++ sync helper avoids unnecessary updates during user interaction
- **Efficient Rendering**: LVGL arc widget is optimized for smooth dragging with minimal layout recalculations
- **Memory Management**: Uses stack-based buffers and efficient string formatting to minimize memory pressure

Best practices observed:
- Separate concerns between UI updates and network calls
- Use debouncing for expensive operations
- Provide immediate visual feedback for better user experience
- Guard against race conditions between user interaction and state synchronization

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and solutions:

**Arc not responding to drag:**
- Check if the arc widget is properly configured as adjustable
- Verify that the popup is visible and not hidden
- Ensure LVGL initialization completed successfully

**Excessive network calls:**
- Confirm debounce script is executing correctly
- Verify that the 200ms delay is working as expected
- Check for any code paths that might bypass the debounce mechanism

**UI state desynchronization:**
- Review C++ sync helper logic for proper guards during drag operations
- Ensure Home Assistant state updates are reaching the device
- Check for any null pointer issues in the sync functions

**Preset buttons not updating correctly:**
- Verify that the correct entity ID is being used
- Check that both UI updates and service calls are executing
- Ensure brightness percentage values are within valid ranges

- [light_popup.yaml:154-189](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml#L154-L189)

- [tab5_custom.cpp:1646-1665](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1646-L1665)

## Conclusion
The brightness control system provides a responsive and efficient interface for controlling light brightness through an intuitive arc gauge. Key strengths include:

- **Smooth User Experience**: Immediate visual feedback with debounced network calls
- **Robust Implementation**: Proper handling of edge cases and user interaction states
- **Performance Optimization**: Efficient resource usage suitable for embedded hardware
- **Maintainable Architecture**: Clear separation between UI, logic, and state management

The system successfully balances real-time responsiveness with network efficiency, providing users with a natural and predictable brightness control experience while minimizing the impact on system resources and network traffic.

## Introduction
This document explains the color management system used by the Tab5 light control popup. It covers:
- Three named white presets (warmwhite, navajowhite, white) and their place on the color temperature spectrum from warm to cool whites.
- The 12 round color swatches arranged in a 4x3 grid and how they are implemented via a reusable component.
- How colors map to Home Assistant light services using color_name.
- Visual feedback mechanisms for selection and interaction.
- How colors are applied to the currently selected light entity.
- Color ordering logic across the palette.
- Accessibility considerations for contrast and readability.
- Extensibility guidance for adding custom color presets.

## Project Structure
The color management UI is centered around a modal popup that groups three glass cards:
- AMPOULE (left): selects one of three lights and toggles power or turns all off.
- LUMINOSITÉ (center): brightness arc with live percentage and shortcuts.
- COULEURS (right): three named whites and a 4x3 grid of 12 round color swatches.

```mermaid
graph TB
A["Light Popup<br/>light_popup.yaml"] --> B["AMPOULE Card<br/>Selection + Power"]
A --> C["LUMINOSITÉ Card<br/>Arc + % + Shortcuts"]
A --> D["COULEURS Card<br/>Whites + 4x3 Swatches"]
D --> E["Reusable Button<br/>light_color_preset_btn.yaml"]
E --> F["Home Assistant Service<br/>light.turn_on with color_name"]
```

## Core Components
- Named white presets: warmwhite, navajowhite, white. These are sent as color_name to Home Assistant’s light.turn_on service to set the light’s color temperature.
- Reusable color preset button: a 78px round button template that renders a colored swatch and calls light.turn_on with a given color_name against the current light entity.
- 4x3 grid of 12 color swatches: gold, orange, orangered, red, deeppink, magenta, blueviolet, purple, blue, cyan, springgreen, green. Each swatch includes a visible icon_color for UI contrast and a color_name for the actual light effect.

Key behaviors:
- All actions target id(current_light_entity), which is set when opening the popup so the same UI controls any of the three lights without hardcoding entities.
- The popup synchronizes title, selector highlight, power icon, and brightness arc via script.tab5_light_popup_show.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Named White Presets (Warm to Cool Spectrum)
- warmwhite: Warm white preset mapped to Home Assistant color_name.
- navajowhite: Mid-warm white preset mapped to Home Assistant color_name.
- white: Cool white preset mapped to Home Assistant color_name.

These three buttons sit at the top of the COULEURS card and provide quick access to common color temperatures. They use the same pattern as other controls: call light.turn_on with color_name against the current light entity.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Open COULEURS Card"]) --> Warm["Tap 'Chaud' (warmwhite)"]
Start --> Cream["Tap 'Crème' (navajowhite)"]
Start --> Cool["Tap 'Froid' (white)"]
Warm --> HA["Home Assistant light.turn_on(color_name='warmwhite')"]
Cream --> HA2["Home Assistant light.turn_on(color_name='navajowhite')"]
Cool --> HA3["Home Assistant light.turn_on(color_name='white')"]
HA --> Light["Apply to current_light_entity"]
HA2 --> Light
HA3 --> Light
```

**Diagram sources**
- [light_popup.yaml:285-339](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml#L285-L339)

- [light_popup.yaml:285-339](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml#L285-L339)

### 12 Round Color Swatches (4x3 Grid)
- Layout: Flex layout wrapping rows with even spacing; each row contains four swatches.
- Swatches: gold, orange, orangered, red, deeppink, magenta, blueviolet, purple, blue, cyan, springgreen, green.
- Each swatch is an instance of the reusable preset button with two variables:
  - color_name: the Home Assistant color name applied to the light.
  - icon_color: the hex color used for the UI swatch to ensure visibility and contrast on the dark background.

Ordering rationale:
- The sequence moves from warm hues through reds and pinks into purples/blues, then to cyan/greens, providing a perceptually smooth transition across the hue wheel. This supports intuitive exploration from warm to cool tones.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Row1["Row 1: Gold → Orange → OrangeRed → Red"]
Row2["Row 2: DeepPink → Magenta → BlueViolet → Purple"]
Row3["Row 3: Blue → Cyan → SpringGreen → Green"]
Grid["4x3 Grid Layout"]
Grid --> Row1
Grid --> Row2
Grid --> Row3
```

### Reusable light_color_preset_btn Component
- Dimensions: 78x78 px with radius 39 px to form a perfect circle.
- Background: Uses icon_color for the swatch fill.
- Border: Glass-style rim with opacity for subtle contrast.
- Pressed state: Reduces background opacity and switches border color to text color for clear visual feedback.
- Action: Calls homeassistant.service light.turn_on with entity_id resolved from current_light_entity and data.color_name set to the provided color_name.

This component centralizes styling and behavior, enabling consistent swatches across the grid and easy maintenance.

```mermaid
classDiagram

+width : 78
+height : 78
+radius : 39
+bg_color : icon_color
+border_width : 2
+border_color : color_glass_rim
+pressed.bg_opa : 55%
+pressed.border_color : color_text
+on_short_click()
}
class LightPopup {
+includes LightColorPresetButton x12
}
LightPopup --> LightColorPresetButton : "reuses via !include"
```

### HSV Color Space Implementation Notes
- The UI does not implement HSV conversion directly in YAML. Instead, it uses Home Assistant’s color_name parameter to apply named colors to lights.
- The icon_color values are chosen for UI contrast and do not need to match the exact light output color; they serve as visual indicators.
- For advanced HSV-based palettes, you would typically compute HSV values in C++ or a script and pass corresponding color_name or RGB values to Home Assistant. In this implementation, the palette is curated as a fixed set of names and display colors.

[No sources needed since this section provides conceptual guidance]

### Applying Colors to Selected Lights
- The current light entity is stored in a global variable and set when the popup opens.
- All color actions target this dynamic entity, ensuring the correct light receives the command regardless of which light was selected.

### Visual Feedback Mechanisms
- Swatch pressed state reduces background opacity and changes border color to improve affordance.
- Selector highlights and power icon recoloring are managed by sensors and scripts to reflect real-time states.
- Brightness arc updates percentage label live during interaction and debounces service calls.

### Color Ordering Logic
- The 12 swatches follow a hue progression from warm to cool:
  - Warm start: gold, orange, orangered, red
  - Transition: deeppink, magenta, blueviolet, purple
  - Cool end: blue, cyan, springgreen, green
- This order supports intuitive navigation and predictable discovery of color families.

**Section sources**
- [light_popup.yaml:341-368](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml#L341-L368)

### Accessibility Considerations
- Contrast: icon_color values are chosen to remain legible on the dark background; borders use a glass-style rim with opacity to enhance visibility.
- Text labels: secondary labels use a dimmed text token for hierarchy while maintaining readability.
- State feedback: pressed states adjust opacity and border color to clearly indicate interaction.
- Tokens: semantic color tokens (e.g., color_text, color_text_dim, color_glass_rim) ensure consistent contrast across the UI.

**Section sources**
- [light_color_preset_btn.yaml:10-19](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_color_preset_btn.yaml#L10-L19)

### Extensibility: Adding Custom Color Presets
To add a new preset:
- Add a new !include line in the COULEURS card with a new color_name and an appropriate icon_color for UI contrast.
- Ensure the color_name is supported by your Home Assistant light integration.
- Optionally, insert the new swatch into the ordered sequence to maintain a logical hue progression.

Example steps:
- Insert a new swatch entry in the grid section of the COULEURS card.
- Choose a color_name recognized by your lights.
- Pick an icon_color that contrasts well with the dark background.

## Performance Considerations
- Debounced brightness updates prevent excessive service calls during drag interactions.
- Using a single reusable button component reduces duplication and simplifies rendering.
- Targeting a dynamic entity avoids repeated entity resolution in each swatch.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and checks:
- Wrong light receiving color: Verify current_light_entity is set correctly when opening the popup.
- Color not applied: Ensure the color_name is supported by the light integration.
- Poor visibility: Adjust icon_color for better contrast against the dark background; verify border and pressed states are configured.
- State mismatch: Confirm sensors update power icon and selector highlights based on light state.

## Conclusion
The color management system provides a clean, reusable interface for selecting named whites and a curated palette of 12 colors. It leverages Home Assistant’s color_name to apply effects to the currently selected light, with strong visual feedback and accessible design. The modular component approach makes it straightforward to extend the palette and maintain consistency across the UI.

## Introduction
This document explains the Home Assistant service integration layer for light control on the Tab5 device. It covers how user interactions trigger Home Assistant services, how entity IDs are resolved dynamically using lambda expressions, and how brightness and color presets are applied. It also documents the configuration of light entities, status synchronization between device and Home Assistant, error handling considerations, and common troubleshooting steps.

## Project Structure
The light control integration spans several files:
- The main ESPHome entry point includes packages and substitutions that bring in user-defined entity IDs.
- User-configurable entity mappings live in a local file to keep production IDs out of version control.
- The light popup UI defines service calls for toggle, turn_on with brightness_pct, and color_name presets.
- Scripts debounce brightness adjustments and centralize state synchronization logic.
- C++ helpers update UI elements based on current light states and selected targets.

```mermaid
graph TB
A["tab5-ha-hmi.yaml"] --> B["Tab5/user_entities.yaml"]
A --> C["Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml"]
A --> D["Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml"]
D --> E["Tab5/ui_components/light_color_preset_btn.yaml"]
C --> F["Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp"]
B --> D
B --> C
```

**Diagram sources**

## Core Components
- Light popup UI: Provides controls to toggle lights, adjust brightness via an arc, set preset brightness levels, and select named colors. All actions target a dynamic entity stored in a global variable rather than hard-coded IDs.
- Debounce script: Ensures only one brightness adjustment is sent after the user stops dragging the brightness arc, preventing service call spam.
- Entity resolution: Uses lambda expressions to resolve the currently selected light entity at runtime, enabling a single popup to control multiple lights.
- Status synchronization: C++ functions update UI icons and labels based on real-time light states pushed from Home Assistant.

Key implementation highlights:
- Toggle uses the light.toggle service against the current entity.
- Brightness presets use light.turn_on with brightness_pct.
- Color presets use light.turn_on with color_name.
- Brightness arc triggers a debounced service call to avoid excessive updates.

## Architecture Overview
The system follows a push-only architecture where Home Assistant pushes state changes to the device. Device interactions initiate service calls to Home Assistant, which then propagate back state updates to refresh the UI.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant UI as "Light Popup (ESPHome)"
participant Script as "Debounce Script"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant Device as "Light Entities"
User->>UI : Adjust brightness arc
UI->>Script : Execute debounce script
Script->>HA : Call light.turn_on<br/>entity_id=current_light_entity<br/>brightness=arc_value
HA-->>Device : Apply brightness
HA-->>UI : Push updated brightness/state
UI->>UI : Update arc and percentage label
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Light Popup Controls and Service Calls
- Toggle: When the power button is pressed, the popup calls light.toggle on the current light entity.
- Brightness presets: Buttons send light.turn_on with brightness_pct values (e.g., 10%, 35%, 65%, 100%).
- Named colors: Preset buttons send light.turn_on with color_name values such as warmwhite, navajowhite, white, plus additional color presets via a reusable component.

All service calls resolve entity_id through a lambda that returns the current light entity, ensuring the same popup can control different lights without duplication.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["User Action"]) --> Choice{"Action Type?"}
Choice --> |Toggle| ToggleCall["Call light.toggle<br/>entity_id=current_light_entity"]
Choice --> |Brightness Preset| BrightnessCall["Call light.turn_on<br/>entity_id=current_light_entity<br/>brightness_pct=<value>"]
Choice --> |Color Preset| ColorCall["Call light.turn_on<br/>entity_id=current_light_entity<br/>color_name=<name>"]
ToggleCall --> End(["Done"])
BrightnessCall --> End
ColorCall --> End
```

### Dynamic Entity Resolution with Lambda Expressions
- The popup sets a global variable to the selected light entity when opened or when switching tabs.
- Every service call references this variable via a lambda expression, allowing a single UI to control multiple lights dynamically.
- This pattern avoids hard-coding entity IDs in the UI and supports reusing components across different contexts.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Popup as "Light Popup"
participant Script as "Show Popup Script"
participant Global as "current_light_entity"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
Popup->>Script : Open popup with light_idx
Script->>Global : Set current_light_entity = selected entity
Popup->>HA : Service call with entity_id=lambda(current_light_entity)
HA-->>Popup : State updates reflected in UI
```

### Brightness Arc Debouncing and Service Calls
- Dragging the brightness arc updates the UI immediately and triggers a debounce script.
- The debounce script waits until the user stops adjusting before sending a single light.turn_on service call with the final brightness value.
- This reduces network traffic and prevents rapid repeated service calls during interaction.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
DragStart["Arc Value Changed"] --> UpdateUI["Update % Label"]
UpdateUI --> Debounce["Execute Debounce Script"]
Debounce --> Wait["Wait for Idle"]
Wait --> SendCall["Send light.turn_on<br/>with brightness"]
SendCall --> End(["Service Sent"])
```

## Performance Considerations
- Debouncing brightness adjustments reduces unnecessary service calls and network usage.
- Push-only architecture minimizes polling overhead; however, it requires reliable automation flows to keep the UI synchronized.
- Using a single popup with dynamic entity resolution avoids duplicating service calls and keeps UI logic centralized.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and mitigations:
- If service calls appear rejected by Home Assistant, ensure the ESPHome integration allows service calls for this device.
- If the UI becomes stale, check that push automations are enabled and not blocked by shared flags or conditions.
- If brightness adjustments do not apply, verify the debounce script is executing and the current light entity is correctly set.
- For multi-entity operations, confirm all entity IDs are valid and reachable in Home Assistant.

**Section sources**
- [troubleshooting.md:43-49](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L43-L49)
- [troubleshooting.md:23-29](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L23-L29)

## Conclusion
The light control integration leverages a clean separation between UI, scripting, and state synchronization. Dynamic entity resolution via lambda expressions enables flexible control of multiple lights through a single interface. Debouncing ensures efficient service calls, while push-based updates maintain UI consistency. Proper configuration of entity IDs and attention to Home Assistant service permissions are essential for reliable operation.

## Introduction
This document describes the light management system that provides a near-fullscreen popup for multi-light control and color management. The popup is organized into three glass cards:
- AMPOULE (left): 3-light selector (Chambre, Salon, LEDs), On/Off toggle for the selected light, and a “Turn all off” action affecting all three lights simultaneously.
- LUMINOSITÉ (center): a live brightness arc with percentage display and four shortcut buttons (10%, 35%, 65%, 100%).
- COULEURS (right): three named white presets (warm, cream, cool) plus a 4×3 grid of twelve round color swatches.

The system supports simultaneous control of multiple entities via group actions, maintains state synchronization between Home Assistant and the UI, and uses debounced updates to ensure smooth interactions and efficient service calls.

## Project Structure
The light management system spans UI components, scripts, globals, sensors, and C++ helpers:
- UI layer: modal popup and three glass cards defined in YAML.
- Control logic: scripts handle opening/syncing the popup and debouncing brightness changes.
- State: global variables track the currently selected light entity.
- Sensors: Home Assistant entity bindings push state changes back to the UI.
- C++ helpers: centralize LVGL updates, brightness sync, and popup rendering.

## Core Components
- Popup container and modal shell: near-fullscreen overlay with header and scrim.
- Three glass cards:
  - AMPOULE: selector buttons for Chambre/Salon/LEDs; power toggle for current selection; “Tout éteindre” for all three.
  - LUMINOSITÉ: adjustable arc (0–255), live percentage label, and four preset shortcuts.
  - COULEURS: three named whites and twelve color swatches using a reusable button template.
- Scripted popup show/sync: sets title, highlights selected light, updates power icon and brightness arc from real HA state.
- Debounced brightness update: single service call after user interaction stabilizes.
- Entity mapping: configurable entity IDs for each light.
- Sensor-driven state sync: pushes state and brightness updates back to UI.

## Architecture Overview
The system follows a clear separation of concerns:
- UI defines widgets and events in YAML.
- Scripts orchestrate popup lifecycle and debounced actions.
- Globals hold shared state (current light entity).
- Sensors bridge Home Assistant states to UI updates.
- C++ functions encapsulate LVGL updates and complex UI logic.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant UI as "Popup UI"
participant Script as "Scripts"
participant Global as "Globals"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant Sensors as "Sensors"
participant Cpp as "C++ Helpers"
User->>UI : Long press light card or select light
UI->>Script : Execute tab5_light_popup_show(light_idx)
Script->>Global : Set current_light_entity
Script->>Cpp : show_light_popup_ui(...)
Cpp-->>UI : Update title, selector highlight, power icon, arc
UI->>HA : light.toggle / light.turn_on / light.turn_off
HA-->>Sensors : State/brightness updates
Sensors->>Cpp : sync_light_popup_brightness(...)
Cpp-->>UI : Update arc and % if popup open and not dragging
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Multi-Light Control and Group Management
- Selector: Three buttons switch the active light without closing the popup. Each triggers script.tab5_light_popup_show with an index.
- Power toggle: Targets id(current_light_entity) so the same UI controls any of the three lights.
- Group action: “Tout éteindre” sends light.turn_off to all three configured entities at once.
- Entity mapping: Configured in user_entities.yaml and referenced by scripts and sensors.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Open Popup"]) --> Select["Select Light Index"]
Select --> SetEntity["Set current_light_entity"]
SetEntity --> SyncUI["Sync Title, Highlight, Power Icon, Arc"]
SyncUI --> Action{"User Action?"}
Action --> |Toggle| Toggle["light.toggle on current_light_entity"]
Action --> |All Off| AllOff["light.turn_off on all three entities"]
Action --> |Brightness| Bright["Debounced brightness update"]
Action --> |Color| Color["light.turn_on with color_name"]
Bright --> End(["Update UI via sensors"])
Color --> End
Toggle --> End
AllOff --> End
```

### Brightness Arc Implementation
- Arc range: 0–255 mapped to percentage display.
- Live feedback: Percentage label updates immediately on value change.
- Debounce: A 200ms delay ensures only one light.turn_on is sent after the drag ends.
- Sync: If the popup is open and not being dragged, sensor updates adjust the arc to reflect actual brightness.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
DragStart["Arc value changed"] --> UpdateLabel["Update % label"]
UpdateLabel --> Debounce["Start 200ms debounce"]
Debounce --> Idle{"Still idle?"}
Idle --> |No| Debounce
Idle --> |Yes| SendService["Call light.turn_on with brightness"]
SendService --> WaitSync["Wait for sensor update"]
WaitSync --> SyncArc["sync_light_popup_brightness updates arc if not dragging"]
```

### Color Picker Integration and Preset Management

### Debounced Update Mechanisms
- Brightness debounce: Ensures a single service call per interaction, improving responsiveness and reducing network load.
- Volume debounce: Similar pattern used elsewhere to avoid spamming devices during continuous adjustments.
- Centralized helper: Uses a restartable script to reset delays on each tick.

```mermaid
Script->>Script : delay(200ms)
Script->>HA : light.turn_on(entity_id=current_light_entity, brightness=arc_value)
```

## Dependency Analysis
- UI depends on scripts for lifecycle and debounced actions.
- Scripts depend on globals for current context and C++ helpers for UI updates.
- Sensors depend on Home Assistant entities and push updates to C++ helpers.
- C++ helpers encapsulate LVGL operations, ensuring no direct LVGL calls from YAML.

```mermaid
Script --> Cpp["tab5_custom.cpp"]
Sensors["tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml"] --> Cpp
Sensors --> UI
Entities["user_entities.yaml"] --> Script
Entities --> Sensors
```

## Performance Considerations
- Debounced brightness updates prevent excessive service calls during drags, improving responsiveness and reducing network overhead.
- Sensor-driven sync avoids UI jumps by skipping updates while the user is actively dragging the arc.
- Reusable templates reduce UI complexity and improve maintainability.
- Centralized C++ helpers minimize direct LVGL calls from YAML, keeping UI logic cohesive and efficient.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Popup not updating brightness: Ensure the popup is open and not currently being dragged; sensor updates will sync automatically otherwise.
- Incorrect light targeted: Verify current_light_entity is set correctly when opening the popup via script.tab5_light_popup_show.
- Color not applied: Confirm the light supports color_name and the entity is reachable.
- Group action not working: Check that all three entity IDs are valid and accessible in user_entities.yaml.

- [tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml:156-189](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml#L156-L189)
- [tab5-scripts.yaml:631-655](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml#L631-L655)
- [user_entities.yaml:13-16](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/user_entities.yaml#L13-L16)

## Conclusion
The light management system provides a robust, user-friendly interface for controlling multiple lights with precise brightness and color management. Its architecture separates UI, logic, state, and hardware integration, ensuring maintainability and performance. Debounced updates and sensor-driven synchronization deliver smooth interactions and accurate feedback, while reusable components simplify future enhancements.

## Introduction
This document explains the light popup interface component: a near-fullscreen modal that presents three glass cards for controlling lights on a 1280×720 display. It covers the modal header, the three-card layout (Ampoule, Luminosité, Couleurs), lifecycle and animation behavior, integration with the shared modal shell, responsive positioning, touch interactions, state synchronization with Home Assistant, and how it is opened from the main dashboard via long-press gestures.

## Project Structure
The light popup is composed of reusable UI components and scripts:
- The popup container defines a scrim, a centered modal card, and a shared header.
- Three glass cards are laid out horizontally inside the modal body.
- A color preset button template is reused to build a grid of color swatches.
- Opening/closing and state sync are coordinated by ESPHome scripts and C++ helpers.

## Core Components
- Modal shell:
  - Scrim: full-screen overlay with configurable opacity; tapping closes the popup.
  - Header: compact title bar with icon, dynamic title label, and close button; body starts below the header with reserved spacing.
  - Modal card: centered near-fullscreen container sized by tokens.
- Cards:
  - Ampoule: selects one of three lights, toggles power, and offers “turn all off”.
  - Luminosity: adjustable arc gauge with live percentage and four shortcut levels.
  - Colors: named white presets plus a 4×3 grid of color swatches using a reusable button template.
- Reusable elements:
  - Color preset button template renders a circular swatch and applies the selected color name to the current light entity.

Key behaviors:
- All actions target the currently selected light entity rather than hard-coded IDs, enabling reuse across multiple lights.
- Live brightness updates refresh both the arc and the percentage label; debouncing ensures a single Home Assistant call per gesture.

## Architecture Overview
The light popup integrates tightly with the shared modal shell and the dashboard’s gesture system:
- Dashboard triggers open via long-press on forecast day cards or internal selectors.
- A script sets the active light entity, reads HA state, and synchronizes UI elements before showing the popup.
- C++ animation helpers provide consistent open/close transitions.
- Closing can be triggered by the header close button or by tapping the scrim.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant U as "User"
participant D as "Dashboard (forecast_daily)"
participant S as "Script (tab5_light_popup_show)"
participant UI as "Popup UI (light_popup)"
participant A as "Animation (C++)"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
U->>D : Long-press light tile
D->>S : Execute script with light_idx
S->>UI : Set current_light_entity<br/>Sync title, selection, power icon, arc
S->>A : animate_popup_open(card, scrim)
A-->>UI : Show scrim + card
U->>UI : Adjust brightness / choose color
UI->>HA : light.turn_on / light.toggle (debounced)
U->>UI : Tap scrim or Close
UI->>A : animate_popup_close(card, scrim)
A-->>UI : Hide scrim + card
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Modal Shell and Header
- Scrim:
  - Full-screen button with configurable opacity; short click executes a provided close lambda.
  - Supports stacking scenarios with lower opacity when nested.
- Header:
  - Compact 52 px title bar with icon, title label, and close button aligned vertically by LVGL.
  - Body starts at a token-defined y-offset to ensure consistent spacing.
  - Close button executes a provided close lambda.

```mermaid
flowchart TD

Icon --> Title["Render title label"]
Title --> CloseBtn["Render close button"]
CloseBtn --> Click{"Short click?"}
Click --> |Yes| ExecClose["Execute close_lambda"]
Click --> |No| End(["Idle"])
```

Behavioral notes:
- Selection highlight and icon colors are synchronized by the show script and HA sensors.
- All actions target the dynamic current light entity to keep the popup reusable.

- Shortcuts:
  - Four buttons set quick brightness levels and update the arc and label immediately.

Debouncing:
- Brightness changes are debounced so only one Home Assistant call is sent after the user stops interacting.

Timing characteristics:
- Open duration uses a tuned constant for responsiveness.
- Close duration is shorter to make dismissal feel snappy.

## Performance Considerations
- Debounced brightness updates reduce unnecessary Home Assistant calls during continuous adjustments.
- Shared modal chrome avoids duplicate style allocations and keeps rendering efficient.
- Using a single scrim and header template minimizes object creation and simplifies layout calculations.
- Live updates are limited to necessary widgets (arc and label), avoiding full redraws.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Popup does not open:
  - Verify long-press handlers on forecast cards are present and call the show script with a valid light index.
  - Ensure the show script receives a valid index and that the current light entity is set before UI sync.
- Incorrect light controlled:
  - Confirm the current light entity is updated by the show script before any action is executed.
- Brightness not updating:
  - Check that the arc value change triggers the debounce script and that the percentage label is updated.
- Header close not working:
  - Ensure the close lambda is correctly passed to the header include and that the animation helper is available.

**Section sources**
- [forecast_daily.yaml:170-262](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/forecast_daily.yaml#L170-L262)

- [modal_header.yaml:1-58](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/modal_header.yaml#L1-L58)

## Conclusion
The light popup delivers a cohesive, near-fullscreen control surface for lights using a consistent modal shell and three focused glass cards. Its design emphasizes reusability (shared header/scrim, templated color swatches), responsiveness (debounced controls, optimized animations), and tight integration with the dashboard through long-press gestures and centralized state synchronization. The architecture keeps configuration modular while ensuring a uniform user experience across different lights and contexts.

## Introduction
This document explains the multi-light selection system that provides a unified, context-aware light control popup for three lights: Chambre (Bedroom), Salon (Living Room), and LEDs (Office). It covers the three-light selector architecture, dynamic entity mapping via user configuration, selection highlighting with cyan borders, real-time icon recoloring based on Home Assistant states, and the synchronization performed by script.tab5_light_popup_show to keep titles, highlights, power icons, and brightness arcs consistent with actual device states.

## Project Structure
The system is composed of:
- A configurable entity map that binds logical names to actual Home Assistant entities
- A shared popup UI component that renders controls for all three lights without duplication
- Scripts that open and synchronize the popup state from Home Assistant
- Sensors that push live updates for light states and brightness attributes
- C++ helpers that update LVGL widgets consistently
