## Core Components
- Dynamic entity mapping: The file user_entities.yaml defines the three light entities used throughout the system. These are referenced as substitutions across scripts and sensors so you can customize per installation without changing logic code.
- Popup UI: light_popup.yaml defines the modal with three glass cards: AMPOULE (selector + power + “all off”), LUMINOSITÉ (brightness arc + % + shortcuts), and COULEURS (named whites + color swatches). All actions target id(current_light_entity) to operate on the currently selected light.
- Script integration: script.tab5_light_popup_show sets current_light_entity, reads HA states for each light, and calls show_light_popup_ui to render title, selection highlight, power icon, and brightness arc.
- Real-time updates: tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml listens to light state and brightness attribute changes and updates both card icons and popup elements via C++ helpers.
- C++ helpers: tab5_custom.cpp centralizes UI updates for selector icons, brightness arc, and popup rendering, ensuring consistent behavior across all triggers.

## Architecture Overview
The popup is context-aware and shared across three lights. Opening or switching within the popup goes through a single script entry point that synchronizes UI with Home Assistant states. Live updates flow from Home Assistant back into the UI via sensor callbacks and C++ helpers.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant UI as "light_popup.yaml"
participant Script as "tab5-scripts.yaml<br/>script.tab5_light_popup_show"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant Helpers as "tab5_custom.cpp"
participant Sensors as "tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml"
User->>UI : Long press / select light
UI->>Script : Execute with light_idx
Script->>HA : Read states (on/off, brightness)
Script->>Helpers : show_light_popup_ui(light_idx, titles, is_on[], brightness[])
Helpers-->>UI : Update title, selector border (cyan), power icon, arc
Note over UI,Helpers : Popup now reflects current light context
loop Live updates
HA-->>Sensors : State/brightness change
Sensors->>Helpers : update_light_card_ui / sync_light_popup_brightness
Helpers-->>UI : Recolor icons, update arc/percentage
end
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Three-Light Selector Architecture
- The selector presents three options: Chambre, Salon, LEDs. Each option button executes script.tab5_light_popup_show with a specific index (0, 1, 2).
- The script maps indices to titles and entity IDs using arrays derived from user_entities.yaml substitutions. It sets a global current_light_entity to scope subsequent actions.
- The same popup handles all three lights; there is no duplicated logic per light.

Key behaviors:
- Title updates to match the selected light
- Selector buttons receive a cyan border when selected
- Power icon color reflects the selected light’s on/off state
- Brightness arc initializes from the selected light’s brightness attribute

**Section sources**
- [light_popup.yaml:55-101](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/light_popup.yaml#L55-L101)
- [tab5-scripts.yaml:631-655](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml#L631-L655)
- [user_entities.yaml:13-16](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/user_entities.yaml#L13-L16)

### Dynamic Entity Mapping
- user_entities.yaml defines the concrete Home Assistant entity IDs for the three lights. These are injected into scripts and sensors via ESPHome variable substitution.
- Changing these mappings allows customization per installation without touching logic files.

Example mapping keys:
- entity_light_chambre
- entity_light_salon
- entity_light_bureau

**Section sources**
- [user_entities.yaml:13-16](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/user_entities.yaml#L13-L16)

### Selection Highlighting Mechanism (Cyan Borders)
- When show_light_popup_ui is called, it iterates over the three selector buttons and applies:
  - Border width and opacity differences between selected and unselected
  - Border color set to an accent color for the selected item (cyan-like) and a neutral rim for others
- This visual cue clearly indicates which light is active in the popup.

**Section sources**
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1667-1703](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1667-L1703)

### Real-Time Icon Recoloring Based on Light States
- For each light, a Home Assistant text_sensor monitors the on/off state. On change, it calls update_light_card_ui to:
  - Color room and light icons appropriately
  - Toggle icon glyph between on/off
  - Update switch label and color
  - If this light matches current_light_entity, also update the popup’s power icon color
- Additionally, update_light_selector_icon is called to recolor the corresponding selector icon in the popup.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml:128-154](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml#L128-L154)
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1413-1435](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1413-L1435)
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1639-1644](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1639-L1644)

### Brightness Arc Synchronization
- At popup open, script.tab5_light_popup_show reads brightness values for all three lights and passes them to show_light_popup_ui, which sets the arc value and percentage label for the selected light.
- During interaction, the brightness arc triggers a debounced service call to adjust brightness after the user stops dragging.
- While the popup is open, brightness attribute updates from Home Assistant are pushed back to the UI via sync_light_popup_brightness, which avoids interfering with user drags.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Arc Value Change"]) --> UpdateLabel["Update % label"]
UpdateLabel --> Debounce["Debounce delay"]
Debounce --> CallHA["Call light.turn_on with brightness"]
CallHA --> End(["Done"])
HAUpdate["Brightness attribute update from HA"] --> CheckPopup{"Popup visible?"}
CheckPopup --> |No| Skip["Skip update"]
CheckPopup --> |Yes| CheckDrag{"Arc being dragged?"}
CheckDrag --> |Yes| Skip
CheckDrag --> |No| SyncArc["sync_light_popup_brightness()"]
SyncArc --> SetArc["Set arc value and % label"]
SetArc --> End
```

### script.tab5_light_popup_show Integration
- Purpose: Centralized entry point to open or switch the light context inside the popup.
- Responsibilities:
  - Validate light_idx
  - Set current_light_entity to the chosen light
  - Read on/off states and brightness for all three lights
  - Call show_light_popup_ui to render title, selector highlights, power icon, and brightness arc
- Triggers:
  - Long press on daily forecast cards for each light
  - Internal selector buttons within the popup

**Section sources**
- [tab5-scripts.yaml:631-655](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-scripts.yaml#L631-L655)

### Entity Configuration in user_entities.yaml
- Defines the three light entities used by the system:
  - entity_light_chambre
  - entity_light_salon
  - entity_light_bureau
- These IDs are substituted into scripts and sensors, enabling per-installation customization without modifying logic.

**Section sources**
- [user_entities.yaml:13-16](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/user_entities.yaml#L13-L16)

### Handling Different Light Types and Capabilities
- The system operates on standard Home Assistant light entities and their common attributes:
  - State: on/off
  - Attribute: brightness (0–255)
- Actions sent to Home Assistant:
  - light.toggle on current_light_entity
  - light.turn_on with brightness_pct or brightness
  - light.turn_off for multiple entities at once
- Named white presets and color swatches use light.turn_on with color_name, allowing compatibility with lights supporting named colors.

## Performance Considerations
- Debounced brightness updates prevent flooding Home Assistant during slider drags, sending a single command after the gesture ends.
- Live brightness sync avoids updating while the user is dragging to prevent knob jumping.
- Reusing a single popup component reduces UI overhead and ensures consistent behavior across lights.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Popup not reflecting correct light:
  - Ensure current_light_entity is set by script.tab5_light_popup_show before actions.
  - Verify user_entities.yaml maps to valid Home Assistant light entities.
- Icons not recoloring:
  - Confirm light_*_state sensors are receiving updates and calling update_light_card_ui and update_light_selector_icon.
- Brightness arc not updating:
  - Check that light_*_brightness attribute sensors are present and trigger sync_light_popup_brightness only when the popup is visible and not being dragged.
- Actions applied to wrong light:
  - Ensure all actions target id(current_light_entity) rather than hardcoded entity IDs.

# Moisture Dashboard Card

## Introduction
This document explains the moisture dashboard card that displays up to 5 BLE plant sensors in a compact, responsive layout. The card uses a dynamic 4-slot system so users always see the most critical plants first:
- Slot 0: driest sensor
- Slot 1: second driest sensor
- Slot 2: median-ranked sensor (labeled “Moy:”)
- Slot 3: wettest sensor

The sorting and UI updates are performed by `sort_and_update_moisture_slots()` whenever any of the five moisture sensors update. Visual indicators include plant icons, color-coded moisture levels, and text labels for pot identity or median status.

## Project Structure
The moisture dashboard is composed of:
- A YAML-defined LVGL card with four fixed slots (icons + value labels).
- A C++ function that sorts current sensor values and assigns them to slots.
- Sensor bindings that trigger the sort/update on each moisture reading.
- Color mapping functions that encode dry/optimal/wet states visually.

```mermaid
graph TB
HA["Home Assistant Sensors<br/>moisture_1..moisture_5"] --> Bind["YAML on_value anchor<br/>&moisture_on_value"]
Bind --> Sort["sort_and_update_moisture_slots()<br/>tab5_custom.cpp"]
Sort --> Slots["LVGL Slot Widgets<br/>icon_pot_sN / val_pot_sN"]
Sort --> Colors["get_humidity_color()<br/>dry=red, optimal=green, wet=blue"]
Slots --> Card["Moisture Card<br/>350x80px, 4 slots"]
```

- [tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml:261-301](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml#L261-L301)

## Core Components
- Dynamic 4-slot card: defined in YAML as a row of four 90x80px widgets, each containing an icon label and a value label.
- Sorting logic: `sort_and_update_moisture_slots()` filters valid readings, sorts them ascending, selects representative indices (driest, second driest, median, wettest), and updates slot icons and labels.
- Color coding: `get_humidity_color()` maps moisture percentage to semantic colors: red for dry, green for optimal, blue for too wet; NaN returns inactive gray.
- Integration: Each moisture sensor triggers the same lambda via `&moisture_on_value`, which calls the sorting function and also refreshes the detail popup.

Key responsibilities:
- YAML defines static UI structure and binds sensor events.
- C++ performs data-driven decisions (sorting, selection, coloring).
- LVGL renders icons and labels based on updated properties.

## Architecture Overview
The moisture dashboard follows a clear separation between configuration (YAML), logic (C++), and rendering (LVGL):

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant S as "Sensor Entity"
participant Y as "YAML on_value"
participant F as "sort_and_update_moisture_slots()"
participant C as "get_humidity_color()"
participant L as "LVGL Labels"
S-->>Y : new moisture value
Y->>F : vals[5], icons[5], slots[4]
F->>F : filter valid, sort ascending
F->>F : select indices (driest, 2nd driest, median, wettest)
loop for each slot
F->>C : color = get_humidity_color(value)
C-->>F : color
F->>L : set icon text (plant icon)
F->>L : set label text ("Pot N" or "Moy : ")
F->>L : apply color to icon and dim color to label
end
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### 4-Slot Layout System
The card is a horizontal flex container with four equal-width slots. Each slot contains:
- An icon label showing a plant icon from a predefined set.
- A value label showing either “Pot N” (for specific pots) or “Moy:” (median slot).

Slot semantics:
- Slot 0: driest sensor
- Slot 1: second driest sensor
- Slot 2: median-ranked sensor labeled “Moy:”
- Slot 3: wettest sensor

The YAML defines these slots statically; their content is dynamically assigned by C++.

**Section sources**
- [moisture_sensors.yaml:14-64](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/moisture_sensors.yaml#L14-L64)

### Sorting and Assignment Logic
`sort_and_update_moisture_slots()`:
- Filters out invalid (NaN) values.
- Sorts valid values in ascending order (driest to wettest).
- Selects indices for display:
  - Driest: index 0
  - Second driest: index 1
  - Median: middle index with safeguards against duplicates
  - Wettest: last index
- Updates each slot’s icon and label accordingly.

Edge cases:
- Fewer than 4 valid sensors: empty slots are cleared and styled inactive.
- Duplicate indices avoided for median when necessary.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Function Entry"]) --> Filter["Filter valid values (ignore NaN)"]
Filter --> Sort["Sort ascending (driest to wettest)"]
Sort --> Select{"Number of valid sensors"}
Select --> |>=4| Pick4["Pick indices: 0, 1, n/2, n-1<br/>Avoid duplicate median"]
Select --> |==3| Pick3["Pick indices: 0, 1, 1, 2"]
Select --> |==2| Pick2["Pick indices: 0, 0, 1, 1"]
Select --> |==1| Pick1["Pick indices: 0, 0, 0, 0"]
Pick4 --> UpdateSlots["Update icons and labels per slot"]
Pick3 --> UpdateSlots
Pick2 --> UpdateSlots
Pick1 --> UpdateSlots
UpdateSlots --> End(["Function Exit"])
```

**Diagram sources**
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1709-1791](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1709-L1791)

### Visual Indicators
- Icons: Plant icons are chosen from a fixed array and assigned to slots based on the underlying sensor identity.
- Color coding:
  - Red: dry (low moisture)
  - Green: optimal range
  - Blue: too wet (high moisture)
  - Gray/inactive: unavailable (NaN)
- Text formatting:
  - Pot slots show “Pot N” where N is the sensor number.
  - Median slot shows “Moy:”.
  - Values are not shown directly in the dashboard slots; only identity and status are presented.

Color thresholds are implemented in `get_humidity_color()`.

### Responsive Design and Integration
- Card dimensions: 350x80px, optimized for compact dashboards.
- Layout: Flex row with even spacing ensures consistent slot sizing.
- Integration points:
  - Triggered by any moisture sensor update via YAML anchor.
  - Also updates the detail popup for comprehensive sensor metrics.

The design prioritizes clarity and quick scanning: critical plants appear first, with visual cues indicating urgency.

## Performance Considerations
- Sorting algorithm: Bubble sort over at most 5 elements is efficient and simple.
- Memory usage: Avoids heavy allocations; uses small buffers and stack-based parsing patterns elsewhere in the codebase.
- UI updates: Only relevant slots are refreshed, minimizing redraw overhead.
- Color computation: Direct mapping without complex calculations.

These choices ensure responsiveness on constrained hardware while maintaining clarity.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and resolutions:
- Empty slots: Occurs when fewer than 4 valid sensors are available; handled by clearing labels and styling inactive.
- Incorrect colors: Verify moisture values are within expected ranges; NaN results in inactive gray.
- Icon mismatch: Ensure icons array aligns with sensor order in the lambda.
- No updates: Confirm YAML anchor is bound to all five sensors and triggers the sorting function.

Validation steps:
- Check sensor states in Home Assistant.
- Inspect LVGL widget IDs match those passed to the sorting function.
- Validate color thresholds in `get_humidity_color()`.

## Conclusion
The moisture dashboard card provides a concise, dynamic view of up to 5 BLE plant sensors, prioritizing critical plants through intelligent sorting and clear visual indicators. Its design balances simplicity and functionality, ensuring users can quickly assess plant health and take appropriate action. The separation of concerns between YAML configuration, C++ logic, and LVGL rendering promotes maintainability and scalability.

## Introduction
This document explains the plant monitoring system implemented on the Tab5 device, focusing on BLE soil moisture sensors and their visualization. The system displays up to five BLE plant sensors on a dashboard card with dynamic sorting by moisture level and color-coded indicators (red for dry, green for optimal, blue for too wet). A long-press opens a detail popup with five fixed glass cards per sensor showing moisture percentage, watering status, fertility (EC µS/cm), light levels (lx), temperature, and battery status. Data flows from Home Assistant into the device via a push-only architecture; the firmware reacts to updates and refreshes UI elements without polling.

## Project Structure
The plant monitoring feature spans UI components, ESPHome sensor wiring, and C++ logic:
- UI components define the layout for the moisture card and the detail popup.
- ESPHome YAML wires BLE-derived entities to LVGL labels through lambdas.
- C++ implements sorting, color mapping, and metric formatting.

## Core Components
- Moisture dashboard card: four slots dynamically filled by sensor rank (driest, second driest, median-ranked sensor labeled “Moy:”, wettest). Icons and values are updated whenever any moisture entity changes.
- Detail popup: five fixed glass cards (one per sensor) opened by long press, each showing moisture %, watering status, EC, lux, temperature, and battery.
- Sensor wiring: ESPHome platform: homeassistant entries for moisture_1..5 and per-metric entities (ec, lux, temp, bat) trigger lambdas that call C++ update functions.
- Color and thresholds: humidity color gradient maps dry/optimal/wet ranges; watering status thresholds align with the same red zone used for alerts.

Key responsibilities:
- Dynamic sorting and slot assignment: sort_and_update_moisture_slots()
- Popup moisture/status update: update_pots_popup_moisture_ui()
- Metric formatting and coloring: update_pot_metric_ui(), get_humidity_color(), get_temperature_color(), get_battery_color()

## Architecture Overview
The system uses a push-only data flow: Home Assistant detects state changes and pushes them to the device via ESPHome services. The firmware is reactive and updates LVGL widgets directly.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant ESP as "ESPHome (tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml)"
participant FW as "C++ (tab5_custom.cpp)"
participant UI as "LVGL UI"
HA->>ESP : State change on moisture_N or pot_N_*
ESP->>FW : Lambda calls sort_and_update_moisture_slots / update_pot_metric_ui
FW->>UI : Update icons, labels, colors (dashboard slots + popup cards)
Note over HA,UI : No polling from device; one-directional push
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Dashboard Moisture Card
- Displays four slots filled by ranking available sensors by moisture value.
- Slot mapping:
  - Slot 0: driest sensor
  - Slot 1: second driest
  - Slot 2: median-ranked sensor (labeled “Moy:”)
  - Slot 3: wettest sensor
- Each slot shows the sensor’s icon and its physical pot number (or “Moy:” for median). Colors reflect moisture level using get_humidity_color().

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Any moisture_N update"]) --> Collect["Collect values[5] from moisture_1..5"]
Collect --> Filter{"Valid values?"}
Filter --> |Yes| Sort["Sort ascending (bubble sort)"]
Sort --> Select["Select indices: 0, 1, n/2, n-1<br/>avoid duplicates"]
Select --> UpdateSlots["Update 4 LVGL slots:<br/>icon, label, color"]
Filter --> |No| Empty["Clear slots / inactive style"]
UpdateSlots --> End(["Done"])
Empty --> End
```

### Detail Popup (Long Press)
- Triggered by long press on the moisture card area.
- Shows five fixed glass cards (card N corresponds to sensor moisture_N), each displaying:
  - Pot name and plant icon colored by moisture level
  - Soil moisture % and watering status: OK (green), Bientôt sec (≤20%, amber), À arroser ! (≤14%, red), Hors ligne (unavailable)
  - Four metrics: Fertility (EC µS/cm), Light (lx), Temperature (°C), Battery (%)
- Values are pushed continuously via lambdas calling update_pots_popup_moisture_ui() and update_pot_metric_ui().

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant UI as "LVGL"
participant ESP as "ESPHome"
participant FW as "C++"
User->>UI : Long press moisture card
UI-->>User : Show pots_detail_popup (5 fixed cards)
loop On each sensor update
ESP->>FW : update_pots_popup_moisture_ui(values[5], cards[5])
FW->>UI : Set icon color, moisture %, status text/color
ESP->>FW : update_pot_metric_ui(label, value, metric)
FW->>UI : Format and color EC/lux/temp/battery
end
```

### Color Coding and Thresholds
- Humidity color gradient:
  - ≤14%: ALERT_RED (dry)
  - 14–22%: yellow-green transition
  - 22–30%: cyan-blue transition
  - ≥30%: blue range toward wet
  - ≥80%: HUMIDITY_WET (too wet)
- Watering status thresholds aligned with humidity color:
  - ≤14%: “À arroser !” (red)
  - ≤20%: “Bientôt sec” (amber)
  - >20%: “OK” (green)
- Temperature and battery use dedicated color helpers for visual cues.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
V["Moisture value v"] --> CheckDry{"v <= 14?"}
CheckDry --> |Yes| Red["ALERT_RED"]
CheckDry --> |No| CheckWet{"v >= 80?"}
CheckWet --> |Yes| Wet["HUMIDITY_WET"]
CheckWet --> |No| Mid["Gradient between 14..30 and 30..80"]
Mid --> Blue["Blue tones (optimal -> wet)"]
```

### Data Refresh Mechanisms
- Every time any moisture_N entity updates, a shared lambda collects all five moisture values, sorts them, and updates both the dashboard slots and the popup cards.
- Per-metric entities (ec, lux, temp, bat) call update_pot_metric_ui() to format and color individual labels.
- The device never polls; it reacts to pushes from Home Assistant.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant ESP as "ESPHome"
participant FW as "C++"
participant UI as "LVGL"
HA->>ESP : moisture_N state change
ESP->>FW : sort_and_update_moisture_slots(vals, icons, slots)
FW->>UI : Update dashboard slots (icons, labels, colors)
FW->>UI : Update popup cards (moisture %, status)
HA->>ESP : pot_N_ec/lux/temp/bat state change
ESP->>FW : update_pot_metric_ui(label, value, metric)
FW->>UI : Format and color metric label
```

### Entity Mapping and Template Sensors
- Entities:
  - moisture_1..5 map to ${entity_plante_N}
  - pot_N_ec, pot_N_lux, pot_N_temp, pot_N_bat map to derived or raw BLE-backed entities for each sensor
- Template sensors:
  - Example template usage demonstrates pre-processing on the Home Assistant side to keep firmware simple and within constraints (e.g., short strings, avoiding large payloads).
  - While this example focuses on weather, the same pattern applies to plant-related templates if needed.

### Alerting and Health Monitoring
- Low battery:
  - Battery values are formatted and colored via get_battery_color(); low thresholds highlight warnings/errors.
- Abnormal readings:
  - Unavailable or NaN values display “--” and inactive styling; popup status shows “Hors ligne”.
- Alerts pipeline:
  - Home Assistant maintains an alert queue and dismissal mechanism; the device can request dismissal events and update UI accordingly.
  - Unavailable count template helps surface broader connectivity issues.

## Performance Considerations
- Sorting algorithm: bubble sort over at most five elements is negligible in CPU cost.
- Push-only architecture avoids polling, minimizing Wi-Fi radio wake-ups and CPU usage when nothing changes.
- Formatting and color calculations are lightweight operations executed only on state changes.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Missing or stale data:
  - If moisture values show “--” or popup status reads “Hors ligne,” check Home Assistant entity availability and push automations.
- Incorrect sorting or duplicate slots:
  - Ensure all five moisture entities exist and report numeric values; invalid/NaN values are filtered out during sorting.
- Battery warnings:
  - Low battery thresholds are visually indicated; verify sensor battery entity updates and consider replacing batteries.
- Alert dismissal:
  - Use the provided scripts to dismiss alerts and re-trigger the screen update automation.

## Conclusion
The plant monitoring system integrates BLE-derived moisture and environmental data into a clear, responsive UI. Dynamic sorting highlights the driest and wettest plants, while the detail popup provides comprehensive per-sensor insights. The push-only architecture ensures efficient operation, and robust color coding and thresholds aid quick interpretation. For reliable communication in embedded environments, ensure consistent Home Assistant pushes, handle unavailable states gracefully, and leverage template processing to keep firmware lightweight.

## Introduction
This document explains the sensor detail popup that appears when long-pressing a moisture sensor card on the dashboard. It covers the modal architecture built from reusable components, the five fixed glass cards per sensor, data binding from BLE/Home Assistant entities to UI widgets, interactive behaviors (close, refresh), navigation across multiple sensors, error handling for disconnected sensors, performance optimizations for smooth scrolling, and accessibility and responsive design considerations.

## Project Structure
The popup is composed of:
- A full-screen modal container with a scrim overlay and a header bar
- Five fixed glass cards, one per sensor, each showing key metrics
- C++ logic that binds live sensor values to labels and status indicators

```mermaid
graph TB
A["pots_popup.yaml<br/>Modal shell"] --> B["modal_scrim.yaml<br/>Tap-to-close overlay"]
A --> C["modal_header.yaml<br/>Icon + title + close button"]
A --> D["pot_detail_card.yaml x5<br/>Fixed glass cards"]
D --> E["LVGL labels:<br/>moisture, status, EC, lux, temp, battery"]
F["tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml<br/>Sensor entities & on_value"] --> G["tab5_custom.cpp<br/>update_pots_popup_moisture_ui / update_pot_metric_ui"]
G --> E
```

## Core Components
- Modal shell: Full-screen container with hidden state by default; includes a scrim and header; hosts five pot detail cards at fixed positions.
- Scrim: Full-screen button with configurable opacity; closes the popup on tap via a lambda callback.
- Header: Reusable header bar with icon, title label, and a close button wired to the same close lambda.
- Pot detail card: Template included five times with variables for index, position, name, and plant icon; contains labels for moisture percentage, watering status, fertility (EC µS/cm), light (lux), temperature (°C), and battery (%).

Key responsibilities:
- pots_popup.yaml composes the modal and instantiates the five cards.
- modal_scrim.yaml provides consistent tap-to-dismiss behavior.
- modal_header.yaml standardizes header chrome and close action.
- pot_detail_card.yaml defines the visual layout and widget IDs bound by C++.
- tab5_custom.cpp updates UI elements based on sensor values and handles states like offline/disconnected.

## Architecture Overview
The popup follows a clear separation between declarative UI (YAML) and imperative updates (C++):
- YAML declares structure, styles, and event handlers (e.g., close button tap).
- C++ functions receive sensor values and push them into LVGL labels and colors.
- Data flows from Home Assistant/BLE entities through ESPHome triggers into C++ helpers that update the UI.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant User as "User"
participant Dashboard as "Dashboard Card"
participant Popup as "pots_popup.yaml"
participant Scrim as "modal_scrim.yaml"
participant Header as "modal_header.yaml"
participant Cards as "pot_detail_card.yaml x5"
participant Sensors as "tab5-sensors-domotique.yaml"
participant Logic as "tab5_custom.cpp"
User->>Dashboard : Long press moisture card
Dashboard->>Popup : Show modal (set visible, opaque)
Popup->>Scrim : Include scrim with close_lambda
Popup->>Header : Include header with close_btn_id and close_lambda
Note over Popup,Header : Header and Scrim share the same close action
loop Sensor updates
Sensors-->>Logic : on_value callbacks with values
Logic->>Cards : update_pots_popup_moisture_ui(values[])
Logic->>Cards : update_pot_metric_ui(label, value, metric)
end
User->>Scrim : Tap scrim
Scrim->>Popup : close_lambda -> animate_popup_close()
User->>Header : Tap close button
Header->>Popup : close_lambda -> animate_popup_close()
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Modal Shell and Navigation
- The modal container is centered, full-width/height, initially hidden, and styled as an invisible layer until opened.
- It includes:
  - A scrim overlay with configurable opacity and a tap handler that calls a close lambda.
  - A header bar with icon, title, and a close button wired to the same close lambda.
  - Five pot detail cards positioned horizontally at fixed X offsets, each representing a specific sensor (Pot 1..Pot 5).

Interactions:
- Opening: Triggered by a long press on the dashboard’s moisture card zone.
- Closing: Either tapping the scrim or pressing the header close button invokes the same animation helper to hide both card and scrim instantly for responsiveness.

**Section sources**
- [pots_popup.yaml:17-45](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/pots_popup.yaml#L17-L45)
- [modal_scrim.yaml:8-16](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/modal_scrim.yaml#L8-L16)
- [modal_header.yaml:45-57](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/modal_header.yaml#L45-L57)

### Glass Cards Layout and Metrics
Each of the five cards displays:
- Plant name and icon (colored by moisture level)
- Moisture percentage (large label)
- Watering status indicator (OK / Soon dry / Water now / Offline)
- Fertility measurement in EC µS/cm
- Light level in lux
- Temperature in °C with gradient coloring
- Battery percentage with color coding

Layout details:
- Fixed width and height, aligned top-left within the modal body area.
- Each metric section uses a transparent container with an icon, label, and value label.

**Section sources**
- [pot_detail_card.yaml:10-81](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/ui_components/pot_detail_card.yaml#L10-L81)

### Data Binding and Update Flow
- Sensor entities are defined in the sensors configuration file and trigger on_value callbacks.
- C++ functions centralize all LVGL updates:
  - update_pots_popup_moisture_ui: Updates icon color, moisture percentage text, and status text/color based on thresholds.
  - update_pot_metric_ui: Formats and colors EC, lux, temperature, and battery values; handles NaN/disconnected states.
- These functions are called from on_value lambdas in the sensors configuration, ensuring continuous synchronization without manual refresh.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Sensor value arrives"]) --> CheckNull{"Label pointer valid?"}
CheckNull --> |No| End(["Skip update"])
CheckNull --> |Yes| Metric{"Metric type"}
Metric --> |Moisture| MoistureUpdate["Set icon color, % text, status text/color"]
Metric --> |EC/Lux| FormatText["Format value string"]
Metric --> |Temperature| TempColor["Apply temperature gradient color"]
Metric --> |Battery| BatColor["Apply battery color scale"]
MoistureUpdate --> ApplyUI["lv_label_set_text + lv_obj_set_style_text_color"]
FormatText --> ApplyUI
TempColor --> ApplyUI
BatColor --> ApplyUI
ApplyUI --> End
```

### Interactive Elements
- Close button: Located in the header; invokes a lambda that calls the popup close helper.
- Scrim tap: Full-screen overlay also invokes the same close lambda.
- Refresh mechanism: No explicit refresh button; values are pushed continuously via on_value callbacks, keeping the UI up-to-date automatically.
- Navigation between sensors: The five cards are fixed to specific sensors (Pot 1..Pot 5); there is no horizontal paging within the popup.

### Error Handling for Disconnected Sensors
- When a sensor value is NaN (disconnected or invalid), the UI shows placeholder text and dims the label color to indicate inactive state.
- For moisture specifically, the status label indicates “Offline” when the value is missing.

Behavior highlights:
- Consistent fallbacks prevent crashes and provide clear user feedback.
- Colors and text are set atomically to avoid partial updates.

**Section sources**
- [tab5_custom.cpp:1805-1866](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L1805-L1866)

### Performance Optimizations
- Instant open/close: The popup opens and closes immediately without fade animations to maximize responsiveness.
- Minimal reflows: Labels are updated in place; no heavy layout changes during updates.
- Centralized updates: All LVGL modifications go through dedicated C++ helpers, reducing redundant operations and ensuring consistent styling.
- Efficient formatting: Uses small stack buffers for string formatting to minimize heap usage.

**Section sources**

### Accessibility and Responsive Design
- Accessibility:
  - Clear status text (OK / Soon dry / Water now / Offline) aids screen readers and users relying on textual cues.
  - Color-coded statuses complement text but do not replace it, supporting color-blind users.
- Responsive design:
  - The modal is full-screen and centers content; cards are fixed-width and arranged horizontally.
  - On different orientations, ensure the modal body Y offset respects header height so content does not overlap the header.
  - Keep scrollable disabled for the modal to avoid accidental scrolling; rely on fixed layout for predictability.

## Performance Considerations
- Avoid unnecessary animations on open/close to keep interactions snappy.
- Batch updates where possible; currently, each sensor triggers independent updates, which is acceptable given the lightweight nature of label changes.
- Use stack-allocated buffers for formatting to reduce memory pressure.
- Ensure that on_value handlers guard against null pointers before updating UI to prevent runtime errors during boot or teardown.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and resolutions:
- Popup does not close:
  - Verify the close lambda is correctly passed to both header and scrim.
  - Confirm the animation helper is invoked and sets the hidden flags on both card and scrim.
- Values not updating:
  - Check that on_value lambdas call the correct update functions.
  - Ensure label pointers are non-null before updates; add guards if necessary.
- Incorrect status or colors:
  - Validate threshold logic in the moisture update function.
  - Confirm metric formatting and color selection paths are executed for each metric type.

## Conclusion
The sensor detail popup provides a consistent, performant, and accessible way to inspect detailed metrics for each moisture sensor. Its modular architecture—using reusable modal components and centralized C++ update logic—ensures maintainability and clarity. Continuous data binding keeps the UI current, while robust error handling and thoughtful UX patterns deliver a reliable experience across devices and orientations.

## Introduction
This document explains the Tab5 architecture with a focus on its push-only paradigm and modular design. The device never polls Home Assistant; instead, HA automations detect state changes and call ESPHome API services to push data to the device. The firmware parses payloads and updates LVGL in one pass, minimizing CPU usage and network overhead. The system is split into multiple YAML packages by concern, plus native C++ logic for performance-sensitive operations. It runs on an ESP32-P4 with LVGL 8.4 rendering in PSRAM and uses native C++ compilation for speed. Offline resilience is built in: the device remains functional during Home Assistant outages (clock, games, diagnostics, last-known UI).

## Project Structure
The root entry point loads substitutions, defines the boot sequence, and includes all packages. Packages are organized by responsibility: tokens, hardware, sensors/diagnostics, sensors/domotique, API logic, styles, globals, scripts, LVGL layout, IMU, HA controls, and alarm clock.

```mermaid

A --> J["tab5-lvgl.yaml"]

```

## Core Components
- Push-only API layer: ESPHome services receive payloads from HA and call C++ handlers to update LVGL safely.
- Globals: Shared typed variables initialized at boot to avoid undefined behavior and gate UI updates until boot completes.
- Hardware: ESP32-P4 board, MIPI-DSI display, touch controller, I2S audio, wake word, OTA, and safe mode.
- LVGL layout: Single-page dashboard with swipe navigation, popups, and game pages marked skip to prevent accidental navigation.
- Scripts: Reusable multi-step actions with debouncing and orchestration for UI transitions, voice assistant, calendar, and games.
- IMU: BMI270 sensor with adaptive polling rate for tap-to-wake and tilt-controlled games.
- Alarm clock: Pure C++ engine for scheduling and announcements, independent of HA availability.

## Architecture Overview
The system follows a strict push-only flow: HA detects changes and calls ESPHome services; the device parses and applies updates to LVGL without initiating any network requests. This eliminates polling cycles, reduces Wi-Fi radio wake-ups, and keeps CPU usage near zero when nothing changes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant ESP as "ESPHome Services"
participant CPP as "C++ Logic"
participant LV as "LVGL Rendering"
HA->>ESP : "Call service tab5_maj_* with payload"
ESP->>CPP : "Invoke parser/update function"
CPP->>LV : "Update labels/widgets safely"
Note over HA,ESP : "No device-initiated requests<br/>Zero polling"
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Boot Sequence and Initialization Order
The boot sequence ensures stable startup:
- Blocking delay to allow GPIO expander stabilization before display reset.
- Resume LVGL and turn on backlight.
- Set media player volume and enable amplifier to avoid audio pops.
- Wait for HA API connection and emit a connected event.
- Mark boot complete and initialize global contexts and weather slots.
- Start alarm refresh and central rotator auto cycle.
- Pre-fetch calendar data for instant popup opening.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Boot"]) --> Delay["Blocking delay for expander stability"]
Delay --> LVGLResume["lvgl.resume + backlight on"]
LVGLResume --> AudioSetup["Set volume + enable amp"]
AudioSetup --> WaitForAPI["Wait for HA API (timeout 30s)"]
WaitForAPI --> EmitEvent{"HA connected?"}
EmitEvent --> |Yes| Connected["Emit esphome.tab5_connected"]
EmitEvent --> |No| LogOffline["Log offline message"]
Connected --> BootComplete["Set boot_complete = true"]
LogOffline --> BootComplete
BootComplete --> InitContexts["Initialize central context + weather slots"]
InitContexts --> AlarmRefresh["Run alarm refresh"]
AlarmRefresh --> RotatorStart["Start central rotator auto"]
RotatorStart --> CalPrefetch["Pre-fetch calendar months"]
CalPrefetch --> End(["Ready"])
```

### Push-Only Data Flow and Payload Parsing
Home Assistant pushes bulk payloads using delimited strings to minimize service calls. The firmware parses these in a single pass and updates LVGL atomically.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant SVC as "ESPHome Service"
participant PARSER as "C++ Parser"
participant UI as "LVGL Widgets"
HA->>SVC : "tab5_maj_previsions_jours_bulk(payload)"
SVC->>PARSER : "parse_and_update_jours_bulk()"
PARSER->>UI : "refresh_daily_forecast() + title update"
Note over HA,SVC : "Payload : semicolon-delimited fields<br/>O(n) parse, single redraw"
```

### Modular YAML Architecture by Concern
Each package has a clear role:
- Tokens: shared dimensions and offsets.
- Hardware: low-level drivers and audio.
- Sensors/Diagnostics: system metrics and network status.
- Sensors/Domotique: home automation entities pushed by HA.
- API Logic: service handlers and lambdas calling C++.
- Styles: global LVGL style definitions to reduce allocations.
- Globals: typed shared variables initialized at boot.
- Scripts: reusable sequences with debouncing and orchestration.
- LVGL: single-page layout with swipe and popups.
- IMU: BMI270 with adaptive polling.
- HA Controls: entities exposed to HA for screen control.
- Alarm Clock: pure C++ scheduling engine.

### Offline Resilience Design
The device maintains functionality during Home Assistant outages:
- Clock, games, and diagnostics work independently.
- Last-known UI state persists until new data arrives.
- Alarm clock uses local SNTP time and cached schedules.
- Safe mode prevents boot loops; reboot timeout avoids zombie states.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
HAOutage{"HA Offline?"}
HAOutage --> |Yes| LocalFeatures["Clock/Games/Diagnostics Active"]
HAOutage --> |No| PushUpdates["Receive HA Push Updates"]
LocalFeatures --> LastState["Maintain Last Known UI"]
PushUpdates --> UpdateUI["Apply New State"]
LastState --> Stable["Stable Operation"]
UpdateUI --> Stable
```

- [alarm_clock.h:4-26](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/alarm_clock.h#L4-L26)

### Technology Stack Choices
- ESP32-P4: High-performance MCU with PSRAM support for LVGL rendering.
- LVGL 8.4: Efficient UI framework running in PSRAM to free internal memory.
- Native C++: Compiled for performance optimization in parsing, animations, and game logic.
- ESP-IDF Framework: Enables experimental features and optimized SDK configurations.
- PSRAM Mode: Hex mode at 200MHz for large UI buffers and assets.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:9-21](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L9-L21)

## Dependency Analysis
Components interact through well-defined boundaries:
- YAML packages depend on globals and styles.
- API logic depends on C++ parsers and LVGL widgets.
- Scripts orchestrate UI transitions and external services.
- IMU feeds game engines and tap-to-wake functionality.

```mermaid
graph TB
Globals["tab5-globals.yaml"] --> API["tab5-api-logic.yaml"]
Styles["tab5-styles.yaml"] --> LVGL["tab5-lvgl.yaml"]
Scripts["tab5-scripts.yaml"] --> LVGL
IMU["tab5-imu.yaml"] --> Games["Game Engines"]
API --> LVGL
Hardware["tab5-hardware.yaml"] --> LVGL
```

## Performance Considerations
- Push-only paradigm eliminates polling overhead.
- Bulk payloads reduce network calls and parse efficiently.
- Global styles minimize LVGL allocations in PSRAM.
- Adaptive IMU polling balances responsiveness and power.
- Native C++ handles performance-critical tasks like parsing and animations.
- PSRAM enables large UI buffers without impacting internal memory.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and mitigations:
- Black screen after software reboot: blocking delay ensures GPIO expander stability.
- HA connection timeout: device continues operating locally with last known state.
- Zombie state prevention: reboot timeout avoids indefinite reboots during HA outages.
- Audio pops: proper amplifier enable sequence after volume setting.
- Wake word conflicts: dynamic model enabling/disabling based on context.

## Conclusion
The Tab5 project implements a robust push-only architecture that minimizes resource usage while providing rich interactive capabilities. Its modular YAML design separates concerns clearly, while native C++ ensures performance for critical operations. The system maintains functionality during Home Assistant outages and leverages ESP32-P4 capabilities with LVGL rendering in PSRAM for optimal user experience.

## Introduction
This document explains the Tab5 boot sequence and initialization order, focusing on how the system ensures a reliable startup of all components: hardware abstraction (display/touch/audio), Wi-Fi co-processor bring-up, Home Assistant API connection, LVGL graphics engine setup, sensor discovery (IMU), and background coordination via the main loop. It also details the custom initialization code in tab5_custom.cpp that guards LVGL updates, parses bulk data, and supports UI animations, and it documents timing considerations for power-on sequences and partial failure handling during boot.

## Project Structure
The ESPHome configuration is split into packages included by a single entry point. The root file defines substitutions, includes, the critical on_boot sequence, and package imports. Hardware, sensors, styles, LVGL layout, scripts, IMU, and alarm logic are each isolated in their own YAML package to keep responsibilities clear and testable.

```mermaid
graph TB

A --> D["Globals: tab5-globals.yaml"]
A --> E["Sensors & Diagnostics"]
A --> F["API Logic & Scripts"]
A --> G["IMU: tab5-imu.yaml"]
A --> H["Alarm & Voice"]
A --> I["Custom C++: tab5_custom.*"]
```

## Core Components
- Entry point and boot orchestration: tab5-ha-hmi.yaml
- Hardware abstraction and peripherals: tab5-hardware.yaml
- LVGL UI layout and gesture routing: tab5-lvgl.yaml
- Shared state and flags: tab5-globals.yaml
- IMU sensor and adaptive polling: tab5-imu.yaml
- Custom C++ layer for LVGL helpers, parsing, and UI logic: tab5_custom.cpp/.h

Key responsibilities:
- Ensure display reset line stabilizes before use (critical for avoiding black screen after software reboot).
- Resume LVGL and turn on backlight safely.
- Wait for Home Assistant API connection with timeout; emit connected event or log failure.
- Initialize LVGL widget references and weather slots once per boot.
- Start wake-word detection if enabled.
- Pre-fetch calendar data in background.
- Provide null-guarded LVGL update functions so early pushes do not crash the UI.

## Architecture Overview
The boot flow is designed to avoid race conditions between hardware init, network availability, and UI rendering. The most critical path is:

1. Power-on and IDF framework start
2. GPIO expander stabilization delay (blocking)
3. LVGL resume and backlight on
4. Media player volume set and amplifier enable (to avoid pop noise)
5. Wait for Home Assistant API connection (timeout 30s)
6. Fire HA event and mark boot_complete
7. Initialize LVGL widget pointers and weather slot arrays
8. Start wake-word detection if enabled
9. Pre-fetch calendar data after short delay

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant FW as "ESPHome FW"
participant HW as "Hardware (Display/Touch/Audio)"
participant NET as "Wi-Fi Co-Proc (ESP32-C6)"
participant HA as "Home Assistant API"
participant LV as "LVGL Engine"
participant UI as "UI Widgets"
FW->>HW : Apply blocking delay for GPIO expander settle
FW->>LV : lvgl.resume
FW->>HW : Turn on backlight
FW->>FW : Set media_player volume
FW->>HW : Enable speaker amp
FW->>NET : Bring up Wi-Fi link (via esp32_hosted)
FW->>HA : Connect native API (wait up to 30s)
alt Connected
FW->>HA : Publish esphome.tab5_connected
FW->>FW : Set boot_complete = true
else Not connected
FW->>FW : Log HA unreachable at boot
end
FW->>UI : Initialize LVGL widget refs and weather slots
FW->>FW : Start micro_wake_word if enabled
FW->>FW : Delay then pre-fetch calendar
```

**Diagram sources**
- [tab5-ha-hmi.yaml:66-162](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/tab5-ha-hmi.yaml#L66-L162)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:116-168](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L116-L168)
- [architecture.md:19-41](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L19-L41)

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Boot Orchestration in tab5-ha-hmi.yaml
- Priority-ordered on_boot steps ensure the GPIO expander has time to stabilize before display reset is asserted.
- LVGL is resumed explicitly because restore_mode on backlight does not trigger transitions reliably on boot.
- Backlight is turned on, media player volume set, and amplifier enabled in a strict order to prevent audio pops.
- The system waits for HA API connectivity with a 30-second timeout; if unavailable, it logs and continues with local UI.
- After connection, it emits an event to HA and sets boot_complete to gate UI updates until safe.
- LVGL widget references and forecast slot arrays are initialized once at boot to avoid repeated allocations.
- Wake-word detection starts only if enabled; otherwise it remains stopped.
- Calendar pre-fetch runs after a short delay to avoid contention with initial UI setup.

Why this order matters:
- Display reset must occur after the GPIO expander settles; otherwise the display may remain off after software reboots.
- LVGL must be resumed before any UI updates; otherwise labels and widgets cannot be painted.
- HA API must be available before pushing data; otherwise UI updates could receive NaN or stale values.
- Widget pointer initialization must happen after LVGL layout exists; otherwise pointers would be invalid.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-ha-hmi.yaml:66-162](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/tab5-ha-hmi.yaml#L66-L162)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:116-168](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L116-L168)
- [architecture.md:19-41](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L19-L41)

### Hardware Abstraction and Timing (tab5-hardware.yaml)
- Display driver uses MIPI-DSI with model M5STACK-TAB5-ST7123; update_interval is never to let LVGL drive redraws from the application loop.
- Touch controller st7123 uses official platform; polling stops automatically when interrupts are attached.
- Backlight LEDC output is controlled via a monochromatic light component; turning on/off triggers LVGL pause/resume.
- Audio chain: ES7210 ADC microphone, ES8388 DAC speaker, i2s_audio bus; buffer_duration tuned to reduce TTS artifacts over WiFi streaming.
- esp32_hosted configures the ESP32-C6 Wi-Fi co-processor over SDIO; PSRAM usage for buffers avoids internal SRAM pressure.

Timing considerations:
- The documented black-screen-after-software-reboot issue was resolved by adding a blocking delay before display reset; removing it risks repeat failures.
- Safe mode is configured to detect repeated crashes and recover gracefully.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:9-36](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L9-L36)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-83](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L83)

- [troubleshooting.md:13-20](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L13-L20)

### LVGL Graphics Engine Setup (tab5-lvgl.yaml)
- The dashboard is a single page (page_main) with gesture handling delegated to C++.
- Swipe gestures route to handle_swipe_gesture() which updates forecast pages and central panel visibility.
- All UI logic is kept out of YAML lambdas; LVGL calls are centralized in C++ helpers to avoid duplication and ensure safety.

Initialization notes:
- LVGL resume is triggered by backlight turn_on; explicit resume is also called in on_boot for robustness.
- Gesture callbacks reference global widget arrays (g_day_slots, g_hour_slots) initialized at boot.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-lvgl.yaml:10-36](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml#L10-L36)
- [tab5-ha-hmi.yaml:121-151](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/tab5-ha-hmi.yaml#L121-L151)

### Sensor Discovery and IMU (tab5-imu.yaml)
- BMI270 IMU is configured on the shared I2C bus; accelerometer axes are internal to avoid flooding HA.
- Adaptive polling switches between 10 Hz at rest and 30 Hz when tilt-controlled games are open; poller is restarted to apply interval changes.
- Tap-to-wake uses acceleration magnitude threshold with debounce; wakes backlight when enabled.

Boot relevance:
- IMU discovery happens during hardware init; no special boot delay is required beyond I2C bus setup.
- Polling rate adjustments are runtime decisions based on game state; they do not block boot.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-imu.yaml:17-31](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L17-L31)
- [tab5-imu.yaml:32-87](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L32-L87)
- [tab5-imu.yaml:117-144](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L117-L144)

### Custom Initialization Code in tab5_custom.cpp
- Provides null-guarded LVGL update functions so early pushes do not crash the UI.
- Parses bulk payloads for daily and hourly forecasts using strtok_r to avoid heap fragmentation.
- Updates weather icons, temperatures, humidity colors, and central panel visibility.
- Implements animations for panels, alerts, swipe transitions, and icon roll-in effects.
- Normalizes UTF-8 text from HA to fix mojibake and ensure correct display.

Why these matter during boot:
- Early HA pushes can arrive before LVGL is fully ready; null checks prevent crashes.
- Bulk parsing reduces network overhead and ensures atomic UI updates without intermediate redraws.
- Animation constants are centralized to control performance and perceived responsiveness.

Note on IMU calibration and NVS storage:
- IMU calibration is exposed via game APIs (e.g., Marble::calibrate()) and used within game contexts rather than during general boot.
- NVS persistence is handled per-game save/load routines; boot does not perform IMU calibration or NVS restoration as part of the core HMI startup.

**Section sources**
- [tab5_custom.cpp:14-32](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L14-L32)
- [tab5_custom.cpp:338-436](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L338-L436)
- [tab5_custom.cpp:454-569](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.cpp#L454-L569)
- [tab5_custom.h:97-127](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.h#L97-L127)
- [tab5_custom.h:213-233](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5_custom.h#L213-L233)

### Main Loop Coordination and Background Tasks
- The dashboard uses LVGL’s event-driven model; the application loop drives redraws and handles gestures.
- Background tasks include:
  - Sensor polling (IMU) with adaptive intervals.
  - Network reconnection attempts (handled by ESPHome/Wi-Fi components).
  - UI updates via push services from HA; updates are gated by boot_complete and api.connected().
  - Central panel rotator cycling through planning/rain/alerts/info panels.
  - Calendar pre-fetch after boot to improve popup responsiveness.

How partial failures are handled:
- If HA API is not connected at boot, the device still renders last known state and local features (clock, arcade, diagnostics).
- Push handlers validate inputs and skip updates if LVGL is not ready or data is invalid.
- Safe mode detects repeated crashes and recovers; OTA end triggers restart after delay.

## Dependency Analysis
The boot sequence enforces a strict dependency order:

```mermaid
graph LR
A["GPIO Expander Stabilization"] --> B["Display Reset & LVGL Resume"]
B --> C["Backlight On"]
C --> D["Media Player Volume Set"]
D --> E["Amplifier Enable"]
E --> F["Wi-Fi Co-Proc Bring-Up"]
F --> G["Home Assistant API Connect"]
G --> H["Set boot_complete"]
H --> I["Initialize LVGL Widget Pointers"]
I --> J["Start Wake Word (if enabled)"]
J --> K["Pre-Fetch Calendar"]
```

**Diagram sources**
- [tab5-ha-hmi.yaml:66-162](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/tab5-ha-hmi.yaml#L66-L162)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:116-168](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L116-L168)

Coupling and cohesion:
- Hardware abstraction is encapsulated in tab5-hardware.yaml; UI logic is separated into tab5-lvgl.yaml and tab5_custom.*.
- Globals centralize shared state to avoid scattered static variables and ensure consistent behavior across packages.
- IMU polling is decoupled from UI; it adapts to game state without blocking boot.

Potential circular dependencies:
- None observed; packages are layered and include order is managed by the entry point.

External dependencies:
- Home Assistant API for data push and voice pipeline.
- ESP32-C6 co-processor for Wi-Fi; SDIO link must be stable to avoid hot retry loops that starve firmware.

## Performance Considerations
- Use of bulk payloads reduces network overhead and ensures atomic UI updates.
- LVGL styles are declared globally to minimize allocations; inline styles would allocate per widget.
- IMU polling adapts to activity to balance responsiveness and power consumption.
- Audio buffer duration is tuned to mitigate TTS stuttering over WiFi streaming.
- Blocking delays are minimized but necessary for hardware stability (e.g., GPIO expander settle).

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common boot issues and techniques:
- Black screen after software reboot: caused by display reset via GPIO expander needing settle time; fix is the blocking delay in on_boot priority 700.
- Device reboots periodically when HA is unreachable: due to api reboot_timeout; raised to 60min to avoid cycles during long outages.
- Wi-Fi co-processor not coming up after OTA: requires full power cycle; soft reboot does not reset the C6.
- Debugging resources: live ESPHome logs, on-screen console overlay, and HA logs for upstream issues.

Recommended debugging steps:
- Check ESPHome logs for boot sequence events and API connection status.
- Use the on-screen console to verify memory, network, and system metrics.
- Validate that boot_complete is set and LVGL widget pointers are initialized.
- Confirm IMU polling rates and tap-to-wake behavior if touch seems unresponsive.

**Section sources**
- [troubleshooting.md:13-20](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L13-L20)
- [troubleshooting.md:83-109](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L83-L109)
- [debugging.md:9-17](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/debugging.md#L9-L17)
- [debugging.md:42-49](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/debugging.md#L42-L49)

## Conclusion
The Tab5 boot sequence is carefully ordered to ensure hardware stability, network readiness, and safe UI initialization. Critical phases include GPIO expander stabilization, LVGL resume, backlight activation, HA API connection, and widget pointer initialization. The custom C++ layer provides robust LVGL helpers and efficient payload parsing to support responsive UI updates. Background tasks like IMU polling and calendar pre-fetch operate independently without blocking boot. Partial failures are handled gracefully, allowing the device to remain useful even when HA is unavailable. For persistent issues, consult the troubleshooting guide and leverage logging and the on-screen console for diagnosis.

## Introduction
This document explains the modular YAML configuration system that composes the Tab5 firmware across twelve focused files organized by concern. The main entry point orchestrates package imports in a strict dependency order while keeping each module isolated and reusable. It also documents how variables are shared between modules, how user entities are substituted at runtime, and how UI elements are bound to Home Assistant entities. Finally, it provides best practices for extending the system while preserving separation of concerns.

## Project Structure
The system is centered on a single root configuration file that:
- Includes C++ sources for games and custom logic
- Declares substitutions from a user-provided entity map
- Defines boot sequence and intervals
- Imports packages (modules) in a precise order so dependencies resolve correctly

## Core Components
- Root orchestrator: loads user substitutions, includes C++ game modules, defines boot flow, and imports packages in dependency order.
- UI tokens: centralizes geometry tokens used by modals and popups.
- Styles: defines colors, fonts, and LVGL styles; sets LVGL component id and rotation.
- Hardware: configures ESP32-P4, display, touch, audio, wake word, voice assistant, and media pipeline.
- Sensors diagnostics: WiFi, antenna selection, API status, uptime, core temp, SNTP time, console updates.
- Sensors domotique: HA entities for devices, lights, temperatures, humidity, plant sensors, headphone detection, speaker enable.
- API logic: service handlers that parse payloads and update UI via C++ helpers.
- Scripts: reusable sequences for games, volume/light/climate debouncing, calendar rendering, central rotator, and more.
- LVGL layout: declarative pages, widgets, gestures, and included UI components.
- IMU: BMI270 motion sensor with adaptive polling and tap-to-wake.
- HA controls: remote control and observation of the device screen from Home Assistant.
- Alarm: alarm clock and meeting announcements with local ringtone and optional HA media URL.

## Architecture Overview
The root file composes the system by importing packages in a specific order. Early packages provide foundational services (hardware, styles, tokens), mid-layer packages add data and logic (sensors, API), and later packages depend on earlier ones (LVGL UI, HA controls, alarm). User substitutions are merged into all packages, enabling centralized customization.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Root as "tab5-ha-hmi.yaml"
participant HW as "tab5-hardware.yaml"
participant ST as "tab5-styles.yaml"
participant TK as "tab5-ui-tokens.yaml"
participant SEN as "tab5-sensors-*.yaml"
participant API as "tab5-api-logic.yaml"
participant SCR as "tab5-scripts.yaml"
participant LV as "tab5-lvgl.yaml"
participant IMU as "tab5-imu.yaml"
participant HA as "tab5-ha-controls.yaml"
participant ALM as "tab5-alarm.yaml"
Root->>TK : Include (geometry tokens)
Root->>HW : Include (board, display, audio)
Root->>SEN : Include (system & home sensors)
Root->>API : Include (service handlers)
Root->>ST : Include (colors, fonts, LVGL styles)
Root->>SCR : Include (reusable scripts)
Root->>LV : Include (pages/widgets)
Root->>IMU : Include (motion/tap-to-wake)
Root->>HA : Include (remote control/observation)
Root->>ALM : Include (alarm engine + UI)
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Root Orchestrator: tab5-ha-hmi.yaml
Responsibilities:
- Loads user entity substitutions from a local file to avoid committing secrets or environment-specific IDs.
- Includes C++ modules for games and custom logic.
- Defines a safe boot sequence with a blocking delay to stabilize the GPIO expander before display initialization, then resumes LVGL, turns on backlight, sets volume, enables speaker, waits for API connection, emits events, initializes globals, starts/stops wake word based on state, synchronizes assist mode, binds LVGL pointers for the central panel, resets alarm floor, refreshes alarms, starts auto-rotator, and prefetches calendar data.
- Imports packages in dependency order to ensure IDs and globals exist when referenced later.

Key behaviors:
- Boot priority ordering ensures hardware stabilization before UI resume.
- Central panel context binding wires LVGL widget IDs into C++ structures for efficient UI updates.
- Package import order guarantees that LVGL-dependent modules load after LVGL itself.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-ha-hmi.yaml:10-163](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/tab5-ha-hmi.yaml#L10-L163)

### UI Tokens: tab5-ui-tokens.yaml
Responsibilities:
- Centralizes geometry tokens for modal cards, header heights, body offsets, calendar grid positioning, and assistant response placement.
- Provides a single source of truth for popup sizing; changing these values adjusts multiple popups consistently.

Best practices:
- Keep token names descriptive and grouped by feature.
- Avoid hardcoding pixel offsets elsewhere; reference tokens instead.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-ui-tokens.yaml:13-33](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-ui-tokens.yaml#L13-L33)

### Styles: tab5-styles.yaml
Responsibilities:
- Defines color palette (dark slate glassmorphism), fonts (Roboto, MDI, weather icons, chess pieces), and LVGL style definitions (cards, buttons, modals, accents).
- Sets LVGL component id and rotation to allow runtime orientation changes for games like pinball.

Best practices:
- Use named color ids rather than hex literals in UI code.
- Keep font glyph sets minimal to reduce flash usage.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-styles.yaml:19-321](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-styles.yaml#L19-L321)

### Hardware: tab5-hardware.yaml
Responsibilities:
- Configures ESP32-P4 board, PSRAM, OTA, logger, I2C bus, GPIO expanders, MIPI DSI display, touchscreen, backlight PWM, I2S audio ADC/DAC, speaker, media player, microWakeWord, voice assistant, HTTP request, online image, restart button, and debug.
- Implements robust audio pipeline with preferred format and sample rate, noise suppression, and automatic gain.
- Integrates wake word models and voice assistant lifecycle hooks to update UI states and manage microphone/speaker resources.

Critical notes:
- Display reset relies on a GPIO expander; a blocking delay during boot prevents black screen issues.
- Wake word and TTS share the I2S bus; careful sequencing avoids conflicts.

- Updates console labels only when the console layer is visible to avoid unnecessary LVGL calls.

Best practices:
- Keep diagnostic updates throttled and conditional on visibility.
- Use helper functions from C++ to update UI labels efficiently.

Best practices:

Design patterns:
- Single entry points per action (e.g., close all games) prevent duplication and missed cleanup.

Best practices:
- Keep layout purely declarative; move logic to C++.

Behavioral flow:
- On acceleration Z update, push axes to game engines, handle tap-to-wake if enabled, and throttle diagnostic sensors.

## Performance Considerations
- Throttle high-frequency sensors (acceleration axes kept internal; pitch/roll/temp published with 60s throttle).
- Use conditional UI updates (e.g., console-only updates when visible) to minimize LVGL overhead.
- Prefer helper functions in C++ for hot paths to avoid string allocations in YAML callbacks.
- Debounce user interactions (volume, brightness, climate targets) to reduce network and UI churn.
- Adaptive IMU polling reduces CPU usage when no fast-input game is active.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and mitigations:
- Black screen after software reboot: Ensure the blocking delay before display init remains in place; it stabilizes the GPIO expander reset line.
- I2S bus conflicts: When playing ringtone or TTS, ensure wake word is stopped and resumed appropriately; alarm and voice assistant pipelines coordinate bus access.
- Volume divergence: Always use the unified volume script; remote changes must be reflected back to the device UI via periodic checks.
- Calendar not updating: Trigger pre-fetch on HA reconnect or manually reload calendar; cache eviction keeps only relevant months.
- Alert dismissal not persisting: Ensure dismiss flows call both local storage and HA scripts to mark alerts as dismissed.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-79](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L79)
- [tab5-alarm.yaml:674-800](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-alarm.yaml#L674-L800)

## Conclusion
The Tab5 firmware’s modular YAML configuration achieves clear separation of concerns through focused packages orchestrated by a root file that enforces dependency order. User substitutions centralize customization, while scripts and C++ helpers encapsulate complex logic. This structure supports extensibility: new features can be added as dedicated modules, integrated via controlled imports, and exposed through well-defined APIs and scripts. Adhering to the documented patterns ensures maintainability, performance, and reliability.

## Introduction
This document explains the Tab5 push-only data flow architecture that eliminates device-side polling. In this design, Home Assistant detects state changes and pushes updates to the device via ESPHome API services named with the tab5_maj_* pattern. The firmware is purely reactive: it does not poll for changes, which reduces CPU usage and network overhead significantly. Updates are event-driven and real-time, triggered only when relevant states change.

The service endpoint pattern centralizes all incoming updates in a single ESPHome configuration file where each feature has dedicated update services (for example, climate, weather, forecasts, alerts, calendar). Each service handler receives a payload and delegates processing to C++ lambda functions that safely update the UI without crashing during boot or connection loss.

Error handling and resilience are implemented on both sides:
- Home Assistant automations use continue_on_error and guard conditions so one failing push does not block others.
- The device maintains last known states and remains useful during Home Assistant outages. A reboot timeout prevents “zombie” devices while avoiding unnecessary reboots during long HA maintenance windows.

**Section sources**
- [0001-push-only-zero-polling.md:1-18](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/decisions/0001-push-only-zero-polling.md#L1-L18)
- [architecture.md:172-183](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L172-L183)

## Project Structure
The push-only architecture spans two main areas:
- Home Assistant side: automations detect state changes and call ESPHome services to push data to the device.
- Device side: ESPHome defines api: services handlers that receive payloads and update LVGL UI through safe C++ lambdas.

```mermaid
graph TB
HA["Home Assistant"] --> |State change detected| Auto["Automation"]
Auto --> |Service call| ESPAPI["ESPHome API Services<br/>tab5_maj_*"]
ESPAPI --> Lambda["Lambda Handlers"]
Lambda --> CPP["C++ Update Functions"]
CPP --> LVGL["LVGL UI Updates"]
```

- [tab5-api-logic.yaml:11-39](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-api-logic.yaml#L11-L39)
- [architecture.md:172-183](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L172-L183)

**Section sources**
- [tab5-ha-hmi.yaml:176-185](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/tab5-ha-hmi.yaml#L176-L185)
- [architecture.md:82-100](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L82-L100)

## Core Components
- Service endpoints: Each feature exposes a dedicated ESPHome service under api: services: with a tab5_maj_* naming convention. Examples include climate updates, weather alerts, bulk forecasts, rain bars, info text, calendar month/day details, and assistant responses.
- Payload contracts: Services accept string payloads or typed variables (target, current, mode, preset, fan, swing, etc.). Bulk payloads use delimited strings parsed by C++ functions.
- Lambda handlers: YAML lambdas validate inputs, parse payloads, and call C++ functions to update UI components safely.
- Globals and context: Shared globals track current page, climate state, alert visibility, calendar view state, and other cross-cutting UI state.

Key responsibilities:
- Home Assistant automations trigger on entity state changes and call the appropriate service with prepared payloads.
- Device-side handlers ensure LVGL updates occur only after boot completion and when connected, preventing crashes and stale rendering.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-api-logic.yaml:41-53](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-api-logic.yaml#L41-L53)

## Architecture Overview
The system follows a strict one-directional data flow: Home Assistant pushes updates; the device never requests its own state. This eliminates polling cycles and minimizes Wi-Fi radio wake-ups.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant Auto as "Automation"
participant API as "ESPHome API Services"
participant Lambda as "Lambda Handler"
participant CPP as "C++ Update Function"
participant UI as "LVGL UI"
HA->>Auto : State change detected
Auto->>API : esphome.tab5_maj_* call
API->>Lambda : Parse payload and validate
Lambda->>CPP : Call update function
CPP->>UI : Safe LVGL update
UI-->>HA : Screen reflects latest state
```

- [automations_examples.yaml.example:25-48](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/HomeAssistant_Config/automations_examples.yaml.example#L25-L48)
- [tab5-api-logic.yaml:41-53](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-api-logic.yaml#L41-L53)
- [architecture.md:172-183](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L172-L183)

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Service Endpoint Pattern
Each feature has a dedicated service endpoint under api: services:. The naming convention uses tab5_maj_* to indicate “update” operations pushed from Home Assistant.

Examples:
- Climate: tab5_maj_clim accepts target, current, mode, preset, fan, swing and updates climate UI and colors.
- Weather alerts: tab5_maj_alerte_meteo_france parses pipe-delimited fields and updates alert icons and date color.
- Forecasts: tab5_maj_previsions_heures_bulk and tab5_maj_previsions_jours_bulk parse semicolon-delimited payloads and refresh forecast cards.
- Rain graph: tab5_maj_pluie_1h updates individual bars and sets has_rain global.
- Info panel: tab5_maj_info_texte updates central info banner with color and dismiss ID.
- Calendar: tab5_maj_calendrier_mois and tab5_maj_calendrier_jour store and render calendar data.
- Assistant response: tab5_assist_reponse renders Markdown and optional image in assistant popup.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["Service Received"]) --> Validate["Validate Variables"]
Validate --> Parse{"Payload Type?"}
Parse --> |Bulk String| Split["Split Delimited Fields"]
Parse --> |Typed Vars| MapVars["Map to Local Variables"]
Split --> Update["Call C++ Update Function"]
MapVars --> Update
Update --> UI["Update LVGL Widgets"]
UI --> End(["Done"])
```

### Home Assistant Automation Triggers
Automations listen for state changes on entities such as weather, climate, calendar, and sensors. When a change occurs, they prepare payloads and call the corresponding ESPHome service.

Key patterns:
- Trigger on entity state changes or time patterns.
- Use continue_on_error to prevent one failure from blocking subsequent pushes.
- Format datetime values explicitly to avoid schema validation failures.
- Use guards like is defined to handle missing template variables gracefully.

Example flows:
- Weather and climate updates trigger a full refresh chain with delays to avoid TCP socket saturation.
- Lightweight alert updates run in a separate automation to minimize latency.
- Shutter state sync triggers a specific service to update shutter UI and motion indicators.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Sensor as "Entity"
participant Auto as "Automation"
participant Service as "esphome.tab5_maj_*"
participant Device as "Device UI"
Sensor-->>Auto : State changed
Auto->>Service : Call with payload
Service-->>Device : Update UI
Note over Auto,Service : continue_on_error ensures partial failures do not block other updates
```

### Device-Side Lambda Processing
Lambda handlers in the ESPHome configuration receive payloads and delegate to C++ functions. They perform:
- Null checks to prevent UI updates before LVGL initialization.
- Parsing of delimited strings using tokenization functions.
- Updating globals and UI elements safely.
- Invoking scripts for reusable multi-step actions.

Important safeguards:
- Check boot_complete and api.connected before LVGL calls.
- Use bounded buffers for large payloads to avoid truncation.
- Update derived UI elements (like page titles) after bulk data changes.

### Error Handling and Connection Recovery
Resilience is built into both Home Assistant and device layers:

Home Assistant health package:
- Detects primary instance inactivity and notifies users.
- Detects unexpected reboots by monitoring uptime drops.
- Detects ESPHome API disconnections and warns about failed pushes.

Device-side recovery:
- Reboot timeout prevents zombie devices while allowing long HA outages without cycling reboots.
- Boot sequence waits for API connection and emits a connected event to HA.
- Last known states remain visible during outages; device stays useful offline.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Start(["System Startup"]) --> WaitAPI["Wait for API Connection"]
WaitAPI --> Connected{"Connected?"}
Connected --> |Yes| Notify["Emit Connected Event"]
Connected --> |No| LogWarn["Log Warning"]
Notify --> Ready["Ready for Push Updates"]
LogWarn --> Ready
Ready --> Monitor["Monitor API Status"]
Monitor --> Offline{"API Disconnected?"}
Offline --> |Yes| Alert["Notify User"]
Offline --> |No| Continue["Continue Normal Operation"]
```

### Offline Resilience and Last Known States
Because the device never polls, it relies on the last pushed state to display information during Home Assistant outages. The firmware maintains:
- Forecast data cached for current views.
- Calendar month and day details stored locally.
- Alarm and reminder lists persisted on-device to ensure announcements still trigger even if HA goes down between push and scheduled time.

This design ensures the device remains functional as a clock, game console, diagnostics tool, and local alarm system even when Home Assistant is unavailable.
