## Performance Considerations
The push-only design delivers significant performance benefits:
- CPU usage stays near zero when no state changes occur because the device never initiates polling cycles.
- Network overhead is minimized since Wi-Fi radio wake-ups only happen when Home Assistant pushes updates.
- Delays between service calls prevent TCP socket saturation when multiple updates are sent together.
- Bulk payloads reduce the number of service calls by packing multiple data points into a single message.

These optimizations make the system suitable for always-on embedded devices with limited resources.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and their resolutions:

Weather, planning, or climate data missing while device appears online:
- Root cause: Push automations gated behind a shared boolean helper that was stuck off.
- Fix: Enable the helper and the guard automation that resets it on HA boot.

Unexpected device reboots during HA downtime:
- Root cause: ESPHome reboot_timeout too short caused cycling reboots when HA was unreachable.
- Fix: Increase reboot_timeout to allow longer outages without cycling.

Black screen after software reboot:
- Root cause: Display reset pin wired through I2C GPIO expander needs settle time.
- Fix: Add blocking delay before display reset sequence.

OTA causing black screen and network loss:
- Root cause: Wi-Fi co-processor link failed to come up after software reboot.
- Fix: Perform full power cycle to reset both P4 and C6 processors.

Connection exhaustion:
- Root cause: Open ESPHome CLI sessions hold connections indefinitely.
- Fix: Close CLI sessions and kill orphaned processes.

**Section sources**
- [troubleshooting.md:23-30](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L23-L30)
- [troubleshooting.md:83-90](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L83-L90)
- [troubleshooting.md:13-20](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L13-L20)
- [troubleshooting.md:93-110](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L93-L110)

## Conclusion
The Tab5 push-only data flow architecture eliminates device-side polling by making Home Assistant responsible for detecting state changes and pushing updates to the device. This design reduces CPU usage and network overhead while providing real-time synchronization through an event-driven model.

The service endpoint pattern centralizes all incoming updates in ESPHome with dedicated tab5_maj_* services for each feature. Lambda handlers process payloads safely and update the UI through robust C++ functions that guard against null pointers and incomplete initialization.

Error handling and resilience are implemented across both layers: Home Assistant automations use continue_on_error and guards to prevent cascading failures, while the device maintains last known states and remains useful during outages. The reboot timeout balances anti-zombie protection with tolerance for long maintenance windows.

This architecture demonstrates how embedded devices can achieve efficient, reliable, and responsive user interfaces by shifting polling logic to the cloud or server side and treating the device as a pure consumer of push updates.

## Introduction
This document explains the technology stack decisions that define the Tab5 system architecture. It focuses on why ESP32-P4 was chosen, how LVGL 8.4 runs in PSRAM for smooth UI rendering under tight memory constraints, why ESPHome was selected for declarative configuration and OTA updates, how TensorFlow Lite Micro enables local wake-word detection, and how Home Assistant’s Wyoming-based STT/TTS pipeline integrates with the device. It also documents the YAML-heavy, minimal-hardcoded-logic approach used to improve maintainability and support AI-assisted development, along with performance trade-offs, memory usage analysis, rejected alternatives, and future scalability considerations.

## Project Structure
The firmware is organized as a set of modular ESPHome packages imported by a single entry point. Each package has a clear responsibility: hardware, sensors, API logic, styles, globals, scripts, LVGL UI, and IMU. The UI layout is declared in YAML, while complex interactions are implemented in C++ helpers. Data flows via push from Home Assistant; the device never polls.

```mermaid
graph TB
HA["Home Assistant"] --> |ESPHome API services| FW["ESP32-P4 Firmware"]
FW --> LVGL["LVGL 8.4 UI (PSRAM)"]
FW --> I2S["I2S Audio (Mic/Speaker)"]
FW --> WW["microWakeWord (TF Lite Micro)"]
FW --> WiFi["ESP32-C6 Wi-Fi (SDIO)"]
FW --> Display["MIPI-DSI Display (1280x720)"]
```

## Core Components
- Platform: ESP32-P4 (RISC-V dual-core up to 400 MHz), 16 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash, MIPI-DSI display, I2C touch controller, I2S audio codec and ADC, ESP32-C6 co-processor over SDIO for Wi-Fi/BLE.
- Framework: ESPHome with ESP-IDF, enabling declarative configuration, OTA, and native components for display, audio, and voice assistant.
- UI: LVGL 8.4 configured entirely in YAML with C++ helpers for complex logic; UI assets and framebuffers reside in PSRAM.
- Voice: Local wake-word detection via microWakeWord (TensorFlow Lite Micro); STT/TTS via Home Assistant’s Wyoming pipeline; TTS streamed back to the device’s I2S speaker.
- Data flow: Push-only from Home Assistant using ESPHome API services; payloads packed into delimited strings and parsed in C++.

## Architecture Overview
The system uses a push-only architecture where Home Assistant detects state changes and pushes updates to the device via ESPHome API services. The device parses payloads and updates LVGL widgets in one pass. The voice pipeline runs local wake-word detection continuously; when triggered, it streams audio to Home Assistant for STT, processes intent, and streams TTS back to the device for playback.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant FW as "ESP32-P4 Firmware"
participant LV as "LVGL"
participant WW as "microWakeWord"
participant I2S as "I2S Mic/Speaker"
participant W as "ESP32-C6 Wi-Fi"
Note over FW,WW : Idle : continuous wake-word detection
WW->>FW : Wake word detected
FW->>W : Stream audio to HA (Wyoming STT)
HA-->>FW : TTS audio stream
FW->>I2S : Play TTS
FW->>LV : Update UI states/colors
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### ESP32-P4 selection and capabilities
- Dual-core RISC-V up to 400 MHz provides headroom for concurrent tasks: LVGL rendering, I2S audio streaming, Wi-Fi handling, and wake-word inference.
- 16 MB PSRAM is essential for the 1280×720 RGB565 framebuffer (~1.8 MB) and other buffers; internal SRAM alone is insufficient.
- MIPI-DSI interface drives the high-resolution display efficiently; touch handled via I2C controller.
- Co-processor ESP32-C6 handles Wi-Fi/BLE over SDIO, keeping radio work off the main core.

Why not other MCUs?
- Lower-end ESP32 variants lack sufficient PSRAM or CPU headroom to sustain 60 FPS LVGL at this resolution while running wake-word detection and audio streaming.
- The ESP32-P4’s combination of CPU power, PSRAM capacity, and dedicated display/audio peripherals makes it uniquely suited for this workload.

Evidence and references:
- Platform and PSRAM configuration: [tab5-hardware.yaml:9-24, 84-87:9-24](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L9-L24)
- Hardware specs and PSRAM necessity: [hardware.md:11-27](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L11-L27)
- Resource cost of wake-word: [voice_assistant.md:23-31](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/voice_assistant.md#L23-L31)

### LVGL 8.4 in PSRAM for smooth UI
- LVGL is configured declaratively in YAML; all heavy graphics buffers (framebuffer, fonts, images) reside in PSRAM to avoid internal SRAM pressure.
- Global style definitions minimize allocations; inline styles would allocate per widget, increasing PSRAM fragmentation.
- Gesture handling delegates complex logic to C++ to keep YAML purely declarative.

Performance implications:
- Framebuffer size ~1.8 MB fits comfortably in PSRAM; LVGL can render at 60 FPS without tearing.
- Declaring styles globally reduces allocations and improves responsiveness.

References:
- LVGL configuration and gesture delegation: [tab5-lvgl.yaml:10-36](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml#L10-L36)
- Style allocation rationale: [architecture.md:104-110](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L104-L110)
- PSRAM framebuffer necessity: [hardware.md:11-27](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L11-L27)

**Section sources**
- [tab5-lvgl.yaml:10-36](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml#L10-L36)
- [architecture.md:104-110](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L104-L110)
- [hardware.md:11-27](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L11-L27)

### ESPHome framework choice
- Declarative configuration simplifies maintenance and enables AI-assisted development through structured YAML.
- Native components for display, audio, and voice assistant reduce custom code complexity.
- OTA updates are built-in; safe mode and boot guards help recover from failures.

Rejected alternatives:
- Custom frameworks would require more low-level driver code and increase maintenance burden.
- Purely C++ firmware would be harder to iterate quickly and less accessible to non-experts.

References:
- Package structure and imports: [architecture.md:19-41](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L19-L41)
- OTA and safe mode: [tab5-hardware.yaml:88-99](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L88-L99)

**Section sources**

- [tab5-hardware.yaml:88-99](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L88-L99)

### TensorFlow Lite Micro for local wake-word detection
- microWakeWord runs continuously in the background, processing I2S frames locally without network transmission during idle listening.
- Model runs on-device in ESP32-P4 memory; resource cost is approximately 5–8% CPU at 400 MHz, leaving ample headroom for UI and audio.
- A second model (“Stop”) is conditionally armed during specific actions (e.g., roller shutter movement) for immediate local control.

Trade-offs:
- Continuous wake-word detection consumes CPU but avoids network overhead and latency.
- On lower-power chips, this would constrain available resources significantly.

References:
- Wake-word integration and resource cost: [voice_assistant.md:23-31](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/voice_assistant.md#L23-L31)
- Second wake-word model usage: [voice_assistant.md:33-36](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/voice_assistant.md#L33-L36)

### Wyoming protocol for STT/TTS communication
- After wake-word detection, audio is streamed to Home Assistant’s Wyoming-based STT pipeline; responses (TTS) are streamed back and played via I2S.
- Preferred playback format is FLAC at 24 kHz mono to match engine outputs and minimize bandwidth while preserving quality.
- Buffer duration and timeout settings mitigate network hiccups and prevent audible gaps.

References:
- Pipeline overview and formats: [voice_assistant.md:43-83](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/voice_assistant.md#L43-L83)
- Media player announcement pipeline: [tab5-hardware.yaml:242-264](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L242-L264)

- [tab5-hardware.yaml:242-264](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L242-L264)

### YAML-heavy configuration with minimal hardcoded logic
- UI layout, entities, and behaviors are defined in YAML; complex logic is centralized in C++ helpers to ensure consistency and safety.
- Globals manage shared state across packages; strict typing and initialization avoid undefined behavior.
- Push-only architecture keeps the device reactive and minimizes network/CPU usage when idle.

References:
- YAML UI and C++ helper separation: [architecture.md:123-163](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L123-L163)

## Dependency Analysis
The system’s dependencies center around ESPHome components and external integrations:
- ESP32-P4 platform and ESP-IDF framework provide base OS and drivers.
- LVGL depends on PSRAM for framebuffer and global styles to minimize allocations.
- microWakeWord depends on I2S microphone input and runs locally.
- Voice assistant depends on ESP32-C6 Wi-Fi for streaming to Home Assistant’s Wyoming pipeline.
- Display and touch depend on MIPI-DSI and I2C controllers respectively.

```mermaid
graph LR
P4["ESP32-P4"] --> LVGL["LVGL 8.4"]
P4 --> WW["microWakeWord"]
P4 --> I2S["I2S Audio"]
P4 --> WiFi["ESP32-C6 Wi-Fi"]
P4 --> Display["MIPI-DSI Display"]
LVGL --> PSRAM["PSRAM"]
WW --> Mic["ES7210 ADC"]
I2S --> DAC["ES8388 DAC"]
```

## Performance Considerations
- CPU utilization: Wake-word detection uses ~5–8% CPU; remaining ~92% covers LVGL, I2S, and Wi-Fi.
- Memory usage: Framebuffer ~1.8 MB in PSRAM; global styles reduce allocations; task stacks for wake-word moved to PSRAM to save internal SRAM.
- Network pacing: Push automation delays between service calls prevent TCP socket exhaustion during large payload updates alongside audio streaming.
- Audio buffer: 500 ms speaker buffer mitigates network hiccups; lowering it risks audible gaps.

Optimization opportunities:
- Monitor PSRAM fragmentation and adjust font/image sizes if needed.
- Tune wake-word VAD to reduce false triggers without sacrificing responsiveness.
- Continue refining push pacing based on observed network conditions.

References:
- CPU cost and headroom: [voice_assistant.md:23-31](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/voice_assistant.md#L23-L31)

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and resolutions:
- Black screen after software reboot: Display reset line via GPIO expander needs stabilization time; ensure blocking delay before display init.
- Post-OTA black screen and no API: ESP32-C6 co-processor link not re-established; perform full power cycle (unplug USB-C for ~15 seconds).
- Audio pop on boot: Amplifier enable must occur after I2S clock is stable; follow boot sequence in on_boot block.

References:
- Display reset timing issue: [tab5-hardware.yaml:37-82](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L37-L82)
- Post-OTA co-processor link failure: [troubleshooting.md:189-203](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L189-L203)
- Boot sequence to avoid pop: [hardware.md:58-69](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L58-L69)

## Conclusion
The Tab5 architecture leverages the ESP32-P4’s dual-core performance and 16 MB PSRAM to run LVGL 8.4 smoothly at high resolution while maintaining real-time audio and wake-word detection. ESPHome’s declarative configuration and OTA capabilities simplify development and maintenance. TensorFlow Lite Micro enables local wake-word detection with minimal network dependency, and the Wyoming protocol integrates seamlessly with Home Assistant for STT/TTS. The YAML-heavy approach enhances maintainability and supports AI-assisted development. Future upgrades should consider PSRAM efficiency, wake-word model tuning, and network pacing optimizations to scale with additional features.

## Introduction
This document highlights the user-facing capabilities of the Tab5 project: a single-page, push-only smart-home dashboard for the M5Stack Tab5 V2 (ESP32-P4). It showcases weather monitoring with 15-day forecasts, climate control via an arc thermostat, light management with brightness arcs and color presets, plant monitoring with BLE sensor integration, voice assistant features including wake-word detection ("Ok Nabu"), local STT/TTS pipeline, and conversation mode with LLM integration, plus an arcade collection of eight games, a calendar/planning system, TV remote control, and a diagnostics console. The design emphasizes zero-polling, offline resilience, and energy efficiency so the device stays responsive even when Home Assistant is unavailable.

## Project Structure
The dashboard lives on one 1280×720 LVGL page with popups and overlays for each feature. Weather, climate, lights, plants, calendar, assistant, TV remote, and console are all reachable from the main screen by taps or long presses; swipe gestures paginate the forecast windows. Arcade games use dedicated fullscreen pages that are excluded from swipe navigation.

```mermaid
graph TB
A["Main Page<br/>page_main"] --> B["Weather Forecast<br/>hourly + daily"]
A --> C["Climate Card<br/>popup"]
A --> D["Lights Popup"]
A --> E["Plant Moisture<br/>BLE sensors"]
A --> F["Calendar Popup"]
A --> G["Assistant Popup"]
A --> H["TV Remote Popup"]
A --> I["System Console"]
A --> J["Arcade Selector<br/>page_arcade"]
J --> K["Game Pages<br/>skip: true"]
```

## Core Components
- Smart home dashboard: time/date, indoor temp/humidity, quick actions, rotating central card (planning/rain/alerts/info), bottom region toggling between weather and switches.
- Weather: swipeable hourly (next 15 slots) and daily (15 days across 3 windows) forecasts with color-coded temperatures and condition icons.
- Climate: compact card and near-fullscreen popup with stacked HVAC modes, 320 px arc thermostat with optimistic target and debounced updates, presets (eco/boost/quiet), and airflow controls.
- Lights: near-fullscreen popup with light selector, live brightness arc with percentage readout and shortcuts, named whites and round color swatches.
- Plants: up to five BLE soil moisture sensors shown in four sorted slots with color coding; long press opens detail cards showing moisture %, watering status, fertility (EC µS/cm), light (lx), temperature, and battery.
- Calendar: monthly grid computed locally from SNTP with work hours inside cells and markers for holidays, school holidays, appointments, birthdays; day tap opens details enriched by Home Assistant on demand.
- Voice assistant: on-device wake-word detection ("Ok Nabu"), microphone icon shows pipeline state, push-to-talk, second wake word "Stop" for shutter stop, and conversation mode with optional LLM routing.
- Arcade: eight fullscreen game consoles with unique controls and NVS persistence, zero HA/network dependency.
- TV remote: Samsung IR remote overlay sending commands through Home Assistant remote services.
- System console: memory/network/system diagnostics, volume, and HA management buttons with confirm overlays.

## Architecture Overview
Tab5 uses a push-only architecture: Home Assistant detects changes and calls ESPHome API services to update LVGL widgets in one pass. Data payloads are packed into delimited strings to minimize network calls. All UI logic runs in native LVGL at 60 FPS; no web stack, no polling. Offline resilience keeps last known state visible and allows clock, arcade, and console to remain usable.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant ESP as "ESPHome API"
participant FW as "Firmware (LVGL)"
HA->>ESP : "tab5_maj_* service call"
ESP->>FW : "payload (packed string)"
FW->>FW : "parse_and_update_*() C++"
FW-->>HA : "UI updated (no poll)"
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Weather Monitoring (15-Day Forecasts)
- Hourly window: next 15 time slots with time, color-coded temperature, rainfall in mm, and two-layer weather icons.
- Daily window: 15-day forecast split across three swipeable pages (5 days per page) with color-coded day names, dual-layer condition icons, and max/min temperatures.
- Tapping a day’s temperature temporarily shows that day’s schedule in the central card.

```mermaid

Hourly --> |No| Daily{"Daily window?"}
Daily --> |Yes| UpdateD["Update 5 daily cards"]
Daily --> |No| End(["Idle"])
UpdateH --> End
UpdateD --> End
```

### Plant Monitoring (BLE Sensor Integration)
- Up to five BLE soil moisture sensors displayed in four sorted slots (driest, 2nd driest, median “Moy:”, wettest) with color coding (red ≤ 14%, green 30–80%, blue ≥ 80%).

### Voice Assistant (Wake Word, Local STT/TTS, Conversation Mode)
- Wake-word detection runs locally with "Ok Nabu"; microphone icon reflects pipeline state (idle/listening/processing/speaking/error).
- Push-to-talk supported; second wake word "Stop" arms only while roller shutter moves to halt it instantly.
- Two modes: standard Home Assistant agent or Discussion mode routed to an optional LLM engine.
- Audio captured at 16 kHz/16-bit over I2S; TTS played via ES8388 DAC with careful boot sequencing to avoid pops.

- Eight fullscreen game consoles, each a dedicated LVGL page declared skip: true so swipe cannot reach them.
- Shared architecture: YAML containers only, content built in C++, lv_timer created on open/destroyed on close, pre-allocated LVGL pools, NVS persistence, zero HA/network dependency.
- Unique controls per game: tilt (Fil d’Or, Arcanoïde), touch D-pad (Coureur d’Or), portrait orientation flip (Neon Apron), touch (Go Tab, Trial Poursuite, Dames Tab, Roi Noir).

## Dependency Analysis
- Push-only data flow: Home Assistant triggers ESPHome API services; firmware parses payloads and updates LVGL widgets without polling.
- Centralized C++ helpers ensure safe UI updates and consistent color mapping; YAML components include reusable templates for consistency.
- IMU polling adapts to active game to balance responsiveness and power.

```mermaid
graph LR
HA["Home Assistant"] -- "tab5_maj_* services" --> ESP["ESPHome API"]
ESP -- "C++ parsers" --> LVGL["LVGL Widgets"]
LVGL -- "User input" --> Scripts["Scripts/Lambdas"]
Scripts -- "HA services" --> HA
```

- [docs/architecture.md:191-221](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L191-L221)

## Performance Considerations
- Zero-polling: device never requests state; CPU stays near idle until pushes arrive.
- Data packing: large datasets (e.g., 15-day forecast) sent as delimited strings and parsed once in C++.
- LVGL optimization: global styles reduce allocations; pre-allocated widget pools in games avoid heap churn.
- Adaptive IMU polling: increases frequency only when tilt-controlled games are open.
- Traffic pacing: delays between pushes prevent collisions with I2S audio streams during TTS playback.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
- Use the system console to re-push the screen, reload automations, restart HA, or reboot the device safely with confirm overlays.
- For logs and payloads, use esphome logs; the console is not a log viewer.
- If the screen freezes, trigger a screen re-push from the console to reset the push flag and automation.

**Section sources**
- [docs/screens.md:193-204](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/screens.md#L193-L204)

## Conclusion
Tab5 delivers a responsive, offline-resilient smart-home dashboard with rich weather visualization, precise climate and light controls, BLE plant monitoring, a capable voice assistant, a full arcade suite, planning tools, TV remote control, and diagnostics—all driven by a push-only architecture that minimizes network traffic and keeps the device efficient and reliable.

## Introduction
This guide helps you get the M5Stack Tab5 V2 (ESP32-P4) up and running as a Home Assistant HMI with ESPHome and LVGL. You will:
- Prepare your environment and hardware
- Configure user entities and secrets
- Flash firmware via USB or set up OTA updates
- Optionally run demo mode without Home Assistant to verify everything works
- Verify installation and resolve common first-time issues

The project is push-only: the device never polls Home Assistant; it reacts to ESPHome native API calls from automations or scripts.

## Core Components

## Architecture Overview
The system follows a push-only architecture: Home Assistant sends updates to the device via ESPHome native services. The device renders an LVGL-based UI directly on the ESP32-P4’s PSRAM and remains functional offline by keeping last known state.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Dev as "M5Stack Tab5 (ESP32-P4)"
participant ESPH as "ESPHome Core"
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant DEMO as "demo_pusher.py"
Note over Dev,HA : Normal operation
HA->>ESPH : Service call tab5_maj_* / state updates
ESPH->>Dev : Push events to LVGL UI
Dev-->>HA : Optional service calls (e.g., light/climate)
Note over Dev,DEMO : Demo mode (no HA required)
DEMO->>ESPH : Connect via aioesphomeapi
DEMO->>ESPH : Push synthetic scenes (weather, climate, planning, alerts)
ESPH->>Dev : Update UI with demo data
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Hardware Requirements
- Device: M5Stack Tab5 V2 (ESP32-P4 variant)
- Processor details:
  - ESP32-P4: RISC-V dual-core up to 400 MHz, 16 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash, MIPI-DSI display, ST7123 touch controller
  - ESP32-C6 co-processor: Wi-Fi 6 and BLE handled transparently via SDIO
- Display: 5-inch, 1280×720 px, RGB565 over MIPI-DSI
- Audio: ES8388 DAC for speaker output; ES7210 ADC for microphone input over I2S
- Power: USB-C; use at least 5V/2A to avoid brownouts under peak load

Why PSRAM matters: LVGL needs a framebuffer sized to the display resolution; the ESP32-P4’s internal SRAM alone is insufficient. With 16 MB PSRAM, the framebuffer resides in external memory, enabling smooth 60 FPS rendering.

- [docs/hardware.md:7-27](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L7-L27)

### Tools and Prerequisites
- Home Assistant instance (any installation method)
- ESPHome add-on or standalone CLI installed
- ESPHome version ≥ 2026.7.0 (enforced by min_version in the entry point)
- Python 3 for generating the API encryption key and running the demo script

Optional but used by default configuration:
- Weather integration (e.g., Météo-France if in France)
- Google Calendar integration for planning
- Home Assistant Voice pipeline for voice assistant features

### Step-by-Step Installation

1. Clone the repository and locate the entry point
   - Clone the repo and change into the directory
   - The main ESPHome config is at the repository root

2. Create your user entities file
   - Copy the example file to create your local mapping
   - Edit the file to replace placeholder entity IDs with your actual Home Assistant entities
   - These substitutions propagate across all packages; no other YAML files need editing

3. Create your secrets file
   - Create a secrets.yaml at the repository root (already gitignored)
   - Include Wi-Fi SSID/password, OTA password, and a generated api_encryption_key
   - Generate the encryption key using the provided Python one-liner

4. Set up Home Assistant automations (optional for full experience)
   - Copy example files from HomeAssistant_Config into your HA configuration
   - Replace placeholders with your own entity names
   - Enable packages if using package includes

5. First flash (USB)
   - Connect the Tab5 via USB-C
   - Run the ESPHome build and flash command or use the ESPHome Dashboard
   - The initial flash must be done over USB; subsequent updates can be OTA

6. OTA updates
   - After the first flash, the device registers with ESPHome’s OTA server
   - Push future builds wirelessly via CLI or Dashboard

Verification steps:
- Confirm the device appears in ESPHome Dashboard and logs show successful boot
- Ensure Wi-Fi connects and the device reports online status
- If using Home Assistant, confirm automations are sending push updates to the device

### Demo Mode (No Home Assistant Required)
Demo mode lets you see the full dashboard on a flashed device without installing Home Assistant. It uses the same ESPHome native API surface that real automations use.

Steps:
- Flash normally, leaving user_entities.yaml unmodified (copy the example as-is)
- Keep secrets.yaml with your Wi-Fi credentials and a valid api_encryption_key
- Note the device’s IP address once connected to Wi-Fi
- Install the demo dependencies and run the script from your PC on the same network
- Watch the screen cycle through synthetic scenes every ~20 seconds
- Stop the script with Ctrl+C; nothing persists outside the device

Interactive mode:
- By default, the script logs when you tap light/climate/shutter controls to confirm touch path
- Disable interactive logging with --no-interactive

Dry-run:
- Validate payloads without any hardware or dependencies using --dry-run

### Boot Sequence and Initialization
The ESPHome entry point defines a careful boot sequence:
- Delay to allow the I2C GPIO expander to stabilize before display reset
- Resume LVGL and turn on backlight
- Set media player volume, then enable amplifier switch to avoid speaker pop
- Wait for Home Assistant API connection with timeout
- Initialize global pointers for UI components and start background tasks (alarm refresh, central rotator, calendar prefetch)

This ordering ensures stable display and audio initialization and avoids common pitfalls like black screens after software reboots.

## Performance Considerations
- LVGL runs natively on the ESP32-P4 with a large PSRAM framebuffer for smooth 60 FPS rendering
- Data packing reduces network overhead by serializing complex payloads (e.g., forecasts) into delimited strings parsed on-device
- Push-only design keeps CPU usage near zero when nothing changes
- Backlight brightness is software-controlled and can be dimmed to reduce power draw
- Use a 5V/2A charger to prevent brownout resets during peak consumption

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common first-time setup issues and fixes:

- Black screen after software reboot
  - Cause: Display reset pin wired through an I2C GPIO expander needs settle time
  - Fix: A blocking delay was added before display reset in the boot sequence; do not remove it without re-testing

- Missing weather/planning/climate data while device is online
  - Cause: Push automations gated behind a shared boolean helper stuck off; guard automation disabled
  - Fix: Turn helper on, re-enable guard automation, trigger push once

- Touch seems dead but touchscreen detects presses
  - Cause: Home Assistant rejecting service calls due to integration options
  - Fix: Enable “Allow service calls” in the ESPHome integration options

- ESPHome API connections exhausted
  - Cause: Leftover esphome CLI processes holding connections
  - Fix: Close CLI sessions; kill orphaned processes

- Device reboots periodically when Home Assistant is unreachable
  - Cause: API reboot timeout too short; device reboots when no API client connected for that duration
  - Fix: Increase reboot timeout to avoid cycles during HA maintenance windows

- Black screen + device off network after OTA
  - Cause: Wi-Fi co-processor link failed to come up after software reboot; hot retry loop starves firmware
  - Fix: Full power cycle (power off and unplug USB-C for ~15 seconds); soft reboot is insufficient

- STT/TTS broken with duplicate entity warnings
  - Cause: Mirroring another Home Assistant instance caused ID collisions
  - Fix: Disable mirroring integration and restart Home Assistant

Verification checklist:
- Device appears in ESPHome Dashboard and shows online status
- Logs indicate successful boot and API connection
- If using Home Assistant, confirm automations send push updates and UI reflects changes
- For demo mode, ensure the script connects and cycles scenes without errors

**Section sources**

## Conclusion
You now have the essentials to install, configure, and verify the Tab5 HMI. Start with a clean clone, copy and edit user_entities.yaml, create secrets.yaml, and flash via USB. Use demo mode to validate functionality without Home Assistant, then integrate automations for a complete experience. Refer to troubleshooting if you encounter common first-time issues, and rely on the push-only architecture to keep performance high and resource usage low.

## Introduction
This document specifies the hardware requirements for the Tab5 project on the M5Stack Tab5 V2 platform. It covers the ESP32-P4 processor capabilities, PSRAM and display interface (MIPI-DSI), touch controller, audio hardware (ES8388 DAC + amplifier), I2S microphone path (ES7210 ADC), GPIO mappings, power and USB-C requirements, Wi-Fi antenna selection, thermal considerations, BLE plant sensor compatibility via Home Assistant, and troubleshooting guidance for common hardware-related issues such as display initialization failures, touch calibration problems, and audio conflicts.

## Project Structure
The Tab5 firmware is organized into configuration files that define hardware peripherals, sensors, UI, and integrations:
- Low-level hardware configuration (display, touch, I2C/I2S, audio, PSRAM, Wi-Fi co-processor): tab5-hardware.yaml
- IMU configuration and game tilt input: tab5-imu.yaml
- System diagnostics and network entities (Wi-Fi, antenna select, power switches, core temperature): tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml
- Architecture overview and integration points: architecture.md
- Hardware reference and pinouts: docs/hardware.md
- Known incidents and fixes: docs/troubleshooting.md

## Core Components
- Main processor: ESP32-P4 (RISC-V dual-core up to 400 MHz; internal SRAM 768 KB; Flash 16 MB; MIPI-DSI LCD peripheral).
- External memory: 16 MB PSRAM (OCT-SPI) required for LVGL framebuffer at 1280×720 RGB565 (~1.8 MB).
- Co-processor: ESP32-C6 handling Wi-Fi 6 and BLE 5 over SDIO (20 MHz).
- Display: 5-inch panel, 1280×720 px, MIPI-DSI 16-bit RGB565.
- Touch: Capacitive multi-touch via ST7123 over I2C with interrupt-driven polling.
- Audio output: ES8388 DAC via I2S with software-controlled amplifier enable.
- Audio input: ES7210 ADC streaming over I2S (16 kHz, 16-bit mono).
- Power: USB-C powered; peak consumption can exceed 1.5 A at 5 V; use a charger rated at least 5 V / 2 A.
- Backlight: PWM via LEDC on GPIO22; dimmable from Home Assistant; auto-on on touch release.

**Section sources**
- [hardware.md:11-27](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L11-L27)
- [hardware.md:30-41](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L30-L41)
- [hardware.md:43-92](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L43-L92)

- [tab5-hardware.yaml:116-167](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L116-L167)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:170-221](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L170-L221)

## Architecture Overview
The system centers on the ESP32-P4 driving a high-resolution MIPI-DSI display and managing I2C/I2S peripherals. The ESP32-C6 co-processor provides Wi-Fi and BLE connectivity transparently to ESPHome components. A PI4IOE5V6408 GPIO expander controls critical reset and enable lines (display reset, touch reset, amplifier enable, antenna switch). PSRAM is essential for smooth LVGL rendering at 60 FPS without tearing.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Boot as "Boot Sequence"
participant P4 as "ESP32-P4"
participant EXP as "GPIO Expander"
participant DISP as "Display (MIPI-DSI)"
participant AUDIO as "Audio (ES8388)"
participant CO as "ESP32-C6 (Wi-Fi/BLE)"
Boot->>P4 : Initialize peripherals
P4->>EXP : Stabilize expander outputs
P4->>DISP : Assert reset after delay
P4->>AUDIO : Configure I2S clocks
P4->>CO : Establish SDIO link (20 MHz)
Note over P4,CO : Wi-Fi/BLE available to ESPHome components
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### ESP32-P4 and Memory
- Dual-core RISC-V up to 400 MHz; internal SRAM 768 KB; Flash 16 MB.
- PSRAM configured in hex mode at 200 MHz; required to hold LVGL framebuffer at 1280×720 RGB565 (~1.8 MB) and avoid internal SRAM pressure.

**Section sources**
- [hardware.md:11-22](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L11-L22)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:84-87](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L84-L87)

### Display (MIPI-DSI)
- Resolution: 1280×720 px; pixel mode 16-bit RGB565; color order RGB.
- Reset pin routed through PI4IOE5V6408 expander; requires a blocking delay before toggling to ensure reliable reset post-boot.
- Update interval set to never (LVGL drives updates).

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:116-128](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L116-L128)
- [troubleshooting.md:13-19](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L13-L19)

### Touch Input (ST7123)
- I2C-based capacitive multi-touch with interrupt pin on GPIO23.
- Calibration ranges mapped to display dimensions (x: 0–720, y: 0–1280).
- On screen release, backlight turns on if off.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:130-149](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L130-L149)
- [hardware.md:30-41](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L30-L41)

### I2C Bus
- Dedicated bus (bsp_bus) on GPIO31 (SDA) and GPIO32 (SCL) at 400 kHz.
- Used by display reset/touch reset via expander and IMU (BMI270) at address 0x68.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:100-104](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L100-L104)
- [tab5-imu.yaml:17-30](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L17-L30)

### Audio Output (ES8388 DAC)
- I2S output via GPIO26 (DOUT/BCLK shared), GPIO29 (LRCLK shared).
- Amplifier enable controlled via GPIO expander; must be enabled only after I2S clock is stable to avoid pop noise.
- Media player uses stereo I2S speaker with external DAC type; buffer duration tuned to reduce stuttering during TTS streaming.

**Section sources**
- [hardware.md:43-68](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L43-L68)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:199-221](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L199-L221)

### Audio Input (ES7210 ADC)
- I2S input via GPIO28 (DIN), GPIO27 (BCLK), GPIO29 (LRCLK), GPIO30 (MCLK).
- Configured at 16 kHz, 16-bit mono; DC offset correction enabled.
- Mic gain set in analog domain to improve SNR before digital processing.

**Section sources**
- [hardware.md:72-83](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L72-L83)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:170-198](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L170-L198)

### GPIO Mapping Summary
- Display reset: PI4IOE5V6408 channel 1, number 4
- Touch reset: PI4IOE5V6408 channel 1, number 5
- Touch interrupt: GPIO23
- Backlight PWM: GPIO22
- I2C SDA/SCL: GPIO31/GPIO32
- I2S BCLK/LRCLK/DOUT/MCLK/DIN: GPIO26/29/26/30/28
- Wi-Fi power and antenna select: PI4IOE5V6408 channels 1/2

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:106-167](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L106-L167)
- [tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml:32-84](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml#L32-L84)

### IMU (BMI270) for Tilt Detection
- I2C device at address 0x68 on bsp_bus; accelerometer range 4G, ODR 100 Hz; gyroscope range 2000 DPS, ODR 200 Hz.
- Acceleration axes published internally to drive games and tap-to-wake logic; pitch/roll/temp throttled for HA diagnostics.
- Adaptive poll rate: 33 ms when active games are open, 100 ms otherwise.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-imu.yaml:17-30](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L17-L30)
- [tab5-imu.yaml:32-144](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-imu.yaml#L32-L144)

### Power and USB-C Connectivity
- USB-C powered; peak current can exceed 1.5 A at 5 V under load (Wi-Fi active, full backlight, audio playing).
- Use a charger rated at least 5 V / 2 A to avoid brownout resets.
- Backlight brightness controlled via PWM; no ambient light sensor present.

**Section sources**
- [hardware.md:87-92](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L87-L92)

### Wi-Fi Antenna Placement and Selection
- Antenna selectable between internal and external via GPIO expander switch.
- Diagnostics expose RSSI, IP/SSID, and status indicators; antenna selection controlled through a template select entity.

**Section sources**
- [tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml:16-84](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml#L16-L84)
- [tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml:199-229](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml#L199-L229)

### Thermal Management Considerations
- Internal core temperature exposed as a diagnostic sensor for monitoring.
- No active cooling; manage performance by adjusting backlight brightness and workload (e.g., reducing push frequency during heavy audio playback).

**Section sources**
- [tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml:169-184](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-sensors-diagnostics.yaml#L169-L184)

### Compatibility with External Components
- BLE plant sensors: Up to five BLE plant monitors integrated via Home Assistant entities pushed to the Tab5; these are managed in the domotique sensors package and displayed on the UI.
- Home Assistant network connectivity: ESPHome API services receive payloads from HA to update UI elements; robust error handling and state checks prevent crashes during HA restarts.

**Section sources**
- [architecture.md:66-77](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L66-L77)
- [architecture.md:77-100](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#L77-L100)

## Dependency Analysis
Key dependencies and interactions:
- ESP32-P4 depends on PSRAM for LVGL framebuffer stability at high resolution.
- Display and touch rely on the PI4IOE5V6408 expander for reset sequencing; incorrect timing causes black screens.
- Audio subsystem shares I2S pins; proper ordering prevents pops and ensures stable streams.
- Wi-Fi/BLE provided by ESP32-C6 over SDIO; failures require full power cycle to re-establish link.

```mermaid
graph LR
P4["ESP32-P4"] --> PSRAM["PSRAM"]
P4 --> DISP["MIPI-DSI Display"]
P4 --> TOUCH["ST7123 Touch"]
P4 --> I2C["I2C Bus"]
P4 --> I2S["I2S Bus"]
I2C --> EXP["GPIO Expander"]
EXP --> AMP["Amplifier Enable"]
I2S --> DAC["ES8388 DAC"]
I2S --> MIC["ES7210 ADC"]
P4 ---|SDIO| C6["ESP32-C6"]
```

**Diagram sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:9-35](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L9-L35)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:100-221](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L100-L221)

**Section sources**
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:9-35](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L9-L35)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:100-221](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L100-L221)

## Performance Considerations
- PSRAM speed and capacity are critical for LVGL performance at 1280×720 RGB565; ensure PSRAM is enabled and running at configured speed.
- I2S buffer tuning reduces TTS stuttering; keep buffer_duration at recommended values to balance latency and continuity.
- IMU poll rate adapts to active games to maintain responsiveness while conserving resources at idle.
- Avoid excessive logging verbosity unless needed; confirmed root cause for boot delays relies on a blocking delay rather than log levels.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide

### Display Initialization Failures (Black Screen After Software Reboot)
- Symptom: Black screen after OTA or software reboot; Wi-Fi/API may still function.
- Root cause: Display reset pin routed through I2C GPIO expander needs settle time; toggling too early has no effect.
- Fix: Maintain the blocking delay before display reset sequence; do not remove without re-testing across multiple reboots.

**Section sources**
- [troubleshooting.md:13-19](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L13-L19)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:116-136](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L116-L136)

### Touch Not Responding
- Symptom: Touch appears dead but controller detects presses.
- Root cause: Home Assistant rejecting service calls due to disabled option.
- Fix: Enable “Allow service calls” in the ESPHome integration options for the device.

**Section sources**
- [troubleshooting.md:43-49](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L43-L49)

### Audio Conflicts and Pop Noise
- Symptom: Loud pop on boot or stuttering TTS.
- Root cause: Amplifier enabled before I2S clock stable; insufficient I2S buffer causing gaps.
- Fix: Ensure boot sequence sets backlight and volume before enabling amplifier; keep buffer_duration at recommended value.

**Section sources**
- [hardware.md:43-68](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L43-L68)
- [tab5-hardware.yaml:199-221](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/Tab5/tab5-hardware.yaml#L199-L221)

### Wi-Fi Co-Processor Link Failure After OTA
- Symptom: Black screen and no API after OTA; device appears online but unreachable.
- Root cause: ESP32-C6 SDIO link did not come up after software reboot; hot retry loop starves firmware.
- Fix: Perform a full power cycle (power off and unplug USB-C for ~15 s); soft reboot is insufficient.

**Section sources**
- [troubleshooting.md:93-109](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#L93-L109)

### Brownout Resets Under Load
- Symptom: Unexpected reboots under high load (Wi-Fi active, full backlight, audio).
- Root cause: Insufficient power supply current capability.
- Fix: Use a USB-C charger rated at least 5 V / 2 A; consider lowering backlight brightness.

**Section sources**
- [hardware.md:87-92](https://github.com/Axellum/M5-Tab5-ESPHome-LVGL/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#L87-L92)

## Conclusion
The Tab5 V2 leverages the ESP32-P4’s MIPI-DSI display engine and substantial PSRAM to deliver a responsive 1280×720 LVGL UI, complemented by an ESP32-C6 co-processor for Wi-Fi/BLE. Correct GPIO sequencing through the PI4IOE5V6408 expander is essential for reliable display and audio operation. Adequate power delivery and careful I2S buffering ensure stable audio playback. The BMI270 IMU enables tilt-based game controls with adaptive polling. For external integrations, BLE plant sensors and Home Assistant connectivity are supported via entity pushes and API services. Following the documented troubleshooting steps resolves the most common hardware-related issues encountered in production.

9. Conclusion

## Introduction
This project is a Home Assistant smart-home dashboard running natively on an M5Stack Tab5 V2 (ESP32-P4), built with ESPHome and LVGL 8.4. It implements a push-only, zero-polling interface: the device never requests state from Home Assistant; instead, automations on the HA side detect changes and push updates directly to the screen via ESPHome API services. The UI is compiled into C++ and rendered locally at 60 FPS using LVGL, without a web stack or browser. Data payloads are packed into delimited strings and parsed on-device for efficient, atomic updates. The device remains fully usable offline (clock, arcade games, diagnostics console) and only reconnects when Home Assistant becomes available again.

The project also includes a voice assistant pipeline that runs wake-word detection locally on the ESP32-P4, streams audio only after wake-word detection, and plays back responses through the built-in DAC and speaker. An optional companion engine can route short home commands deterministically and open conversation to a lightweight LLM path. Finally, the project ships eight experimental arcade game consoles that run entirely offline with NVS persistence and zero network dependency.

This documentation introduces both beginners and experienced developers to the design principles, data flows, and capabilities of the Tab5 HMI, using terminology consistent with the codebase such as push-only, LVGL components, ESPHome packages, and NVS persistence.

## Project Structure
At the root, the entry point `tab5-ha-hmi.yaml` loads user substitutions, defines the boot sequence, and imports modular ESPHome packages. Each package has a clear responsibility: hardware, sensors, styles, globals, scripts, LVGL layout, IMU, and HA controls. The LVGL layout lives in `Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml`, which declares the single-page dashboard (`page_main`) and includes reusable UI components under `ui_components/`. Game modules are included as separate C++ files and exposed as dedicated LVGL pages marked `skip: true` so swipe navigation cannot reach them.

```mermaid
graph TB
Entry["Entry Point<br/>tab5-ha-hmi.yaml"]
PkgUI["Packages<br/>hardware, sensors, styles, globals,<br/>scripts, lvgl, imu, ha-controls"]
LVGL["LVGL Layout<br/>Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml"]
Components["Reusable Components<br/>ui_components/*.yaml"]
Games["Game Pages<br/>page_arcade + per-console pages"]
Cpp["C++ Logic<br/>tab5_custom.h/.cpp + game modules"]
Entry --> PkgUI
PkgUI --> LVGL
LVGL --> Components
LVGL --> Games
PkgUI --> Cpp
```

## Core Components
- Push-only architecture: Home Assistant detects state changes and calls ESPHome API services (`tab5_maj_*`). The firmware parses payloads and updates LVGL widgets atomically.
- Modular YAML architecture: The configuration is split across multiple packages by concern, each independently readable and maintainable.
- Native LVGL rendering: The UI is built in C++ and rendered at 60 FPS in PSRAM, using vector fonts and global style definitions to minimize allocations.
- Data packing strategies: Multi-value datasets (e.g., 15-day forecast, hourly weather, alerts) are serialized as delimited strings on the HA side and parsed in C++ in one pass.
- Offline resilience: All lambdas guard against missing connections and uninitialized UI; last known state persists on screen, and the device stays usable without Home Assistant.
- Voice assistant: Local wake-word detection, streaming audio only after wake-word, real-time pipeline state feedback, and optional conversation routing via a companion engine.
- Arcade games: Eight fullscreen LVGL pages with preallocated widget pools, NVS persistence, and zero HA/network dependency.

Practical examples:
- Weather monitoring: A single bulk push delivers 15 days of daily forecasts and hourly slots; the device parses and renders icons, temperatures, and rainfall bars instantly.
- Voice commands: Wake word triggers local capture; Home Assistant performs STT, intent processing, and TTS; the Tab5 displays transcription and Markdown replies while playing audio.
- Plant moisture: Up to five BLE plant sensors are pushed and sorted dynamically; long press opens detail cards showing moisture, watering status, fertility, light, temperature, and battery.

## Architecture Overview
The system follows a unidirectional data flow: Home Assistant pushes updates to the Tab5 via ESPHome API services. The device’s LVGL layer updates widgets based on parsed payloads. The voice assistant pipeline captures audio locally, streams it only after wake-word detection, and plays back TTS through the ES8388 DAC.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant HA as "Home Assistant"
participant ESP as "ESPHome Services<br/>tab5_maj_*"
participant CPP as "C++ Parser<br/>tab5_custom.cpp"
participant LV as "LVGL UI<br/>Tab5/tab5-lvgl.yaml"
HA->>ESP : "Push payload (delimited string)"
ESP->>CPP : "Call parser function"
CPP-->>LV : "Update widgets atomically"
Note over LV : "Rendered at 60 FPS in PSRAM"
```

## Detailed Component Analysis

### Push-Only Data Flow
The device never polls Home Assistant. Automations detect changes and call ESPHome API services with payloads. The firmware parses these payloads and updates LVGL widgets in one pass, avoiding repeated redraws and minimizing CPU usage.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Change["State Change in HA"] --> Automation["Automation Triggered"]
Automation --> Service["esphome.tab5_maj_* Service Call"]
Service --> Parse["C++ Parser (strtok_r)"]
Parse --> Update["LVGL Widgets Updated"]
Update --> Render["60 FPS Rendering in PSRAM"]
```

### Data Packing Strategy
Multi-value datasets are serialized as delimited strings on the HA side and parsed in C++ in a single pass. For example, a 15-day forecast is sent as one string with semicolon-separated fields, reducing network calls and socket pressure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Build["HA Builds Delimited String"] --> Send["Single API Service Call"]
Send --> Receive["Device Receives Payload"]
Receive --> Tokenize["C++ Tokenizer (strtok_r)"]
Tokenize --> Apply["Apply to LVGL Widgets"]
```

### LVGL Components and Layout
The dashboard is a single LVGL page (`page_main`) with functional areas: clock/date, weather forecast, central rotating card, climate/light controls, plants, TV remote, assistant popup, calendar popup, and console overlay. Navigation uses touch gestures and swipe on the lower band for weather pagination. Reusable components under `ui_components/` include popups, cards, and templates.

```mermaid

+info_panel
}
```

### Voice Assistant Pipeline
The Tab5 acts as a local voice satellite. Wake-word detection runs on-device, streaming audio only after detection. The pipeline includes STT, intent processing, and TTS, with visual feedback via microphone icon colors. Optional conversation routing supports deterministic home commands and open chat.

### Arcade Games (Experimental)
Eight fullscreen LVGL pages implement games with preallocated widget pools, NVS persistence, and zero HA/network dependency. Each game has a uniform API (`open()`, `close()`, `is_open()`, `on_imu(...)`) and runs independently of the dashboard. One exception rotates the screen to portrait for pinball gameplay.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
Open["Open Game Page"] --> Init["Create lv_timer & Preallocate Widgets"]
Init --> Loop["Game Loop (lv_timer)"]
Loop --> Input["Touch/IMU Input"]
Input --> State["Update Game State"]
State --> Render["Render LVGL Objects"]
Render --> Close["Close Game"]
Close --> Cleanup["Destroy lv_timer & Free Resources"]
```

## Dependency Analysis
The project’s dependencies are structured around modular ESPHome packages and C++ modules. The entry point includes all necessary headers and source files, while LVGL components are declared in YAML and implemented in C++. Games are isolated sub-modules with no shared state with the dashboard.

## Performance Considerations
- Push-only reduces CPU and network usage when nothing changes.
- Data packing minimizes network calls and socket pressure.
- LVGL rendering uses global styles and preallocated widget pools to avoid heap churn.
- Adaptive IMU polling switches between 10 Hz at rest and 30 Hz during tilt-controlled gameplay.
- Traffic pacing delays prevent collisions between large payload pushes and active I2S audio streams.

[No sources needed since this section provides general guidance]

## Troubleshooting Guide
Common issues and mitigations:
- API connections exhausted: Use data packing to reduce service calls and monitor socket usage.
- Stale state: Ensure HA-side automations fire correctly; the device does not pull state.
- Boot audio pop: Amplifier enable occurs after media player volume set and I2S clock stability.
- Wake word disabled: Toggle via UI switch; ensure micro_wake_word is started in boot sequence.

## Conclusion
The Tab5 project demonstrates a robust, efficient, and resilient approach to embedded IoT dashboards. By combining push-only architecture, modular YAML, native LVGL rendering, data packing, and offline resilience, it delivers a responsive and feature-rich Home Assistant interface on the M5Stack Tab5 V2. The inclusion of a voice assistant and experimental arcade games showcases the potential of AI-generated code and embedded development on powerful microcontrollers like the ESP32-P4. Whether you are exploring smart home automation or experimenting with embedded AI, this project provides a solid foundation and practical examples for building advanced, localized interfaces.
